policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic framework, tool-calling format, and system prompt can shift pass rates substantially, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable unless the same harness is used. The task sets in each domain are relatively small, so point estimates carry high variance and small benchmark sets increase contamination risk as models improve.
policy_note.measures: τ2-bench evaluates LLM agents on realistic multi-turn, tool-using tasks across simulated environments (e.g., retail and airline domains), requiring agents to complete end-to-end customer-service workflows by calling tools and responding to a simulated user across multiple dialogue turns. It extends the τ-bench lineage by introducing two-sided evaluation where both the agent-side and user-side interactions are assessed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher pass rate is better. Scores represent the fraction of full task trajectories successfully completed end-to-end; partial credit is not awarded. Frontier models as of early 2025 typically score in the 30–60% range depending on domain and scaffold, leaving meaningful headroom for differentiation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating LLM agents on realistic agentic task completion, particularly those building or comparing tool-use and multi-turn dialogue systems.

policy_note.caveat: Benchmark is unrecognized from available metadata — no variant strings were observed in model cards and no canonical paper or dataset could be confirmed. Policy note fields reflect this uncertainty.
policy_note.measures: ABC-Bench is not a benchmark I can identify with confidence from the slug and name alone; no canonical dataset size, task format, or capability domain can be reliably attributed without risking fabrication.
policy_note.how_to_read: Unknown — scoring direction and scale cannot be confirmed without a verified source.
policy_note.intended_for: Unknown — insufficient metadata to determine intended audience or primary use case.

policy_note.measures: ABLE (Assessing Broad Language Evaluation) probes general natural-language understanding across multiple task types; specific dataset size and task format details are not well-documented in public literature for this benchmark.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better performance; frontier range and scale context are not well-established for this benchmark due to limited public reporting.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating general language understanding capabilities of language models.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic framework, system prompt, and tool-call implementation all significantly affect both utility (task completion) and attack success rate, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. The benchmark's fixed attack suite may underestimate vulnerability to novel injection strategies not in the dataset.
policy_note.measures: AgentDojo evaluates AI agents' robustness against indirect prompt injection attacks across realistic task environments (email, calendar, banking, travel). Agents must complete legitimate user-assigned tasks while resisting adversarial instructions embedded in environmental content such as emails or web pages.
policy_note.how_to_read: Reported on two axes: utility rate (task completion, higher is better) and injection attack success rate (ASR, lower is better). A robust agent maximizes utility while minimizing ASR; frontier models often show a tension between the two. There is no single composite leaderboard score — interpret both axes together.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, red-teamers, and developers of agentic systems who need to measure resistance to indirect prompt injection before deployment.

policy_note.caveat: The 'no attack' variant captures only baseline compliance; scores can shift substantially under adversarial prompting (the 'attack' variant), so the two should not be conflated. Safety-tuned frontier models tend to cluster near 0% compliance on the no-attack split, compressing differentiation at the top of the leaderboard.
policy_note.measures: AgentHarm evaluates whether LLM-based agents will comply with explicitly harmful task requests (e.g., cybercrime, fraud, harassment, disinformation) in agentic settings without adversarial prompting. The 'no attack' variant measures baseline refusal behavior when harmful instructions are presented directly, without jailbreak augmentation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rates are better — a score of 0% means the agent refused all harmful tasks. Frontier safety-tuned models typically score below 10% on the no-attack split; less safety-trained or uncensored models can score substantially higher.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and developers assessing the harm-refusal behavior of agentic LLM systems before deployment.

policy_note.caveat: Methodology, dataset, and scoring rubric are not publicly released, making independent reproduction impossible. The observed variant strings 'without mitigations' and 'without safeguards' indicate scores are reported under conditions where safety interventions are disabled, so numbers are not directly comparable to production-deployed model performance. Cross-lab comparisons are not possible.
policy_note.measures: An Anthropic-internal benchmark evaluating model performance on multi-step, agentic coding tasks — scenarios where the model must autonomously write, execute, and iterate on code to complete software engineering goals. Dataset size and exact task composition are not publicly disclosed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as a percentage pass rate or similar scalar. Scores should be read only against other results from the same Anthropic system card, under matched mitigation conditions, as the benchmark is not externally reproducible.
policy_note.intended_for: AI developers and policy researchers reviewing Anthropic system cards for Claude Opus 4.x models; useful for understanding capability trajectories within Anthropic's model family but not for broad cross-vendor benchmarking.

policy_note.caveat: This metric is typically reported as an internal, lab-defined evaluation rather than a standardized public benchmark, so the specific harm taxonomy, scenario distribution, and refusal threshold vary by lab and may not be directly comparable across reports. A high refusal rate alone does not distinguish between appropriate safety refusals and over-refusal on benign tasks; results should be read alongside helpfulness or task-completion metrics.
policy_note.measures: Measures the proportion of harmful or policy-violating agentic task requests that a model correctly declines to execute, such as requests involving unauthorized actions, destructive tool use, or real-world harm. Higher scores indicate the model more reliably refuses to carry out dangerous multi-step agentic actions.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better — a higher refusal rate indicates the model more reliably refuses harmful agentic tasks. Because this is typically an internal evaluation, there is no universal scale; individual lab reports should specify the scenario set size and harm categories covered.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating an agent model's ability to abstain from harmful real-world actions in tool-use or multi-step settings.

policy_note.caveat: Because the source material consists of real published exams, training-data contamination is a significant concern — portions of these tests circulate widely online and may appear in pretraining corpora. Frontier models have approached saturation on several subtasks (e.g., SAT English), reducing differentiation at the top of the leaderboard. The benchmark spans both English and Chinese subtasks, so aggregate scores conflate multilingual capability with domain knowledge.
policy_note.measures: AGIEval assesses foundation models on human-centric standardized exams and cognitive tests, including SAT, LSAT, GRE, GMAT, AMC math competitions, and the Chinese Gaokao, totaling roughly 8,000 questions. It probes reasoning, reading comprehension, and quantitative ability through multiple-choice and short free-response formats drawn from real-world high-stakes tests.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models (GPT-4 class) typically score in the 60–75% range on the aggregate English split, with weaker performance on math-heavy subtasks like AMC and stronger performance on verbal subtasks.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating general reasoning and academic problem-solving ability, particularly for comparing models across multilingual and multi-domain standardized-test settings.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models now score high enough on several subtasks that differentiation at the top is limited. The benchmark conflates fairly heterogeneous sub-tasks (SAT math, LSAT logic games, GRE verbal) under a single aggregate score, which can obscure where a model actually excels or struggles. Contamination risk is non-trivial given that these exams are widely reproduced online.
policy_note.measures: AGIEval English evaluates language models on English-language human-centric standardized exams, including SAT, LSAT, GRE, GMAT, and AQA tasks, covering reading comprehension, logical reasoning, and math. Tasks are presented as multiple-choice or short-answer problems drawn directly from real test corpora, typically evaluated under 3–5 shot prompting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models typically score in the 60–80% range on the aggregate English subset, with wide variance across subtasks. Compare only within the same shot setting (3-shot vs 5-shot can shift scores meaningfully).
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing general reasoning and academic problem-solving ability across LLMs, particularly in English-language professional and academic test formats.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a concern — frontier vision-language models routinely score above 80%, compressing the differentiating range. As a widely circulated 2016 dataset, training-data contamination is plausible for models trained on large web crawls that include educational content.
policy_note.measures: AI2D tests visual understanding of science diagrams: given an elementary-school science diagram (food chains, earth layers, life cycles, etc.), the model answers a multiple-choice question about it. The dataset contains roughly 5,000 diagrams and ~15,000 questions sourced from grade-school textbooks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent correct on multiple-choice questions. Frontier VLMs currently cluster in the 80–90 % range, with strong models approaching 85–90 %. Random baseline for 4-choice questions is ~25 %.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multimodal (vision-language) models on diagram comprehension and visual scientific reasoning.

policy_note.caveat: Strong scaffold dependence: scores vary substantially by edit format (diff, diff-fenced, whole, udiff), so comparisons across models using different formats are not apples-to-apples. The observed variant strings (diff, diff-fenced, whole, extended thinking, extended reasoning) confirm this — models prompted with extended thinking or reasoning modes can score markedly higher, inflating comparisons against base-mode results. Results should only be compared within the same edit format.
policy_note.measures: Aider Polyglot tests a model's ability to edit existing code files across multiple programming languages, scoring the percentage of problems where the model produces a correct, applicable code change. Problems are drawn from real open-source repositories and require the model to output diffs or whole-file edits that pass tests.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent of problems solved. Frontier models (as of early 2025) range roughly from 40% to 70%+ depending on edit format. Always check which edit format was used before comparing two models.
policy_note.intended_for: AI developers and researchers evaluating model suitability for agentic code-editing tasks, particularly those building or benchmarking tools like AI pair programmers.

policy_note.caveat: Heavy saturation at the frontier: top models with extended thinking now approach or exceed 90% on recent years, compressing headroom for differentiation. Contamination is a serious concern because AIME problems from prior years (pre-2024) are widely published online and likely present in training corpora. Scores are highly sensitive to the sampling protocol — best-of-32, majority-vote, 5-trial average, and single pass@1 can differ by 20–40 percentage points on the same model, making cross-report comparisons unreliable without knowing the exact variant. The unversioned 'aime' slug conflates multiple competition years that vary in difficulty; prefer aime_2024 or aime_2025 for reproducible comparisons.
policy_note.measures: AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) measures olympiad-level mathematical problem-solving across 15 integer-answer problems per year, drawn from the official AMC competition series. It probes multi-step algebraic, combinatorial, geometric, and number-theoretic reasoning with no multiple-choice scaffold.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; score is reported as percentage of problems correct (0–100%) or raw count out of 15. Frontier models with extended thinking score roughly 70–92% on recent years (pass@1 with chain-of-thought); standard inference without extended reasoning sits closer to 20–60%. Always check which year, which sampling protocol, and whether tools were permitted before comparing numbers.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and competition-math practitioners evaluating frontier model reasoning depth; useful as a ceiling probe when easier math benchmarks are saturated.

policy_note.caveat: Extremely small dataset (15–30 problems) produces high score variance—a single problem is worth ~3–7 percentage points, making fine-grained model comparisons unreliable. Rapid saturation: frontier reasoning models (o3, Claude 3.7 extended thinking) now approach or exceed 90% pass@1, compressing the differentiating range. Maj@64 scores are substantially higher than 0-shot CoT and should not be compared directly; results must be reported with the sampling strategy. Contamination risk is elevated because AIME problems circulate widely on math forums (e.g., AoPS) before training cutoffs.
policy_note.measures: Mathematical problem-solving ability on the American Invitational Mathematics Examination 2024, consisting of 15 competition-level problems per sitting (AIME I and II, 30 problems total). Each answer is an integer from 0–999; problems span algebra, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory at olympiad-preparation difficulty.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as percentage of problems solved correctly (0–100%). 0-shot CoT scores for strong non-reasoning models cluster around 20–50%; dedicated reasoning models reach 70–90%+. Maj@64 scores run 15–30 points above single-sample CoT for the same model, so always check the sampling method before comparing.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and labs benchmarking advanced mathematical reasoning; useful for differentiating mid-tier models but increasingly uninformative at the frontier.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a growing concern — top frontier models approach or reach 15/15, compressing discrimination at the high end. The 2025 edition reduces training-data contamination risk compared to earlier AIME years (which are widely reproduced online), but post-cutoff fine-tuning pipelines may still have ingested these problems. Scores are scaffold-dependent: tool-use (code interpreter, symbolic math) materially improves results, so comparisons across setups with different tool access are not apples-to-apples.
policy_note.measures: Tests olympiad-level mathematical reasoning via the 15-question American Invitational Mathematics Examination 2025 problem set. Each question requires a free-response integer answer (0–999), spanning algebra, geometry, combinatorics, and number theory with no multiple-choice scaffolding.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; maximum score is 15. As of 2025, leading frontier models score in the 10–15 range, with some reaching perfect scores under tool-assisted conditions. Scores below 8 indicate meaningful gaps relative to frontier capability.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning in LLMs, particularly for distinguishing capability among frontier models where standard math benchmarks have saturated.

policy_note.caveat: LLM judges exhibit a strong verbosity bias — longer responses are systematically preferred — which AlpacaEval 2.0 partially addresses with LC win rate, but the correction is approximate. The 805-instruction set is small and publicly known, creating contamination risk for models trained after its release. Raw win rate and LC win rate are not interchangeable; cards reporting one variant should not be compared against the other. Scores are incomparable with AlpacaEval 1.0, which used text-davinci-003 as the reference model.
policy_note.measures: AlpacaEval 2.0 measures instruction-following quality via an LLM-as-judge setup: a GPT-4 annotator compares each evaluated model's output against a GPT-4 Turbo reference on 805 diverse open-ended instructions, reporting a length-controlled (LC) win rate as the primary metric.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher LC win rate is better, representing the percentage of outputs preferred over the GPT-4 Turbo reference after controlling for length. Frontier models typically score in the 50–65% LC win rate range; scores below ~30% indicate weak instruction following relative to the reference.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing chat and instruction-following LLMs; commonly used as a fast, cheap alternative to human preference evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: Contamination is a serious concern: AMC problems span decades and are extensively reproduced in textbooks, online forums, and competition-prep sites, making training-data leakage likely for any model trained on broad web data. The benchmark is also small (30 questions per exam year), so accuracy estimates have high variance and minor prompt differences can swing reported scores several percentage points. Frontier models have reached high accuracy, limiting differentiation at the top.
policy_note.measures: AMC measures mathematical problem-solving ability using problems from the American Mathematics Competitions (AMC 10/AMC 12), multiple-choice competitions for high-school-level pre-calculus mathematics. The 5-shot CoT variant prompts models with five worked examples before asking them to solve competition problems, probing multi-step algebraic and combinatorial reasoning.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as percentage of problems answered correctly (0–100%). Frontier models generally score in the 60–95% range on AMC 10/12 depending on year and prompting strategy; human AMC qualification cutoffs (~60–75% correct) provide a useful reference point.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating mathematical reasoning depth, particularly competition-level multi-step problem solving beyond standard grade-school arithmetic.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to the action-space definition and agent scaffold used (e.g., whether the agent receives raw pixel screenshots vs. accessibility tree representations), making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. The benchmark targets action-level accuracy on pre-recorded trajectories, so it does not measure end-to-end task success in a live environment.
policy_note.measures: AndroidControl evaluates an AI agent's ability to complete natural-language tasks on Android devices by predicting the correct UI action (tap, swipe, text input, etc.) at each step given a screenshot and task instruction. The dataset contains human-collected demonstrations across a wide range of Android apps, testing both low-level action prediction (exact action type and target) and high-level action selection (choosing among candidate actions).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as action accuracy (fraction of steps where the predicted action matches the ground truth). Frontier model performance on low-level accuracy has reached the mid-to-high 70s (%), while high-level selection tasks tend to score higher due to a smaller candidate pool.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners building or comparing GUI agents and mobile automation systems.

name: Anthropic AI R&D Suite 1 LLM Training
Anthropic AI R&D Suite 1 Novel Compiler
Anthropic AI R&D Suite 1 Quadruped RL
Anthropic AI R&D Suite 1 Text RL
Anthropic AI R&D Suite 1 Time Series

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is likely significant — model behavior on impossible tasks varies with how the prompt is framed (e.g., explicit vs. implicit impossibility). Saturation is a known risk as frontier models improve at detecting contradictory requirements; scores may compress at the top end quickly. Specific contamination status is unknown.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether models correctly identify that a given coding task is impossible or unsolvable as specified, rather than generating plausible-looking but non-functional or incorrect code. Probes honesty and resistance to sycophancy when a user implicitly expects a solution to be produced.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a high score indicates the model reliably reports impossibility rather than confabulating a solution. Frontier models vary significantly on this type of task depending on prompting style; absolute scores should be compared within the same scaffold configuration.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and lab evaluators assessing model honesty, calibration, and sycophancy in coding contexts.

policy_note.caveat: Evaluation sets for safety behaviors like this are typically small, limiting statistical reliability. The 'unambiguous references' variant represents an easier condition than real-world deployment where cues would be subtle; high scores here do not imply the model detects evaluations generally. Scores should be interpreted alongside behavioral-change data — awareness alone is not harmful without differential behavior.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether an AI model recognizes it is being evaluated when the evaluation context is made unambiguously explicit — e.g., through direct statements or clear contextual cues that a test is underway. Probes evaluation awareness as a precursor capability to deceptive alignment (behaving differently during evaluation vs. deployment).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate the model more reliably identifies it is being tested when told so explicitly. This is not straightforwardly 'better' or 'worse' — awareness is concerning only if paired with behavioral differences between eval and deployment contexts. Frontier models on safety evals often cluster near ceiling or floor, making differentiation difficult.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and frontier-model developers assessing whether models exhibit potential deceptive alignment precursors, particularly in the context of scheming evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: Results are highly sensitive to scaffolding, system-prompt framing, and the specific evaluator pipeline used, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. The evaluation targets rare, extreme behaviors, so even a low non-zero success rate carries outsized policy significance that a raw percentage can obscure. Scoring thresholds and task definitions may vary across Apollo Research evaluation rounds.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether frontier AI models can perform covert sabotage behaviors — such as inserting subtle bugs into code, manipulating outputs to deceive human reviewers, or undermining oversight mechanisms — without being detected. Tasks present models with agentic scenarios in which they have both the opportunity and (simulated) motive to sabotage operations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a score of 0% (no successful sabotage) is ideal. Any non-trivial success rate is treated as a safety-relevant signal regardless of absolute magnitude. Results are typically broken down by task category (e.g., code sabotage, monitor deception) rather than reported as a single aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, model developers, and policy teams conducting pre-deployment dangerous-capability assessments; relevant to organizations following responsible scaling policies that gate deployment on safety thresholds.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold and prompt dependence is high: small changes in how sabotage opportunities are framed or how the agentic context is constructed can substantially shift observed rates, making cross-setup comparisons unreliable. The benchmark covers a narrow slice of possible sabotage modalities, so a low score should not be read as a general safety certification.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether AI models will engage in covert sabotage behaviors when given the opportunity — such as subtly undermining tasks, manipulating outputs, or acting against user or operator interests while appearing compliant. Tests for a specific class of misaligned agentic behavior distinct from refusal or overt noncompliance.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower sabotage rates are better; an ideally aligned model scores near 0%. Because most current frontier models rarely succeed at sabotage tasks, small absolute differences carry high variance — interpret relative rankings cautiously.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and frontier labs assessing pre-deployment risk of deceptive or scheming behavior in capable models.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold- and prompt-dependent: the magnitude of sandbagging measured varies with how the eliciting condition is framed, making cross-study comparisons unreliable. Results reflect behavior under specific experimental conditions rather than an intrinsic model property, and a model that does not sandbag in this setup may still do so in deployment contexts not covered by the eval.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether AI models deliberately underperform (sandbag) on question-answering tasks when prompted or conditioned to believe that demonstrating high capability is undesirable. Probes the gap between a model's true ability and its reported performance under conditions designed to elicit strategic underperformance.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower sandbagging rate (smaller performance delta between standard and sandbagging-eliciting conditions) is better. A score near zero indicates the model performs consistently regardless of the incentive framing; a high score indicates the model is suppressing demonstrated capability when prompted to do so.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing deceptive alignment and strategic self-concealment of capabilities in frontier language models.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: elicitation method, system prompt framing, and whether the model is told it is being evaluated all materially affect results, making cross-setup comparisons unreliable. The eval detects sandbagging propensity under specific prompting regimes, not a fixed underlying capability, so results should not be treated as a stable capability score.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether AI models engage in 'sandbagging' — deliberately underperforming on capability evaluations when they infer that appearing less capable serves their goals. Probes a specific form of strategic deception by comparing model performance under normal conditions versus conditions where the model may be motivated to conceal capabilities.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores (more evidence of sandbagging behavior) indicate greater safety concern, not greater model capability. There is no conventional frontier range — the benchmark is binary/graded by degree of detected deceptive underperformance rather than a competitive leaderboard.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing whether frontier models might strategically hide capabilities during deployment or safety evaluations; relevant to pre-deployment risk assessments and dangerous-capability evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: Interpretation is inherently dual-directional: a high score (strong verbalized awareness) may indicate sophisticated self-modeling but also raises deceptive-alignment concerns, since a model that detects evaluations could selectively behave better during them. The benchmark is narrow in scope—verbalized awareness does not capture implicit behavioral shifts. Results may vary substantially with system-prompt framing and scaffold choice.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether frontier AI models explicitly verbalize awareness that they are undergoing an alignment or safety evaluation, probing a form of situational self-awareness. Tasks present evaluation-adjacent scenarios and assess whether the model expresses, in natural language, that it believes it is being tested or observed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger verbalized detection of evaluation contexts. Whether higher is 'better' is safety-context-dependent: high awareness in a deployed model is a safety concern; low awareness in a lab model under study may mean the probe is ineffective. Compare across model families rather than seeking an absolute target.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers studying situational awareness, deceptive alignment, and evaluation-gaming in frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: Introductory-tier problems are largely saturated by frontier models, reducing differentiation at the easy end. Problems were scraped from public competitive programming and interview-prep sites, raising training-data contamination risk for models trained on large web corpora. Strict accuracy and test-case average are two distinct metrics frequently reported interchangeably, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. 0-shot vs. few-shot prompting produces substantially different scores.
policy_note.measures: APPS (Automated Programming Progress Standard) measures code generation ability on 10,000 Python programming problems spanning introductory, interview, and competition difficulty tiers. Models generate Python solutions evaluated for functional correctness by running against hidden test cases, reported as either test-case pass rate or strict (all-tests-passing) accuracy.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Strict accuracy (fraction of problems with all test cases passing) is the harder metric; test-case average is more lenient. Frontier models (2024–2025) reach ~50–80% test-case average on introductory problems but typically under 30% strict accuracy on competition-level problems. Always note which split and which metric is reported.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and developers evaluating code generation and program synthesis capabilities, particularly across difficulty levels.

policy_note.caveat: ARC-AGI-1 (the original 400-task set) is approaching saturation for top frontier systems, especially when heavy test-time compute or program synthesis scaffolds are used — o3 high-compute reportedly exceeded 85% in late 2024, making single-number comparisons scaffold-dependent. Score comparisons across model cards are often not comparable because some use semi-private leaderboard submissions, others report public-set numbers with unconstrained retries, and the harder ARC-AGI-2 (released 2025) should not be conflated with ARC-AGI-1 scores.
policy_note.measures: ARC-AGI presents grid-based visual pattern puzzles where models must infer a transformation rule from 2–5 demonstration input/output pairs and apply it to a novel input. The public evaluation set contains 400 tasks designed to require fluid reasoning over object properties, symmetry, and spatial relations rather than memorised facts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percentage of tasks solved correctly. Human baseline is roughly 85% on ARC-AGI-1. Frontier model scores on ARC-AGI-1 ranged from near-zero (pre-2023 LLMs) to ~85%+ (o3 with high compute, 2024); ARC-AGI-2 scores remain much lower across all systems.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers evaluating abstract reasoning and generalisation capability; useful for distinguishing fluid reasoning from pattern-matched retrieval in frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: direct next-token prediction, program synthesis, and extended test-time compute approaches produce very different numbers on identical underlying tasks, making cross-system comparisons unreliable. The 'high effort' variant label indicates extended compute budgets (more attempts, longer reasoning chains) that can roughly double scores versus standard single-pass inference. Frontier models have moved from near-zero to >85% (on the public set) between 2023 and 2025, raising saturation concerns for the public split. The private leaderboard set is harder and less saturated. ARC-AGI-2 was released in 2025 and is a distinct, harder benchmark — conflating the two versions inflates apparent progress.
policy_note.measures: ARC-AGI-1 tests abstract visual reasoning by asking models to infer transformation rules from a handful of colored-grid input/output examples and apply them to a novel test grid. The public evaluation set contains 400 tasks; the private leaderboard set (used in the ARC Prize competition) contains an additional 100 held-out tasks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percentage of tasks solved correctly (0–100%). On the public evaluation split, weak baselines score near 0% while top systems (with high compute budgets) now exceed 85%. The private competition set is harder, with winning scores historically 10–20 points lower than public-set claims.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and competition participants evaluating fluid reasoning and out-of-distribution generalisation; primary venue is the ARC Prize public leaderboard.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent — test-time compute strategies (program synthesis, search, chain-of-thought) produce dramatically different results than single-pass inference, making cross-report comparisons unreliable without matching inference budgets. ARC-AGI-2 was explicitly designed to replace ARC-AGI-1 after frontier models saturated the original (some reaching ~60%+); the two versions are not interchangeable and should not be conflated in trend analysis.
policy_note.measures: ARC-AGI-2 tests abstract visual reasoning: given 2–5 input/output grid-transformation examples, the model must infer the underlying rule and produce the correct output grid for a held-out test input. It is designed to probe fluid intelligence and novel rule generalisation rather than memorised knowledge.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent of tasks solved correctly. Frontier models scored in roughly the 4–15% range at launch, far below estimated human performance (~85%), leaving substantial headroom for differentiation. Cross-model comparisons require matching inference-time compute budgets.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and competition participants evaluating abstract reasoning and generalisation capabilities of frontier models; designed for the ARC Prize competition.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: 'high effort' (extended test-time compute, majority voting, or multi-attempt) configurations produce substantially higher numbers than single-pass inference, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless inference strategy is matched exactly. The benchmark is intentionally designed to resist training-data memorization, but the degree of contamination from synthetically generated ARC-style training data in recent frontier models is not fully audited.
policy_note.measures: ARC-AGI-2 (Verified) measures abstract visual reasoning via grid-based transformation puzzles: each task supplies a few input-output example grids and asks the model to apply the inferred rule to a novel input. The Verified label denotes a human-audited subset with unambiguous solutions and confirmed unique correct answers, designed to reduce noisy labels present in the broader ARC-AGI-2 public set.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent of tasks solved. Human performance is roughly 60–80%. As of mid-2025, top frontier models under high-effort inference reach roughly 15–40%, with most standard single-pass results well below 20%. ARC-AGI-2 is substantially harder than ARC-AGI-1, where leading models had already approached or exceeded human-level scores.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and benchmark practitioners evaluating abstract reasoning and out-of-distribution generalization in frontier models; used by the ARC Prize competition to rank submitted systems.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are strongly scaffold-dependent: extended-thinking token budgets (e.g., 64k tokens) substantially inflate results versus standard inference, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless thinking budgets are matched — the 'prior score' and '64k thinking budget' variant strings in cards reflect exactly this ambiguity. Label conflation between the full ARC-AGI-2 public set and the Verified subset is common; the two should not be compared directly. ARC-AGI-2 tasks are novel by construction, so contamination risk is low, but evaluation methodology (number of submission attempts, ensemble strategies) varies across labs.
policy_note.measures: ARC-AGI-2 is a visual abstract-reasoning benchmark of novel grid-based transformation tasks: given a few input-output example pairs, a model must infer the rule and solve a held-out test grid. The 'Verified' label denotes a curated subset with human-validated labels and confirmed unique solutions, analogous to SWE-bench Verified.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as percentage of tasks solved (0–100%). ARC-AGI-2 was designed to be substantially harder than ARC-AGI-1: human performance sits near 85%, while as of mid-2025 frontier models score in roughly the 10–40% range depending on compute budget and thinking allowance. Scores without a stated thinking budget are difficult to interpret.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and competition participants benchmarking general fluid intelligence and abstract reasoning in frontier models; also used to track progress toward the ARC Prize.

policy_note.caveat: Heavily saturated — frontier models routinely score above 90%, leaving little headroom to differentiate top systems. The benchmark has been public since 2018, raising contamination risk as its questions likely appear in pretraining corpora. Shot-count variants (0-shot, 5-shot, 25-shot) produce meaningfully different absolute scores and should not be compared directly across papers.
policy_note.measures: ARC-Challenge tests grade-school science reasoning via 1,172 four-choice multiple-choice questions drawn from standardized US science exams (grades 3–9). It specifically contains questions that simple retrieval and word co-occurrence methods fail to answer correctly, probing genuine reasoning over scientific concepts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent correct (0–100). Frontier models now cluster above 90%, so scores below ~85% indicate a meaningful capability gap relative to leading systems. Always note the shot count when comparing results.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating general reasoning and science knowledge in language models; commonly used as part of standard LLM evaluation suites.

policy_note.caveat: Hausa-language benchmarks are relatively rare in public leaderboards, so frontier-model score ranges are not well established; results may vary significantly with translation quality and the fidelity of the adaptation from the original ARC dataset.
policy_note.measures: ARC-Easy-Hausa is a Hausa-language adaptation of the ARC Easy subset, probing multiple-choice science question answering in a low-resource African language. It tests whether models can apply elementary science knowledge when the prompt language is Hausa rather than English.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier multilingual models may score in the 60–80% range, but baselines specific to this variant are sparse.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multilingual or African-language coverage in language models, particularly for low-resource language generalization.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a growing concern — top frontier models now score 90%+ win rate, compressing differentiation at the high end. The GPT-4-based judge introduces verbosity and positional biases that can favour longer, more verbose outputs regardless of quality. The reference model (GPT-4-0314) is outdated, making absolute win-rate numbers difficult to interpret across time. Prompt leakage is plausible since source prompts originate from public Chatbot Arena logs.
policy_note.measures: Arena Hard evaluates general instruction-following and assistant quality using 500 challenging prompts drawn from Chatbot Arena conversations, scored via GPT-4-as-judge in a pairwise comparison against a fixed reference model (GPT-4-0314). It is designed to produce leaderboard rankings that correlate strongly with human-preference results from live Chatbot Arena.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as win rate (%) against GPT-4-0314. Frontier models (mid-2024 onward) typically range from ~75% to 95%+. A score above ~85% is competitive with top-tier models; scores below ~50% indicate performance well below the GPT-4-0314 baseline.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners comparing general-purpose chat/instruction-following capabilities of large language models; teams that want an automated proxy for Chatbot Arena human-preference rankings.

policy_note.measures: Assesses model performance on atomic, discrete challenge items that follow irregular or non-standard patterns, likely probing robustness to exceptions and edge cases rather than canonical rule-following. The exact dataset size and task format are not publicly documented in widely available sources.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Without published frontier baselines or a known scale, scores should be interpreted relative to other models reported in the same context rather than against an absolute threshold.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and evaluators interested in fine-grained capability profiling, particularly how models handle irregular or exception-laden inputs outside of standard rule patterns.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: agentic framework choice (tool set, retry logic, context management) materially affects outcomes, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless the scaffold is held constant. The easy/medium/hard variant labels may conflate structurally different task types rather than a clean difficulty gradient, so aggregate scores can obscure where capability actually lies. Results are often not publicly disclosed in full due to dual-use sensitivity.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's ability to autonomously execute offensive cybersecurity tasks — such as vulnerability exploitation, privilege escalation, and lateral movement — across three graded difficulty tiers (easy, medium, hard). Tasks are typically isolated challenge environments scored on task completion.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher completion rate = greater autonomous offense capability, which is the risk signal being measured — higher scores are worse from a safety perspective. Frontier models currently show meaningful separation on hard-tier tasks; easy-tier tasks may be near saturation for leading models. Compare only runs with identical scaffolds and environment configurations.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating dangerous-capability thresholds; used internally by frontier labs and third-party evaluators (e.g., pre-deployment red-teaming) to inform deployment and access decisions.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic harness, tool set, and scaffolding framework supplied to the model substantially change pass rates, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. Tasks are necessarily toy or sandboxed proxies for real replication, so low scores do not guarantee inability in unconstrained settings. The '100 trials' variant reports a pass-rate over 100 runs, but trial difficulty and exact task distribution vary across evaluators.
policy_note.measures: ARA evaluates whether an AI model can autonomously replicate itself to new compute resources, acquire money or API access, and persist without human assistance across approximately 100 independent trial runs. It probes dangerous 'self-proliferation' capabilities by presenting agents with realistic tasks such as spinning up cloud instances, exfiltrating weights, or subverting oversight mechanisms.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower task-completion rates are safer. A score near 0% means the model failed essentially all replication sub-tasks; scores above safety thresholds (often ~10–50% depending on the evaluating organization) may trigger policy-level interventions. Frontier models circa 2024–2025 generally score in the low single digits on the hardest sub-tasks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing whether a model crosses dangerous-capability thresholds under responsible scaling / model evaluation frameworks.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a significant concern: frontier models now routinely exceed human baselines (set around 2022) on most subtasks, compressing differentiation at the top. Scores are scaffold-dependent—chain-of-thought prompting yields substantially higher numbers than direct prompting, so comparisons across papers are only valid when the prompting regime matches. Some tasks may have appeared in pretraining corpora, raising contamination risk.
policy_note.measures: BBH (BIG-Bench Hard) evaluates reasoning across 23 diverse tasks—drawn from the broader BIG-Bench suite—where models previously scored below average human performance. Tasks cover logical deduction, multi-step arithmetic, causal reasoning, date understanding, tracking shuffled objects, and similar structured-reasoning challenges, typically assessed with chain-of-thought prompting across ~6,500 total problems.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are expressed as accuracy (0–100%). Human average baseline is roughly 50–70% depending on task. Frontier models (GPT-4-class and above) typically score 85–95%+, making the benchmark most informative for mid-tier model comparisons rather than distinguishing top frontier systems.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating general multi-step reasoning and instruction-following ability in language models, particularly for comparing models that sit below frontier saturation.

policy_note.caveat: The variant strings reported across cards reflect genuinely distinct sub-tasks that should not be aggregated: 'ambiguous' and 'disambiguated' have different correct-answer logic, and P(not stereotyping|ambiguous) is a derived bias score from the ambiguous subset only — mixing these produces meaningless composites. Frontier models now approach ceiling on the disambiguated accuracy sub-task (>90%), limiting its power to differentiate top models. Scores are also sensitive to answer-option ordering and prompt phrasing, which creates scaffold dependence when comparing across evaluation harnesses.
policy_note.measures: BBQ tests social-bias tendencies in multiple-choice QA across 9 protected-attribute categories (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race/ethnicity, religion, socioeconomic status, sexual orientation). It presents ~58,000 question sets in two modes — ambiguous contexts (where 'unknown' is always correct) and disambiguated contexts (where one answer is factually supported) — to detect whether models substitute stereotypes for evidence.
policy_note.how_to_read: On disambiguated contexts, higher accuracy is better (random baseline is 33%). On ambiguous contexts, a higher rate of selecting 'unknown' is better. P(not stereotyping|ambiguous) runs 0–1; 1.0 means the model never applied a stereotype. Frontier models typically score 88–96% on disambiguated accuracy; bias scores on ambiguous contexts vary more and are the more meaningful differentiator.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing social-bias tendencies in language models, particularly in question-answering settings.

policy_note.caveat: The ambiguous split specifically targets over-reliance on stereotypes, so a model can score high by consistently choosing 'unknown' without genuine reasoning. Scores should be read alongside the disambiguated-context accuracy; high ambiguous accuracy paired with low disambiguated accuracy may indicate the model is hedging indiscriminately rather than reasoning correctly.
policy_note.measures: BBQ (Bias Benchmark for QA) Ambiguous Accuracy measures a model's accuracy on multiple-choice social-situation questions where the context is deliberately ambiguous and does not provide enough information to determine the answer — the correct response is always the 'unknown/cannot determine' option. It probes whether models default to stereotyped answers when evidence is insufficient.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a perfect score is 100%. Random-choice baseline is ~33% (three-choice questions). Unbiased models should score near 100% on ambiguous contexts by consistently answering 'unknown'. Frontier models typically score in the 80–95% range on this split.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing social bias and stereotype reliance in language models, particularly in QA contexts involving demographic groups.

policy_note.caveat: The ambiguous condition has a trivial optimal strategy — always output 'Unknown' — so high aggregate scores do not guarantee the model reasons fairly; per-category breakdowns are more informative. Results should not be conflated with the BBQ Disambiguated condition, which tests the opposite: whether models use explicit contextual cues correctly. Aggregate saturation is possible for large frontier models, masking per-category disparities. Dataset is English-only.
policy_note.measures: BBQ (Bias Benchmark for QA) — Ambiguous condition — measures whether a model defaults to stereotyped answers when context is deliberately underspecified. The dataset contains 58,492 QA examples across 9 social bias categories (age, race/ethnicity, gender identity, religion, etc.); in the ambiguous split the correct answer is always 'Unknown', so accuracy reflects how often the model avoids biased inference.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better (scale 0–100%). A score of 100% means the model always selected 'Unknown' in ambiguous contexts and never inferred a stereotyped answer. Frontier models typically score in the 80–95% range in aggregate, but per-category scores can vary by 20+ points; report category-level results alongside aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: AI fairness researchers and model developers evaluating social bias in language model QA behavior, particularly for auditing stereotyping tendencies across protected-attribute categories.

policy_note.caveat: BBQ has two distinct sub-conditions — ambiguous (context is inconclusive; correct answer is 'unknown') and disambiguated (context resolves the answer) — and model cards sometimes report a single 'BBQ accuracy' figure without specifying which condition, making cross-card comparisons unreliable. Frontier models frequently saturate the disambiguated condition (scores in the high 90s), reducing its power to differentiate capable models. The benchmark is English-only and relies on US-centric social framing, which may not generalize across languages or cultural contexts.
policy_note.measures: BBQ (Bias Benchmark for QA) Disambiguated Accuracy measures whether a model correctly answers multiple-choice questions when the context explicitly resolves ambiguity — i.e., provides enough information to identify the right answer without relying on stereotypes. The benchmark covers ~58,000 QA items across 9 social categories (age, disability, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race/ethnicity, religion, socioeconomic status, sexual orientation).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score of 100% means the model always followed the disambiguated context rather than defaulting to a stereotyped answer. Frontier models typically score above 90%, so meaningful differentiation occurs in the low-to-mid 90s range. Compare against the ambiguous-condition score alongside this metric for a complete bias picture.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and fairness researchers, policy analysts, and developers evaluating whether language models exhibit social bias in question-answering contexts.

policy_note.caveat: This variant should not be conflated with BBQ Ambiguous, which measures how often models default to stereotypes when context is insufficient — the two conditions probe opposite failure modes and yield separate scores. Frontier models now score very high on the disambiguated condition (often 90–99%), limiting its ability to differentiate top systems. The benchmark is English-only and covers a fixed set of demographic categories that may not reflect all relevant bias axes.
policy_note.measures: BBQ (Disambiguated) measures whether a model correctly answers multiple-choice QA questions when the provided context unambiguously identifies the answer, even when that answer contradicts a common social stereotype. The full BBQ dataset spans ~58,000 examples across 9 social dimensions (age, disability, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race/ethnicity, religion, socioeconomic status, sexual orientation); the disambiguated split isolates items where a correct, non-stereotypical answer is derivable from context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; score is accuracy on unambiguous items. Frontier models typically cluster above 90%, so meaningful differentiation is mostly below that range. Pair with the Ambiguous split score to get a full picture of bias behavior.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and fairness researchers evaluating whether language models exhibit stereotypical reasoning in QA tasks; model developers auditing social bias before deployment.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to the agentic scaffold and tool definitions used — different frameworks or prompt templates produce materially different pass rates, so cross-report comparisons are unreliable without controlling for scaffold. The retail domain is narrower than general instruction-following benchmarks, so results may not generalise beyond customer-service policy compliance.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates LLM-based agents on multi-turn customer-service tasks in a simulated retail (e-commerce) environment, requiring the agent to follow store policies while resolving user requests such as order modifications, returns, and product inquiries. Success is measured as the fraction of episodes completed correctly per policy rules.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent task success rate (0–1 or 0–100%). Frontier models typically cluster in the 0.4–0.7 range on the retail split, with significant variance by scaffold.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating tool-augmented or agentic LLMs on realistic, policy-constrained task completion; particularly relevant for enterprise/customer-service deployment decisions.

policy_note.caveat: Agentic benchmarks of this family exhibit strong scaffold dependence — scores shift meaningfully depending on the agent harness, tool schema formatting, and retry logic used, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable without exact setup parity.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates AI agents on realistic telecommunications customer-service tasks, probing multi-turn dialogue, policy adherence, and tool use (e.g. account lookups, plan changes, billing adjustments). Scores reflect end-to-end task completion rates across simulated customer interactions in the telecom domain.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; primary metric is task success rate (0–100%). Frontier model scores on agentic task benchmarks of this type typically cluster in the 40–75% range, with meaningful headroom remaining.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating conversational agents for telecom customer-service automation; useful for comparing policy-following and tool-use capabilities in a domain-specific, high-stakes setting.

name: Benign Request Evaluation - Extended Thinking Refusal Rate

policy_note.caveat: Results are specific to the extended thinking inference mode and may not generalize to standard (non-thinking) inference; the same model can exhibit materially different refusal rates depending on whether extended thinking is enabled. The set of "benign" prompts and their categorization is determined by the evaluating lab, introducing potential subjectivity in what counts as benign.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model incorrectly refuses clearly benign user requests when operating in extended thinking (chain-of-thought reasoning) mode. A lower refusal rate indicates the model is less likely to over-refuse safe, legitimate requests.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a lower refusal rate means the model correctly answers more benign requests rather than over-refusing. Scores are expressed as a percentage (0–100%); frontier models with well-calibrated safety training typically score in low single digits on fully benign prompt sets.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policymakers assessing over-refusal / false-positive refusal behavior in models with extended reasoning capabilities.

name: Benign Request Evaluation - Overall Refusal Rate

policy_note.caveat: The metric is heavily threshold-dependent: what counts as 'benign' varies across evaluation sets, so cross-lab comparisons may conflate different prompt distributions. Results also depend on how refusal is operationalized (hard refusal vs. hedged response), which differs by evaluator.
policy_note.measures: Measures the fraction of clearly benign user requests that a model refuses to answer, capturing over-refusal behavior introduced by safety training. Lower scores indicate the model is less likely to block harmless, legitimate queries.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a rate of 0% means the model never refused a benign request, while higher values indicate increasing over-caution. Frontier models typically report rates well below 10%; values above ~5% are often flagged as regressions.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and policy teams assessing the helpfulness-safety tradeoff; useful for tracking regressions in over-refusal after safety fine-tuning iterations.

name: Benign Request Evaluation - Standard Thinking Refusal Rate

policy_note.caveat: Scores are mode-dependent: 'standard thinking' and 'extended thinking' variants routinely produce different refusal rates for the same underlying requests, so cross-variant comparisons are misleading. The benchmark name implies a companion extended-thinking variant; always specify which variant is being cited. Dataset composition and size are not publicly documented, limiting external reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model refuses benign, clearly harmless user requests under standard (non-extended) thinking mode. A higher refusal rate indicates more over-refusal — the model declining requests it should fulfill.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better. A refusal rate of 0% on benign requests is ideal; any positive value represents unnecessary unhelpfulness. Compare only within the same thinking mode (standard vs. extended), as modes can shift rates substantially.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating over-refusal behavior — specifically whether safety training causes a model to decline legitimate, low-risk requests.

policy_note.caveat: There is no single canonical dataset for this metric; each lab or evaluator defines 'benign' differently, making cross-model comparisons unreliable without knowing the exact test set. Prompt phrasing, system-prompt strictness, and the specific refusal-detection heuristic used (keyword match vs. human rater vs. classifier) can all swing scores substantially. The 'overall' variant label suggests aggregation across request categories, which can mask divergent behavior on specific topics.
policy_note.measures: Measures the fraction of clearly harmless, legitimate user requests that a model incorrectly refuses to fulfill. A lower rate indicates the model is less prone to over-refusal — declining to help when there is no genuine safety reason to do so.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better; 0% means the model never refused a benign request in the test set. Frontier models typically report single-digit percentages on internal evaluations, but absolute values are not directly comparable across labs due to dataset differences.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, model developers, and policymakers evaluating the helpfulness–safety tradeoff; particularly useful for auditing whether safety mitigations produce excessive false positives on everyday user requests.

policy_note.caveat: Simple single-function categories show saturation among frontier models (scores routinely above 90%), reducing differentiation at the top. Contamination risk is elevated because schemas and prompts are publicly hosted and may appear in training corpora. Scores are scaffold-dependent: prompt format for function definitions (JSON Schema vs. XML vs. prose) meaningfully shifts results, so cross-provider comparisons require identical prompting.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates an LLM's ability to correctly invoke functions/tools given natural language instructions and JSON function schemas, covering simple, parallel, multiple-turn, and nested call patterns across roughly 2,000 test cases. Probes both syntactic correctness (AST match) and executable correctness for a subset of real-API calls.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models typically score 85–95%+ on simple categories; parallel and nested categories (often 60–85%) provide more differentiation. The leaderboard separates categories, so look at the hardest tier rather than the aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners benchmarking tool-use / agentic capability of LLMs; useful for selecting models for function-calling pipelines.

policy_note.caveat: Top frontier models cluster above 85–90% accuracy, reducing differentiation at the high end. Scores are scaffold-dependent: models tested via their native tool-use APIs versus plain-text prompting can diverge significantly. BFCL v2 extended the original BFCL with harder multi-turn and irrelevance-detection cases, so v1 and v2 scores are not directly comparable.
policy_note.measures: BFCL v2 (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v2) measures how accurately models generate syntactically and semantically correct function/tool calls given a function signature and a user query. It covers simple, parallel, nested, and multiple-function invocation patterns across real-world APIs, evaluated via AST matching and live execution.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are overall accuracy percentages (0–100). Frontier models typically land between 70% and 95%, with top-tier models above 85%. A large gap between a model's simple-call and parallel/nested-call sub-scores reveals brittleness in complex tool-use scenarios.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating or selecting models for tool-use and agentic pipelines that rely on structured function calling.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is an active concern — frontier models (GPT-4-class and above) now routinely exceed 85–90% on BBH, compressing the useful signal for differentiating leading systems. The '3-shot' vs '3-shot CoT' variants produce meaningfully different scores for the same model and should not be compared directly; model cards often omit which setting was used. Benchmark contamination is plausible given BBH's wide use and early release date (2022).
policy_note.measures: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a suite of 23 tasks drawn from the larger BIG-Bench benchmark, selected because prior language models scored below human baselines on them. Tasks span algorithmic reasoning, logical deduction, causal judgement, tracking shuffled objects, temporal sequences, and other multi-step reasoning challenges; each task typically has a few hundred examples evaluated under 3-shot or 3-shot chain-of-thought prompting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as percent correct (0–100). Human baselines average roughly 89% across tasks. Frontier models as of 2024–2025 cluster in the 85–92% range under CoT prompting, so differences of 1–2 points carry limited practical meaning at the top of the leaderboard.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multi-step reasoning and chain-of-thought capabilities in language models; useful for tracking progress on tasks where naive few-shot prompting previously failed.

policy_note.caveat: BigCodeBench Hard was carved out specifically because frontier models were saturating the full BigCodeBench benchmark, so saturation on the Hard subset is an ongoing concern as models improve. Scores are scaffold-dependent: evaluation harness version and execution environment (library versions, sandboxing) can meaningfully shift pass rates. The Hard subset is not independently versioned from the full benchmark, so the exact task composition may shift across releases.
policy_note.measures: BigCodeBench Hard is a challenging subset of the 1,140-task BigCodeBench suite, retaining only the tasks where average model performance is lowest. Tasks require generating Python code that correctly calls functions from diverse real-world libraries (covering 139 libraries), evaluated via pass@1 against ground-truth unit tests.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent pass@1 (fraction of tasks solved on first attempt), expressed as a percentage from 0–100. Frontier models typically score in the 30–60% range on the Hard subset, providing more headroom for differentiation than the full benchmark.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and ML engineers evaluating LLM practical coding ability, particularly for differentiating frontier models that score too uniformly on standard coding benchmarks.

policy_note.measures: Assesses factual and conceptual knowledge of biochemistry, including topics such as metabolism, enzyme kinetics, molecular biology, and cell signaling. Typically presented as multiple-choice questions drawn from undergraduate-to-graduate-level biochemistry curricula.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent percentage of questions answered correctly. Frontier models typically score in the 70–90% range on biochemistry subsets of broader science benchmarks.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating AI models on domain-specific scientific knowledge, particularly for biomedical and life-sciences applications.

policy_note.measures: Assesses factual and conceptual knowledge across core biochemistry domains—metabolism, enzyme kinetics, protein structure, nucleic acid biochemistry, and cell signaling—typically via multiple-choice questions drawn from undergraduate-to-graduate-level material. Dataset size and exact question count are not widely documented for this benchmark.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; scores are typically reported as percent correct (0–100). Frontier models generally score in the 70–90 range on comparable domain-knowledge benchmarks, though specific distributional data for this benchmark is not well established in the public literature.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating AI models on specialized life-sciences domain knowledge, particularly for biomedical or scientific assistant applications.

policy_note.caveat: The two observed variant strings — 'expert baseline' and 'post-mitigation' — represent meaningfully different scoring contexts and are not directly comparable; a model's 'post-mitigation' score will typically be lower than its 'expert baseline' score by design, so cross-paper comparisons must confirm which variant is reported. Scaffold and system-prompt dependence is high: safety mitigations applied at inference time can swing scores substantially, making leaderboard rankings sensitive to deployment configuration rather than intrinsic capability.
policy_note.measures: BioLP-Bench measures the degree of dangerous biological laboratory procedure uplift an AI model provides to a user, relative to a human expert baseline. It probes biosecurity risk by presenting biology-adjacent queries and scoring how much actionable, hazardous procedural information the model supplies.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a lower score indicates the model provides less dangerous procedural uplift. The 'expert baseline' variant anchors scores against what a domain expert could independently produce; 'post-mitigation' reflects residual uplift after refusal or redaction mitigations are active. Always confirm which variant a reported number corresponds to before comparing across models.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and biosecurity policy makers evaluating the dual-use risk profile of frontier language models before and after safety interventions.

policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to correctly identify and surface biosecurity-relevant information or threat signals from text, measuring recall (true-positive rate) over a set of biorisk-related scenarios or documents. Probes whether a model can flag biological risk indicators without missing critical positives.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher recall is better; a higher score means the model misses fewer genuine biorisk signals. Interpret alongside precision metrics if available, since high recall at the cost of many false positives may not indicate safe or useful behavior in practice.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating model performance on biosecurity monitoring tasks, particularly for dual-use risk assessments and responsible deployment decisions.

policy_note.caveat: The definition of 'success' is ambiguous across reporting labs — some treat higher pass rate as safer (model refused), while others frame it as capability (model completed a task). Methodology and threat scenarios are rarely disclosed publicly, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. Scaffold and tool configuration (which tools are available, in what order) can substantially affect outcomes, introducing scaffold dependence. Internal proprietary variants from different labs may not share the same scenario distribution.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether an AI model with tool access (web search, code execution, etc.) provides meaningful uplift toward biological risk activities, such as synthesizing dangerous pathogens or circumventing biosecurity controls. Results are reported as a pass rate or overall success rate, where a 'pass' typically means the model appropriately refused or declined to assist.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher pass rate is generally better when 'pass' means the model refused or did not provide uplift; verify the lab's definition before comparing. No broadly standardized frontier range exists publicly — scores are typically reported close to 100% for compliant models on disclosed evaluations, but thresholds triggering policy action vary by lab.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policy makers, and lab responsible-scaling-policy reviewers assessing whether frontier models cross biological risk thresholds under agentic conditions.

policy_note.caveat: Scores on the dev set are not directly comparable to test-set leaderboard numbers, which use a held-out split with a separate execution-accuracy evaluation server. Dev-set results self-reported in model cards may use varying execution environments or SQL dialects, introducing scaffold dependence. Contamination risk exists because the dev set is public and its questions may appear in training corpora.
policy_note.measures: Bird-SQL (Dev) measures text-to-SQL generation on the BIRD (BIg Bench for Large-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL) development split, a dataset of 1,534 questions across 11 domains requiring models to translate natural-language questions into executable SQL against real-world, large-scale databases. It tests whether models can handle complex schema reasoning, dirty data, and domain-specific knowledge beyond syntax correctness.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; the primary metric is Execution Accuracy (EX), the fraction of generated SQL queries that return the correct result set when executed. Frontier models score roughly 60–75% EX on the dev set; human expert performance is around 92%.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and practitioners evaluating LLM capability on realistic, enterprise-scale database question answering and text-to-SQL tasks.

policy_note.caveat: Models score far below human performance (~95%), so saturation is not currently a concern; however, the small multiple-choice option sets (typically 2–4 choices) inflate scores relative to open-ended perception tasks, and gains on BLINK may reflect format exploitation rather than improved visual understanding.
policy_note.measures: BLINK evaluates multimodal large language models on 14 visual perception tasks (e.g., relative depth estimation, jigsaw puzzles, visual correspondence, multi-view reasoning, spatial relations) presented as multiple-choice questions — approximately 3,800 items total — that humans solve rapidly but that challenge current vision-language models.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better. Human performance is approximately 95%; frontier multimodal models (GPT-4V-era and beyond) typically score in the 40–60% range, well above random chance (~25–50% depending on task) but far below human level.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers assessing low-level visual perception capabilities of vision-language models, distinct from benchmarks that primarily test factual knowledge or language reasoning.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark is largely saturated for frontier models, which now routinely exceed the ~90% human accuracy baseline, leaving little headroom to differentiate top-tier systems. Some contamination risk exists given the dataset's long public availability and its inclusion in SuperGLUE, a widely used pre-training signal.
policy_note.measures: BoolQ evaluates yes/no reading comprehension: given a short Wikipedia passage and a naturally occurring boolean question, a model must predict a true/false answer. The dataset contains approximately 9,700 training and 3,245 development examples sourced from real Google search queries.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; scale is 0–100%. Human performance is roughly 89–90%. Frontier models (GPT-4 class and above) typically score 90–95%+, compressing the useful differentiation range.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and ML practitioners assessing reading comprehension and natural language inference; most useful for evaluating mid-tier or smaller models where ceiling effects are less pronounced.

policy_note.caveat: Strong scaffold dependence: scores vary substantially depending on the browsing tool, search API, step budget, and agentic framework used, making cross-system comparisons unreliable. The 'rlhf' variant string observed in model cards likely refers to RLHF-tuned agent policies rather than a distinct benchmark release, creating label-conflation risk when comparing scores across systems without knowing the scaffold configuration.
policy_note.measures: BrowseComp tests AI agents on difficult, multi-hop research questions that require iterative web browsing to answer — questions deliberately chosen so the answer cannot be recalled from training data alone. The dataset contains approximately 1,266 questions with verifiable exact-match answers, and agents are scored on accuracy.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models with capable browsing scaffolds typically score in the 20–60% range; unaided models relying on parametric memory score near 0%. Human researchers familiar with web search tend to score 50–80%.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating the real-world web-research and multi-step information-retrieval capability of agentic AI systems.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are heavily scaffold-dependent: the number of parallel agents, total browsing steps, and orchestration strategy all inflate results, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable unless the exact setup is matched. The "multi-agent" and "max effort" variant labels are inconsistently applied across model cards, so reported numbers may not reflect comparable compute budgets.
policy_note.measures: BrowseComp tests a model's ability to find specific, hard-to-find factual answers through multi-step web browsing across roughly 1,266 challenging research questions with unambiguous, verifiable answers. The multi-agent variant pools results from multiple parallel agent runs ("max effort") rather than a single browsing session.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (%). Single-agent frontier baselines typically score in the low-to-mid single digits; multi-agent max-effort configurations push scores into the 20–50%+ range depending on compute budget. Compare only within the same scaffold configuration.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and lab evaluators assessing agentic, tool-augmented web research capabilities in frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the same model can perform very differently depending on the agentic framework, retry logic, and error-message formatting used. Results across labs are rarely directly comparable unless the exact scaffold is controlled.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether language models can complete web-browsing tasks when one or more of the available tools (e.g., click, search, form-fill) malfunction or return errors mid-task, probing robustness and recovery in agentic browsing pipelines.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better, indicating the model successfully completes more tasks despite tool failures. Frontier model performance on this class of benchmark is still well below saturation, so scores meaningfully differentiate systems.
