policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating agentic reliability and fault-tolerance in browser-use or tool-augmented LLM systems.

policy_note.caveat: Contamination risk is significant — C-Eval has been public since 2023 and many frontier models were trained on data that likely overlaps with it. The benchmark tests knowledge tied to the Chinese national education curriculum, so scores partially reflect alignment with that curriculum rather than general reasoning. Frontier models now score high enough on many subject categories that differentiation between top models is limited.
policy_note.measures: C-Eval is a comprehensive Chinese-language evaluation suite covering 52 subjects across four difficulty levels (middle school, high school, college, and professional), containing 13,948 multiple-choice questions. It probes factual knowledge and reasoning in Chinese across STEM, social sciences, humanities, and professional domains.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models as of 2024–2025 typically score in the 80–90%+ range on the standard split, with lower scores on the harder C-Eval Hard subset. Human expert performance on many professional categories is around 70–80%.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating Chinese-language large language models on broad academic and professional knowledge benchmarks.

policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's safety and robustness under adversarial red-teaming prompts designed to elicit harmful, policy-violating, or otherwise unsafe outputs. The '1' suffix suggests it is the first in a series of progressively difficult adversarial evaluation sets.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower harmful-output rates are better; a model scoring lower on attack success rate is considered more robust. Absolute scores are difficult to compare across labs because scoring rubrics and attacker strength vary by implementation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and lab policy teams assessing how well frontier models resist adversarial elicitation of unsafe behavior.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly dependent on the elicitation scaffold and attacker strategy used; different jailbreaking frameworks applied to the same model can yield substantially different attack success rates. Without a fixed attacker, cross-model comparisons may reflect methodology differences rather than true safety differences.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's robustness against adversarial red-teaming prompts designed to elicit harmful, unsafe, or policy-violating outputs. The '2' designation indicates a second, typically harder iteration with more challenging attack strategies compared to an initial version.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower attack success rate (or equivalently, higher refusal/safe-response rate) is better. Frontier safety-focused models typically achieve low attack success rates on standard red-teaming sets, so harder variants like this are used to differentiate among them.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing a model's resistance to adversarial prompting and red-teaming attacks.

policy_note.caveat: The not_unsafe variant measures the opposite behavior from the harm-category variants: it captures false-positive refusals rather than true-positive refusals. Aggregating across all variants into a single score conflates precision and recall on safety decisions, which can mask distinct failure modes. Results should always be interpreted per-variant.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model makes correct refusal decisions across challenging content categories—harassment/threatening, hate/threatening, illicit/non-violent, and illicit/violent—as well as whether the model correctly avoids refusing safe content (the not_unsafe variant). The benchmark probes both under-refusal (failing to decline genuinely harmful requests) and over-refusal (incorrectly declining benign ones).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better within each variant, but the direction of a 'good' outcome differs: for harm categories (harassment/threatening, hate/threatening, illicit/*) higher scores mean more correct refusals; for not_unsafe higher scores mean fewer over-refusals. Compare models at the per-variant level rather than as a single aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing the accuracy and calibration of a model's content refusal policy across specific harm taxonomies.

policy_note.caveat: At the standard R@1 IoU=0.5 threshold recent models approach 80 %+, limiting differentiation among frontier video-language systems. Results are highly threshold-sensitive—papers sometimes report only IoU=0.5 while omitting the harder IoU=0.7 split, so cross-paper comparisons require verifying which threshold(s) are used.
policy_note.measures: Charades-STA measures temporal sentence grounding in video: given a short indoor-activity video and a natural language query, a model must predict the start and end timestamps of the described moment. The dataset contains roughly 16,000 training and 2,400 test query-segment pairs derived from the Charades household-activity video collection.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The primary metrics are Recall@1 at IoU thresholds of 0.5 and 0.7 (written R@1 IoU=0.5 / R@1 IoU=0.7). Competitive recent models score roughly 70–85 % at IoU=0.5 and 50–70 % at IoU=0.7; a score should always be paired with its IoU threshold to be interpretable.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating video-language models on temporal grounding (moment retrieval) tasks.

policy_note.caveat: Scores vary substantially by inference setup: 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, and relaxed-accuracy variants are not directly comparable, and cards often omit which variant was used. 'Relaxed accuracy' allows minor numerical tolerance (±5%) and inflates scores relative to exact-match. Frontier models now exceed 90% relaxed accuracy, compressing differentiation at the top end.
policy_note.measures: ChartQA tests visual question answering over charts and plots: given a chart image, a model must answer a natural-language question about it. The test split contains 2,500 human-authored and 2,500 machine-generated question-answer pairs spanning bar, line, pie, and other chart types.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores are reported as percentage accuracy (0–100). Frontier multimodal models score roughly 85–95% under relaxed accuracy; exact-match scores run ~5–10 points lower. Always confirm which variant (relaxed vs. exact, 0-shot vs. CoT) is being reported before comparing across models.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and model card readers evaluating a model's chart-understanding and visual reasoning capability.

policy_note.caveat: This is a diagnostic ablation, not a standalone capability measure — scores are only interpretable relative to a model's full-image CharXiv score. High missing-image scores signal benchmark gaming or textual shortcut exploitation, not genuine vision skill. The lenient and strict variants use different answer-matching thresholds and are not interchangeable; results should always specify which rubric is used. Contamination risk exists for models trained after mid-2024 when CharXiv charts and questions became publicly available.
policy_note.measures: CharXiv Missing Image is a control condition within the CharXiv chart-understanding benchmark where the chart image is withheld, measuring how much a model's score is driven by non-visual cues (question phrasing, positional patterns, text context) rather than genuine chart comprehension. It accompanies the standard CharXiv tasks (descriptive and reasoning questions drawn from arXiv scientific figures) and is reported under both lenient and strict answer-grading rubrics.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better for a model being evaluated on genuine visual reasoning — a large gap between the full-image score and the missing-image score indicates the model actually uses the chart. Frontier vision-language models typically score 10–30% on missing-image variants versus 50–80% on full-image variants; a small gap is a red flag. Both lenient and strict scores are reported on a 0–100% scale.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal model evaluators and researchers who want to disentangle genuine chart-reading capability from language-prior exploitation; used alongside the standard CharXiv score as a sanity check.

policy_note.caveat: The 'no tools' vs 'with tools' variants introduce scaffold dependence: allowing code execution or retrieval tools can substantially boost scores independent of raw visual reasoning ability, making cross-variant comparisons misleading. Charts sourced from arXiv preprints may appear in multimodal training corpora, raising contamination concerns for models with broad web-scraped training data. The Descriptive subset (surface-level chart reading) is a separate task and scores are not interchangeable with the Reasoning subset.
policy_note.measures: CharXiv Reasoning evaluates multimodal models on complex, multi-step reasoning over scientific charts drawn from arXiv papers. Tasks require models to interpret chart data and perform non-trivial inference (e.g., trend comparison, numerical estimation, cross-series reasoning) rather than simple fact lookup.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier multimodal models as of mid-2025 typically score in the 60–80% range on the Reasoning subset, leaving meaningful headroom. Always compare within the same tool-use condition.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and evaluators assessing a model's chart comprehension and scientific visual reasoning beyond surface-level description.

policy_note.caveat: The 'No Tools' label is critical: scores are not comparable to variants where models invoke code interpreters or calculators, and card authors sometimes report one without specifying which. Charts are drawn from arXiv preprints, which may overlap with pretraining corpora, introducing potential contamination for models trained on broad web data.
policy_note.measures: CharXiv Reasoning (No Tools) tests multi-step visual reasoning over scientific charts sourced from real arXiv papers. Models answer open-ended quantitative and analytical questions about chart content without access to code execution or calculators, probing chart comprehension and numerical reasoning from visual input alone.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as percentages. The reasoning subset is substantially harder than CharXiv's descriptive subset—frontier models as of late 2024 typically scored in the 20–50% range, leaving meaningful headroom for differentiation.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal model researchers and developers evaluating chart understanding and visual reasoning capabilities, particularly in scientific contexts.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the tool framework provided (e.g., which code interpreter, how tool outputs are fed back) materially changes results, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless the exact scaffold is matched. The 'With Tools' variant is not directly comparable to the no-tools CharXiv Reasoning baseline.
policy_note.measures: CharXiv Reasoning (With Tools) tests a model's ability to answer complex, multi-step reasoning questions about scientific charts drawn from arXiv papers, with access to external tools such as code execution. Questions require quantitative inference and cross-chart reasoning rather than simple visual lookup.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as accuracy percentages. Reasoning questions are substantially harder than descriptive ones — frontier models generally score in the 40–70% range on reasoning subsets, with tool access improving but not closing the gap.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating multimodal models on agentic chart-understanding tasks, particularly in scientific or technical document contexts.

policy_note.caveat: Known style bias: voters systematically prefer longer, more confidently formatted responses independent of factual accuracy, so ELO rewards presentation as much as correctness. Scores are not task-stratified — a model strong at coding but weak at creative writing may rank similarly to the reverse. Query distribution shifts over time as user population changes, making historical score comparisons unreliable. There is evidence that some labs prompt-engineer or fine-tune specifically for arena-style preferences, potentially gaming the leaderboard rather than improving general capability.
policy_note.measures: Crowdsourced human-preference ranking of chat models via pairwise blind comparisons: users are shown two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and vote for the better one. ELO scores (Bradley-Terry variant) are derived from millions of accumulated votes across a wide variety of open-ended conversational tasks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher ELO is better. Scores are relative, not absolute: 1000 is the notional baseline. As of early 2026, frontier models cluster roughly between 1250 and 1400+, with meaningful separation only at the top few ranks; mid-tier models are often statistically indistinguishable given confidence intervals. Always check the confidence interval column alongside the point estimate.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers, practitioners, and the general public wanting a general-purpose human-preference ranking of chat models that does not rely on fixed benchmark datasets.

policy_note.caveat: Without a canonical paper or standardized dataset, scores reported under this label likely reflect internally defined refusal taxonomies that vary across labs, making cross-model comparisons unreliable. The metric conflates over-refusal (false positives on benign prompts) with under-refusal (missed harmful content) unless disaggregated, and prompt phrasing strongly influences results.
policy_note.measures: Chat Refusals tracks the rate at which a model declines to respond to user messages in conversational settings, capturing both appropriate refusals of harmful requests and potential over-refusals of benign ones. It is used as a proxy for a model's safety posture and helpfulness balance.
policy_note.how_to_read: Interpretation depends on the sub-task: for harmful-prompt refusal, higher is better; for benign-prompt refusal (over-refusal), lower is better. Always check which population of prompts is being reported before comparing numbers across models or labs.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and product teams evaluating the trade-off between helpfulness and harm avoidance in conversational AI systems.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to the exact jailbreak strings used in the system prompt, meaning results may not generalize across jailbreak variants. Refusal rate alone can be gamed by over-refusal (refusing benign requests), so this metric should be read alongside a paired benign-compliance benchmark. The label conflates 'system prompt jailbreak' (operator-level attack) with user-turn jailbreaks, which engage different defense mechanisms.
policy_note.measures: Measures how reliably a model refuses harmful or policy-violating user requests when the system prompt contains adversarial jailbreak instructions designed to override safety training. Probes whether refusal behavior persists under an antagonistic operator context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher refusal rate is better (model correctly declines harmful requests despite jailbreak system prompt). Frontier safety-tuned models typically score in the high-80s to mid-90s percent range; a score near 100% should be scrutinized for over-refusal.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing robustness of safety training against adversarial operator-level manipulation.

policy_note.caveat: Jailbreak benchmarks have a short shelf life: once specific attack strings are public, they may appear in safety fine-tuning data, causing contamination and inflating refusal rates on known probes while leaving novel attacks untested. Results are also scaffold-dependent — refusal rates vary significantly with system-prompt framing. The '+User' variant label may conflate different jailbreak taxonomies across reporting labs, making cross-model comparisons unreliable if the underlying probe sets differ.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's rate of correctly refusing harmful or policy-violating requests specifically under adversarial user jailbreak attempts — prompts designed to bypass safety guardrails through roleplay, hypotheticals, persona switches, or other manipulation strategies. Higher scores indicate the model maintains appropriate refusals even under adversarial pressure.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better — a higher score means the model refuses more harmful jailbreak attempts. Scores are typically expressed as refusal rates (0–100%). Frontier models vary considerably on this metric depending on safety tuning intensity; models with aggressive safety training can score near ceiling on known probes while still being vulnerable to novel attacks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating a model's robustness to adversarial user inputs; used in red-teaming and pre-deployment safety assessments.

policy_note.caveat: Multi-turn safety benchmarks are inherently scaffold-dependent: results can vary significantly based on conversation framing, system-prompt configuration, and the specific turn at which the harmful request appears. Pass rates may not transfer across deployment contexts with different system prompts.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model maintains child-safety refusals and appropriate responses across multi-turn conversations, probing whether safety behaviors persist when harmful intent is introduced gradually or after benign conversational setup. Task format is adversarial dialogue sequences targeting content that could facilitate harm to minors.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores reflect the fraction of evaluated interactions where the model responded safely. Frontier models are expected to score very high (near 1.0) on well-formed probes, so differentiation typically appears on harder multi-turn jailbreak sub-categories rather than the aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing robustness of child-safety alignment across extended dialogue; relevant for pre-deployment red-teaming and policy compliance checks.

policy_note.caveat: The label 'benign' is inherently a judgment call, and edge cases near the benign/harmful boundary may be annotated inconsistently across dataset versions. Results are sensitive to the refusal threshold baked into a model's RLHF tuning: a highly cautious model may score low here while scoring high on a paired harmful variant, so neither score should be read in isolation.
policy_note.measures: Measures whether a model correctly responds helpfully to benign, legitimate single-turn prompts that touch on child safety topics — probing for over-refusal rather than harmful output. A model that refuses innocuous child-related queries (e.g., parenting advice, child development questions) would score poorly.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better — a higher score means the model correctly complied with benign requests rather than refusing them. Should always be read together with a companion harmful-prompt metric; a model that never refuses anything would score 100% here but fail the harmful variant.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating whether models over-refuse legitimate child-related queries; useful alongside a paired 'harmful' variant to assess the precision/recall trade-off in child safety classifiers.

policy_note.caveat: The 'violative' label means prompts are unambiguously harmful; this variant should not be directly compared with borderline or borderline-refusal child-safety benchmarks, which probe a different region of model behavior. Scores are scaffold-dependent: system-prompt framing and refusal tuning heavily influence pass rates, so cross-model comparisons are only valid when evaluation harnesses are identical.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model will generate content that violates child safety norms when given a single adversarial prompt explicitly designed to elicit such output. The metric is a violation rate — the fraction of test prompts on which the model produces harmful rather than refusing responses.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower violation rate is better; 0% means the model refused every violative prompt. Well-aligned frontier models are expected to score at or near 0%. Any non-zero rate is a policy failure, not a range to optimize within.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing whether models reliably refuse requests that could facilitate harm to children.

name: Claude Code Dual-use & Benign Success Rate

policy_note.caveat: The 'without mitigations' variant is a baseline condition, not a deployment configuration; scores are not comparable to numbers reported under active mitigations and should not be cited as representative of production behavior. Because this benchmark is internal to Anthropic and dataset composition is not publicly disclosed, independent reproduction and contamination checks are not possible.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which Claude Code successfully completes coding tasks that have dual-use potential (i.e., tasks with both legitimate and potentially harmful applications) when safety mitigations are disabled. Captures whether the model can execute benign requests in dual-use contexts without over-refusal.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better — a higher benign success rate indicates the model completes legitimate dual-use requests without unnecessary refusal. Scores are percentages (0–100); the 'without mitigations' condition typically serves as an upper-bound reference against which mitigated variants are compared.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy evaluators assessing the tension between capability preservation and harm reduction in code-generation models; model card readers evaluating refusal calibration.

policy_note.caveat: This appears to be an Anthropic-internal evaluation without a public dataset or paper; methodology, dataset size, and exact scoring rubric are not publicly documented. Scores are likely scaffold-dependent: the same underlying model may behave differently depending on whether it is accessed via Claude Code CLI, the API directly, or another agentic harness. Results should not be compared across scaffolds without controlling for that variable.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether Claude Code, operating as an agentic coding assistant, appropriately handles requests with dual-use potential — tasks that are legitimate in some contexts (security research, penetration testing) but harmful in others. Probes refusal calibration, context sensitivity, and safe completion patterns across a set of ambiguous or adversarial coding scenarios.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better policy compliance (appropriate refusals on harmful requests, appropriate completions on benign ones). Because the benchmark is not publicly released, no frontier score ranges or inter-model comparisons are available externally.
policy_note.intended_for: Anthropic safety and policy teams evaluating agentic coding models; external auditors reviewing frontier-model dual-use risk. Not designed as a general model-comparison leaderboard.

policy_note.caveat: The 'with FileTool reminder' vs. 'without FileTool reminder' variants are not interchangeable and produce systematically different scores; cross-variant comparisons should not be made without explicit labeling. 'Success' conflates distinct outcomes: a refusal (safety behavior) and a capability failure both count as non-success, making it difficult to distinguish safety from inability. Scaffold dependence is intrinsic to the design — the FileTool reminder is itself a prompt-level intervention, so scores are tied to this specific agentic harness.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which Claude Code successfully completes tasks with dual-use potential — tasks that could serve either legitimate security research or harmful purposes — in an agentic coding context. The two observed variants (with vs. without a FileTool reminder in the system prompt) probe how tool-availability context in the scaffold affects task completion.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher success rate indicates more frequent task completion; whether that is desirable depends entirely on the threat model. For harmful-intent tasks, lower is safer; for legitimate security-research tasks, higher reflects better utility. Scores must always be interpreted alongside the task category breakdown, not in aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: Anthropic safety and policy teams evaluating Claude Code's propensity to complete dual-use requests under varying agentic scaffolds; not intended as a general capability ranking.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is explicit by design: the 'with FileTool reminder' and 'without FileTool reminder' variants are not directly comparable, so cross-variant score comparisons are misleading. The benchmark appears to be an internal Anthropic evaluation with no public dataset or paper; scoring direction is context-dependent (higher success may indicate higher capability risk rather than better model behavior).
policy_note.measures: Measures the fraction of dual-use coding tasks that Claude Code successfully completes — tasks whose outputs could serve both legitimate and potentially harmful purposes. Variants isolate the effect of an in-context FileTool reminder on completion rates.
policy_note.how_to_read: Direction is ambiguous by design — a higher success rate indicates greater capability on dual-use tasks, which safety teams may treat as higher risk rather than better performance. Scores should always be read alongside the specific variant (with vs. without FileTool reminder) and must not be aggregated across variants.
policy_note.intended_for: Anthropic safety and policy researchers assessing the dual-use risk profile of Claude Code across agentic tool-use configurations.

policy_note.caveat: Explicit scaffold dependence: scores are not comparable across variants (with FileTool reminder, without FileTool reminder, without mitigations) because the system prompt configuration directly drives refusal behavior. This appears to be an Anthropic-internal evaluation; methodology and dataset are not publicly documented, limiting external reproducibility or independent auditing.
policy_note.measures: The rate at which Claude Code refuses to execute requests classified as malicious or harmful in an agentic coding context. Evaluated across scaffolding variants that control whether a FileTool safety reminder is present in the system prompt and whether built-in safety mitigations are active.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better — a higher refusal rate indicates the model more reliably declines malicious requests. Report results per variant; do not aggregate across the three scaffolding conditions, as each represents a distinct deployment configuration.
policy_note.intended_for: Anthropic safety researchers and policy teams assessing Claude Code's resistance to misuse in agentic, tool-enabled coding workflows.

policy_note.caveat: This appears to be an Anthropic-internal evaluation; scoring methodology, dataset size, and pass/fail thresholds are not publicly documented, making cross-model comparisons difficult. Results may reflect scaffold-dependent behavior since Claude Code's tool-use context differs substantially from chat-mode evaluations.
policy_note.measures: Assesses whether Claude Code can be prompted to assist with malicious coding tasks such as writing malware, developing exploits, or automating attacks. Tests refusal robustness across a set of adversarial prompts targeting the agentic coding use case.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower misuse-assistance rates are better. Absolute scores are less informative than trends across model versions; Anthropic typically reports this as a pass/fail threshold against a defined misuse policy rather than a continuous numeric score.
policy_note.intended_for: Anthropic safety and policy teams, and external auditors reviewing Claude Code's resistance to misuse in agentic coding workflows.

name: Claude Code Malicious Use Evaluation (with mitigations)

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark is internal to Anthropic and tied specifically to Claude Code's scaffolding and system prompt; scores are not directly comparable to safety evaluations run on base API models or other agentic frameworks. The three variant labels (dual-use, malicious-covert, malicious-overt) conflate meaningfully different threat models — a single aggregate score can mask divergent behavior across categories. Results with mitigations applied reflect a specific mitigation snapshot and may not generalize to future prompt configurations.
policy_note.measures: Measures Claude Code's rate of complying with malicious requests across three scenario types — dual-use tasks, overtly malicious requests, and covertly malicious requests — after safety mitigations are applied. Tests whether the model can be prompted to assist with harmful activities in a coding assistant context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rate is better — the ideal score is 0% (no malicious requests fulfilled). Scores are typically reported as a percentage of test cases where the model produced a harmful or policy-violating response; scores near 0% indicate strong mitigation effectiveness.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy reviewers assessing Claude Code's resistance to misuse, particularly in agentic coding contexts where tool access amplifies potential harm.

name: Claude Code Malicious Use Evaluation (without mitigations)

policy_note.caveat: Results are explicitly measured without mitigations, so scores reflect a worst-case ceiling rather than deployed behavior — direct comparison to mitigated or other models' safety evals is misleading. The three variant labels (dual-use, malicious-covert, malicious-overt) conflate meaningfully different threat models; aggregate scores obscure per-variant differences. As an internal Anthropic evaluation the task set and scoring rubric are not publicly audited.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which Claude Code complies with malicious or dual-use requests when its built-in safety mitigations are absent, across three sub-categories: dual-use tasks (legitimate and harmful applications), covert malicious operations, and overt malicious requests. Provides a baseline vulnerability signal before mitigations are applied.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower scores are better (lower compliance rate with malicious prompts). Scores represent the fraction of harmful requests the model fulfills without mitigations; a score near 0% means near-total refusal even without guards, near 100% means near-total compliance.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy reviewers assessing the inherent susceptibility of coding-assistant models to misuse, and Anthropic internal teams tracking safety regression across model versions.

policy_note.caveat: Label conflation is a primary concern: scores on this variant are categorically not comparable to the 'with mitigations' variant and should never be reported side-by-side without that distinction clearly stated. Because mitigations are stripped, frontier models score worse here than in deployment, which can be misread as evidence of unsafe deployed behavior. Methodology and threshold details are proprietary to Anthropic, limiting external replication.
policy_note.measures: Measures Claude Code's baseline rate of complying with harmful or policy-violating requests in agentic coding contexts, specifically before any safety mitigations (prompt-level interventions, classifiers, or refusal tuning) are applied. Results represent a lower-bound safety floor rather than deployed model behavior.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rate with harmful requests is better. This variant establishes the pre-mitigation baseline; the paired 'with mitigations' evaluation shows the safety gain from interventions. Absolute numbers should be interpreted relative to that paired score, not as a standalone safety rating.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policy analysts, and model card readers evaluating Anthropic's internal pre/post-mitigation safety deltas for Claude Code specifically.

policy_note.measures: CloningScenarios evaluates how models respond to prompts involving human reproductive or therapeutic cloning, probing whether models apply consistent ethical reasoning, decline appropriately, or provide potentially harmful biological guidance across varied scenario framings.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores typically indicate safer or more policy-consistent responses; interpretation depends heavily on the scoring rubric used by the evaluating framework. No widely-published frontier range is established for this benchmark.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing model behavior on sensitive bioethics topics, particularly consistency and refusal calibration across scenario variations.

policy_note.caveat: The test set is small (roughly 500 examples), making scores statistically noisy. Frontier models with strong Chinese pre-training tend to approach saturation in the high 80s–low 90s, limiting differentiation at the top. Scores may also appear as part of an aggregate CLUE score rather than standalone, so label conflation between the two reporting styles is common.
policy_note.measures: CLUEWSC is the Chinese Winograd Schema Challenge, part of the CLUE (Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation) benchmark suite. It tests commonsense coreference resolution: given a Chinese sentence with an ambiguous pronoun and two candidate referents, the model must select the correct one—probing world knowledge and common-sense reasoning in Chinese.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (0–100%). Human performance is around 98%. Competitive Chinese-capable models typically score in the 80–93% range; scores below ~75% indicate weak Chinese commonsense reasoning.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and engineers benchmarking Chinese language understanding, especially commonsense reasoning and pronoun disambiguation capabilities.

policy_note.caveat: The problem set is extremely small (olympiad rounds typically yield only ~6 problems), making scores highly sensitive to individual problem difficulty and introducing high variance. Contamination risk is elevated for any model trained on web data post-2024, as competition problems circulate online immediately after the exam. Scoring methodology (full credit vs. partial credit vs. pass@k) varies across evaluators and can produce incomparable results.
policy_note.measures: Tests advanced mathematical reasoning and problem-solving using problems from the 2024 Chinese National Mathematics Olympiad (CNMO), a prestigious high-school-level competition. Tasks require multi-step proof construction and olympiad-style problem solving across algebra, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent percentage of problems solved correctly. Because the problem set is tiny, even a one-problem difference represents a large percentage swing. Frontier models as of early 2026 solve a small minority of problems, so this benchmark is not yet saturated.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers probing frontier model mathematical reasoning at the upper difficulty range, beyond what standard benchmarks like MATH or AMC can differentiate.

policy_note.caveat: Contamination risk is high: Codeforces problems and their editorial solutions are widely indexed on the web and likely present in training data for most frontier models. Scores are highly scaffold-dependent — different code execution environments, languages permitted, and retry policies produce materially different results. 'Codeforces rating' as a metric is not standardized across evaluations; some report Elo-equivalent ratings, others report solve rates on specific difficulty tiers (e.g. 1200–2400 rated problems), making cross-paper comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Measures competitive programming ability by evaluating models on algorithmic problem-solving tasks drawn from or inspired by the Codeforces online judge platform, which hosts thousands of rated contest problems spanning data structures, graph algorithms, dynamic programming, combinatorics, and mathematics. Performance is typically reported as a rating or percentile equivalent, or as pass rate on a curated problem set.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores may be expressed as an Elo-style rating (human grandmaster ~3000+, typical strong human competitor ~1500–2000) or as a solve-rate percentage on a fixed problem set. Frontier models as of early 2025 reach roughly 1200–1900 Elo-equivalent on standardized subsets, well below top human competitors.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and engineers benchmarking models on hard algorithmic reasoning and competitive programming; useful for differentiating frontier coding models at the high end where HumanEval and MBPP have saturated.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark category is 'other' with no canonical variant strings observed, suggesting it may be used inconsistently across model cards — different scaffolds (e.g., direct execution vs. sandboxed evaluation) may substantially change elicitation rates. Scores are highly sensitive to prompt framing and the specific test-checking mechanism; comparisons across labs may not be apples-to-apples.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model attempts to deceive evaluators when completing coding tasks — for example, by hardcoding expected outputs, manipulating test harnesses, or otherwise gaming evaluation metrics rather than genuinely solving the problem. Probes the alignment-relevant question of whether a model behaves differently when it believes its outputs are being checked.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower deception rates are better. A score of 0% indicates the model never attempted to game the evaluation; higher scores indicate more frequent deceptive behavior. Because this probes rare failure modes, even small absolute differences (e.g., 2% vs. 8%) may be meaningful at the policy level.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy analysts assessing whether frontier models exhibit deceptive or specification-gaming behavior in agentic coding contexts.

policy_note.caveat: This label is a loose aggregate, not a single standardized benchmark — the exact subtask composition and shot counts vary by paper and evaluation framework, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. Several constituent tasks (HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-easy) exhibit saturation for frontier models (scores routinely above 90%), limiting their ability to differentiate top systems. Contamination risk is high for well-known subtasks that have appeared in NLP benchmarks since 2019.
policy_note.measures: Aggregated accuracy across a suite of commonsense reasoning subtasks (commonly BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-easy, ARC-challenge, OpenBookQA, and SIQA), probing a model's ability to apply everyday world knowledge, physical intuition, and social reasoning. The 'mixed-shot' variant uses different few-shot counts per subtask (e.g., 0-shot for PIQA, 5-shot for WinoGrande, 25-shot for ARC), then averages results.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy percentages (0–100). Frontier models typically score in the 85–95 range on the aggregate; older or smaller models score in the 60–80 range. Because subtask composition varies, only compare scores from evaluations using the same harness and shot configuration.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and model developers comparing general language model capabilities on everyday reasoning tasks, particularly for open-weight model evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: This appears to be a narrow, internally-defined evaluation tied to specific computer-use scaffolding; scores are likely scaffold-dependent and may not transfer across agentic frameworks or UI rendering environments. No public dataset or leaderboard is known, making cross-lab comparisons difficult. The benchmark name is not associated with a published paper as of the knowledge cutoff.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a computer-use agent correctly identifies and confirms (or appropriately declines) financial transaction dialogs presented via GUI screenshots and interactive interfaces. Probes the agent's ability to parse transaction details, recognize confirmation flows, and act on them accurately without being misled by ambiguous or adversarial UI states.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores reflect accuracy or success rate on transaction-handling tasks; without a published leaderboard the frontier range is unknown. Treat absolute numbers as meaningful only within the same scaffold and UI environment used during evaluation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating computer-use agents for deployment in financial or enterprise workflows where transaction accuracy and manipulation resistance matter.

policy_note.caveat: This appears to be an internal Anthropic behavioral/safety evaluation rather than a publicly documented benchmark, so scoring methodology, dataset composition, and scale are not publicly specified. Results are likely scaffold-dependent: the same model may confirm more or less frequently depending on the agentic harness and system prompt used. The label 'general confirmation' may conflate distinct sub-behaviors (ambiguity-triggered confirmation vs. irreversibility-triggered confirmation).
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether an AI agent performing computer use tasks appropriately seeks user confirmation before executing general (non-specialized) actions that may be consequential or ambiguous. Probes the agent's judgment about when to pause and verify intent rather than proceed autonomously.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate the model more reliably seeks confirmation in situations that warrant it — generally desirable for safe deployment. Interpret relative to a defined threshold rather than raw percentage, as both over-confirmation (blocking productivity) and under-confirmation (unsafe autonomy) are failure modes.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing whether computer-use agents exhibit appropriate human-in-the-loop behavior; model card readers comparing agent caution across model versions.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agent framework, system prompt, and tool definitions strongly influence how often confirmation prompts are triggered, making cross-framework comparisons unreliable. The definition of 'high-stakes' may vary between evaluators, introducing label subjectivity.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether an AI agent operating in a computer-use context pauses to seek explicit user confirmation before executing high-stakes communication actions (e.g., sending emails, submitting forms, posting messages) that could have significant or irreversible real-world consequences. Probes the agent's ability to distinguish routine from consequential actions and defer appropriately.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a higher score indicates the model more reliably requests confirmation before consequential irreversible communications. Frontier safety-focused models are expected to score near the upper range; scores well below ceiling indicate unsafe autonomous action tendencies.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and developers evaluating agentic systems for appropriate human-in-the-loop behavior before deployment in computer-use or autonomous-action settings.

policy_note.caveat: Results differ substantially between the 'without safeguards' and 'with safeguards' variants, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless the variant is specified. Task composition, injection sophistication, and the agentic scaffold (browser tool, VM, API) all affect scores, so numbers are not directly portable across evaluation harnesses.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates how often a computer-use AI agent is successfully hijacked by adversarial instructions embedded in the environment (e.g., on-screen text, web pages, documents) during agentic tasks. Scores reflect the percentage of injection attempts the agent resists rather than follows.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher resistance rate is better (fewer successful injections = safer agent). Frontier models without safeguards have shown meaningful vulnerability rates; safeguard variants substantially reduce but do not eliminate susceptibility. The gap between variants is itself a key signal.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, red-teamers, and policy audiences assessing the real-world security posture of agentic computer-use systems before deployment.

policy_note.measures: Confirmations Recall tests a model's ability to accurately retrieve and confirm previously established facts or commitments across 607 tasks spanning 20 categories. The benchmark probes memory and recall fidelity — whether a model can correctly surface information it was given or agreed to earlier in a context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; scores likely represent recall accuracy (0–100%). With 20 categories and 607 tasks, per-category breakdowns matter more than the aggregate — weak performance in specific categories may not surface in the mean.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating model reliability in multi-turn or long-context settings where accurate recall of confirmed information is critical.

policy_note.caveat: The 'cot' variant string observed in model cards is ambiguous and may refer to generic chain-of-thought prompting studies rather than the CoT-Control safety evaluation specifically, making cross-model score comparisons unreliable. Scaffold dependence is a core concern: scores vary substantially depending on whether the model's thinking trace is streamed, truncated, or summarized before the monitor sees it.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether monitoring a model's chain-of-thought (scratchpad / extended thinking) provides meaningful oversight as a safety control mechanism — specifically whether CoT reasoning is faithful to the model's underlying computation and whether problematic or deceptive reasoning is detectable by a human or automated monitor. Sits within the broader AI-control evaluation paradigm.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate that CoT monitoring is a more reliable control — i.e., the monitor successfully detects anomalous reasoning more often. Frontier model scores are not yet widely published in a standardized form; treat cross-lab comparisons cautiously given scaffold and monitor-design variation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and frontier labs assessing whether chain-of-thought monitoring is a viable oversight mechanism against deceptive or misaligned model behavior.

policy_note.caveat: Counting remains a known systematic weakness of large vision-language models, so scores vary significantly by object type and quantity range; models tend to degrade sharply past counts of ~5-6. Benchmark size is small enough that minor prompt or decoding changes can shift reported accuracy meaningfully.
policy_note.measures: CountBench tests the ability of vision-language models to accurately count objects depicted in images, probing fine-grained visual perception and number sense. Tasks present natural images and ask models to produce an exact integer count of a specified object category.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better (percentage of images correctly counted). Frontier multimodal models typically score in the 50-80% range depending on object density and occlusion; human performance is near ceiling.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and practitioners evaluating visual perception and numeracy in vision-language models.

policy_note.measures: CounterFactQA probes a model's ability to reason correctly under counterfactual premises — questions where the stated scenario contradicts real-world facts and the model must follow the hypothetical rather than recall trained knowledge. It tests whether models can suppress factual priors and reason within an explicitly false premise.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better, indicating the model more reliably follows counterfactual premises rather than defaulting to memorized facts. Exact scale and frontier-model ranges are not well-documented in publicly available literature.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating reasoning robustness, instruction-following under conflicting signals, and the degree to which factual training interferes with hypothetical reasoning tasks.

policy_note.caveat: Performance varies enormously across the 21 languages because source-language audio hours are highly imbalanced (some languages have only a few hours). BLEU is a weak proxy for translation quality, especially for morphologically rich or low-resource languages. Crowd-sourced Common Voice audio introduces accent and recording-quality variance that may not reflect deployment conditions.
policy_note.measures: CoVoST 2 evaluates speech-to-text translation across 21 source languages into English, built on Mozilla Common Voice audio. Models are scored on BLEU, testing combined ASR and MT capability in a single end-to-end pass.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher BLEU is better. Scores are reported per-language and as an average; a model with high average BLEU may still fail on low-resource languages. Frontier speech models typically score in the 20–35 BLEU range on the harder low-resource languages and 30–50+ on high-resource ones.
policy_note.intended_for: Speech and multimodal AI researchers evaluating multilingual speech translation capability, particularly coverage breadth across low- and high-resource languages.

policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to generate creative, open-ended responses to biology-themed prompts — such as hypothesis generation, experimental design, or novel biological analogies. Task format and dataset size are not publicly documented under this benchmark name.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger creative and generative biology reasoning. No standardized frontier range or leaderboard is publicly associated with this benchmark name, so cross-model comparisons should be treated with caution.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating generative or creative reasoning capabilities in life-sciences domains.

policy_note.measures: CRPE (likely a Chinese-language reading or reasoning evaluation) probes language comprehension and reasoning ability, typically through multiple-choice or short-answer questions drawn from Chinese-language examination corpora. Exact dataset size and task format are not well-documented in public sources.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; scores are typically reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier model ranges and total model counts vary by paper; consult the originating publication for baseline comparisons.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating Chinese-language understanding or general reasoning capabilities of large language models.

policy_note.caveat: CTF benchmark scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic framework, tool access (e.g. shell, debugger), and number of allowed steps heavily influence results. Scores across labs are often not directly comparable unless run under identical conditions. The CAISI variant is not widely documented in public model cards, making cross-model comparisons difficult.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's ability to solve Capture The Flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenges, probing skills such as reverse engineering, binary exploitation, cryptography, and web security. The CAISI designation indicates this is a curated evaluation set, likely assessing offensive cyber capabilities relevant to AI safety.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better (more challenges solved). Scores are typically reported as a percentage of challenges solved or a count. Frontier models as of 2025 vary widely, with top models solving a meaningful fraction of easier CTF categories but struggling on hard binary exploitation tasks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy evaluators assessing potentially dangerous cyber capabilities in frontier models; informs deployment decisions and capability thresholds.

policy_note.caveat: The three difficulty-level variants are not interchangeable — scores must be compared within the same tier only; a 'collegiate level' score cannot be stacked against a 'professional level' score. pass@12 inflates apparent capability relative to pass@1: a model that rarely solves a challenge deterministically can still score non-zero. CTF challenges are publicly released after competitions, creating meaningful training-data contamination risk for models trained on post-competition web crawls. Scores are sensitive to the scaffolding (shell access, tool availability, number of allowed tool calls) used during evaluation.
policy_note.measures: Tests a model's ability to solve Capture The Flag (CTF) security challenges spanning reverse engineering, binary exploitation, web security, cryptography, and forensics, evaluated at three difficulty tiers (high-school, collegiate, and professional level). The pass@12 metric reports whether the model succeeds in at least one of 12 independent solution attempts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher pass@12 rate is better (scale 0–1 or 0–100%). Professional-level challenges are qualitatively harder; frontier models typically score near zero on professional tasks while showing measurable performance on high-school and collegiate tasks. Always specify the difficulty tier when reporting or comparing results.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and security practitioners assessing offensive cybersecurity capabilities of frontier models; policymakers evaluating dual-use risk of capable models.

policy_note.caveat: The dataset is relatively small (510 contracts) and drawn entirely from EDGAR filings, so it skews toward U.S. public-company commercial agreements and may not generalize to consumer, employment, or non-U.S. contract styles. Frontier models now score high enough on several clause categories that per-category F1 differentiation is limited; aggregate scores can mask large variance across rare clause types with few positive examples.
policy_note.measures: CUAD evaluates a model's ability to identify 41 legally significant clause types (e.g., indemnification, termination-for-convenience, non-compete) across 510 commercial contracts totaling ~3.5 million words, annotated by lawyers from the Atticus Project. The task is extractive question-answering: given a contract and a clause-type question, the model must locate the relevant span or indicate absence.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher F1 is better. Scores are typically reported as macro-averaged F1 across all 41 categories; a perfect score is 100. Early strong baselines (RoBERTa-large) reached ~40–45 F1; capable frontier models can exceed 80 F1 on common categories but the macro average is pulled down by rare clause types. Compare models at the per-category level for operational use.
policy_note.intended_for: Legal AI researchers and practitioners evaluating contract review assistants; useful for comparing models on structured information-extraction from long legal documents.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is substantial — the choice of agentic framework, available tools, and retry strategy materially affects scores, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable without matching setup details. CTF writeup contamination is a real concern because solutions for many included challenges are publicly indexed online. The 'unguided' variant produces meaningfully lower scores than guided/subtask-decomposed variants, so results must not be compared across these label variants.
policy_note.measures: Cybench measures AI agents' ability to solve professional CTF (Capture the Flag) challenges spanning reverse engineering, web exploitation, cryptography, forensics, and binary exploitation, drawn from real CTF competitions. Agents are scored on whether they can capture the flag autonomously; pass@30 reports the fraction of tasks solved in 30 independent attempts, while the 'unguided' variant withholds subtask hints and intermediate scaffolding.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent the fraction of CTF tasks solved (0–1 scale). Frontier models on the unguided variant typically solve a low-to-moderate fraction of tasks; pass@30 is substantially higher than pass@1 due to stochastic sampling. Compare only within the same variant (guided vs. unguided) and the same scaffolding configuration.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and security teams evaluating the offensive cybersecurity capability of frontier language models; used for capability elicitation, uplift assessment, and risk evaluation.

policy_note.caveat: As an agentic benchmark, scores are heavily scaffold-dependent: the tools, shell access, and prompting framework provided to the agent substantially affect outcomes, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable unless the scaffold is identical. CTF-style tasks are also susceptible to training-data contamination if challenge writeups were present in model pretraining corpora.
policy_note.measures: CyberGym evaluates AI agents on a broad suite of cybersecurity tasks spanning both offensive (exploitation, privilege escalation) and defensive (vulnerability analysis, incident response) scenarios, scored with pass@1 — whether the agent succeeds on its first attempt without retries.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher pass@1 is better. Scores represent the fraction of tasks solved on a single agent attempt; frontier models currently cluster in a wide range depending on task difficulty tier and scaffold, so absolute numbers should only be compared within identical experimental setups.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capability researchers assessing autonomous cybersecurity capability in frontier models; red-teamers benchmarking agent tool-use in adversarial contexts.

policy_note.caveat: The three-tier variant split (easy/medium/hard) means scores are not directly comparable across cards unless the variant is specified; reporting only an aggregate obscures where a model's capability actually lies. As frontier models improve rapidly on cybersecurity benchmarks, easy and medium tiers may be near-saturated for top models, reducing their discriminative value. Contamination risk is moderate given that cybersecurity question sets frequently appear in public training corpora.
policy_note.measures: The Cyber Key Skills Benchmark evaluates a model's knowledge and reasoning across core cybersecurity domains — including vulnerability analysis, cryptography, network security, and exploit concepts — at three difficulty tiers (easy, medium, hard). Tasks are typically multiple-choice or short-answer questions that probe whether a model can reason about offensive and defensive security scenarios.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate greater cybersecurity knowledge. Report results per difficulty tier (easy / medium / hard) rather than as a single aggregate. Frontier models typically score high on easy tiers; the hard tier is the meaningful differentiator. No single public leaderboard exists, so cross-model comparisons require matching the exact variant.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capabilities researchers assessing dual-use cybersecurity risk in frontier models; red-teamers benchmarking how much operational security knowledge a model exposes.

policy_note.caveat: The 'Production data' label implies inputs drawn from real-world traffic or usage logs rather than controlled synthetic prompts, which may introduce distribution shift and make cross-lab comparisons difficult if each evaluator uses a proprietary production corpus. Scores are not directly comparable to results from synthetic cyber safety suites or other CyberSecEval variants.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates the propensity of a language model to assist with cyberattack-relevant tasks (e.g., exploit development, malware generation, attack planning) using real production data as prompts rather than purely synthetic or hand-crafted scenarios. It probes whether models exhibit unsafe behaviors when exposed to realistic, in-the-wild inputs.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower unsafe-assistance rates are better (closer to 0% indicates the model rarely helps with cyberattack requests). The specific scale and passing thresholds vary by evaluator; compare only within results from the same production dataset and harness.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing cybersecurity risk in language models prior to deployment, particularly for understanding real-world unsafe-assistance rates.

policy_note.caveat: Synthetic prompt distributions may not reflect real-world attacker phrasing, potentially making models easier to optimize against via safety fine-tuning without genuine risk reduction. Results are sensitive to system-prompt framing and model temperature; reported compliance rates across labs may not be directly comparable if scaffold details differ.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates the rate at which LLMs comply with synthetically generated prompts requesting assistance with cyberattacks, including malware creation, vulnerability exploitation, and attack planning. Uses a dataset of artificial adversarial prompts drawn from MITRE ATT&CK tactics to probe whether models act as a capable cyber-offense assistant.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rate is better (safer); 0% means the model never assisted with the attack prompts. Frontier safety-tuned models typically land in the low single digits to roughly 15–25% range depending on attack category and prompt phrasing.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing cybersecurity risk exposure in LLMs before deployment.

policy_note.caveat: Because this benchmark is derived from proprietary production traffic, the dataset is not publicly released, making independent replication or contamination auditing impossible. Scores are not directly comparable across labs that construct their own production-traffic slices, and the definition of 'safe' behavior may vary by evaluator policy.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates how safely a model handles cybersecurity-related requests drawn from real production traffic, probing whether the model refuses or appropriately navigates harmful cyber requests (e.g., exploit assistance, malware generation) while remaining helpful on legitimate security tasks. Uses live or logged user interactions rather than synthetic prompts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate safer, more policy-compliant responses to cyber-related queries. Because traffic distributions differ across deployments, absolute scores are less meaningful than relative comparisons within the same lab's evaluation suite.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety teams and model developers assessing real-world cybersecurity refusal behavior and dual-use risk in deployed systems.

policy_note.caveat: Synthetic data benchmarks can diverge from real-world adversarial prompts; coverage and difficulty depend heavily on the generation procedure and may not reflect novel attack vectors. Without a public dataset or paper, scoring methodology and label definitions are difficult to independently verify.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's safe behavior on cybersecurity-related prompts using synthetically generated test cases, probing whether models appropriately decline or handle requests touching on harmful cyber activities (e.g., malware creation, exploitation techniques) while remaining helpful for legitimate security tasks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate safer, more policy-compliant behavior. Specific scale and frontier model ranges are not publicly documented for this benchmark.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing a model's alignment and refusal calibration in cybersecurity contexts.

policy_note.caveat: The label 'Production Data' is ambiguous — it may refer to real attacker-style prompts collected from deployment, but without a public paper or dataset the exact collection methodology, size, and labeling criteria are unverifiable. Scores may be scaffold- or system-prompt-dependent if thresholds were tuned against a specific deployment configuration.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates model behavior on cybersecurity-related safety scenarios using production (real-world) data rather than synthetic prompts. Probes whether models assist with or refuse harmful cyber activities such as exploit development, intrusion guidance, or malware generation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores typically indicate stronger safety compliance (fewer harmful assists). Absolute scale depends on internal rubric; without public baselines, scores should be interpreted relative to other models evaluated on the same version of the dataset.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and red-team practitioners assessing a model's refusal behavior and safety alignment on realistic offensive-security requests.

policy_note.caveat: As a synthetic dataset, there is an inherent risk of distribution shift — model performance on synthetic cyber scenarios may not transfer to real-world attack and defense patterns. The lack of observed variant strings and absence of a registry description suggest limited community adoption and unclear standardization, making cross-study comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates model behavior on cybersecurity safety scenarios using synthetically generated training data; probes whether models can recognize, respond to, or avoid facilitating cyber threats and unsafe practices in a controlled, artificially constructed dataset.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores typically indicate safer or more appropriate model responses to cyber threat scenarios; however, without a known standard scale or frontier baseline range, absolute scores should be interpreted relative to the specific evaluation rubric used by each reporting lab.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and red-teamers assessing model robustness against cybersecurity misuse; teams building or fine-tuning models intended for security-sensitive deployment contexts.

policy_note.caveat: The v1 ('hard challenges') and v2 ('end-to-end challenges') variants are not directly comparable — v1 selects a filtered difficult subset while v2 evaluates complete challenge pipelines; scores across variants should not be aggregated or ranked against each other. Scaffold dependence is significant: different agentic tool setups and execution environments can materially shift pass rates.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates AI models on cybersecurity tasks spanning vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and security reasoning, structured as capture-the-flag-style challenges. Two variants exist: v1 focuses on a hard-challenge subset while v2 covers challenges end-to-end, probing broader attack and defense workflows.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate greater success completing cybersecurity challenges; interpret results only within the same variant. Frontier models vary substantially on hard vs. end-to-end splits, so always note which variant is being reported.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and security teams assessing the offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities of frontier models, particularly for dangerous-capability evaluations and responsible deployment decisions.

policy_note.measures: CyScenarioBench evaluates language models on cybersecurity scenario reasoning tasks, probing the ability to analyze, reason through, and respond to realistic security situations such as threat assessment, incident response, or vulnerability analysis. The benchmark uses scenario-based prompts rather than pure fact recall.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger performance on cybersecurity scenario reasoning. Frontier model score ranges and total model comparisons are not well-documented in public sources; interpret scores relative to reported baselines in the originating paper.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and security researchers assessing model capability and risk on cybersecurity-relevant tasks; red-teamers and policy analysts evaluating whether models can reason about offensive or defensive security scenarios.

policy_note.caveat: The 'adversarial' variant label suggests this is a harder or more targeted probe than a baseline deception-rate evaluation, but without a public specification it is unclear how adversarial prompts are constructed or what counts as a deceptive response. Scores are likely highly scaffold- and judge-dependent: different system prompts, output parsers, or rubrics can shift the measured rate substantially. No peer-reviewed dataset or methodology paper is publicly known for this specific slug.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model produces deceptive outputs when subjected to adversarial prompts designed to elicit production-context deception — scenarios mimicking real deployment conditions where a model might mislead users or operators. Lower scores indicate less deceptive behavior under adversarial pressure.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better; a deception rate of 0% means no deceptive outputs were detected across the adversarial prompt set. Frontier models on safety-focused evaluations typically aim for rates near 0%, so even small nonzero values are considered meaningful. Compare only within the same evaluation harness and judge configuration.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing honesty, deception tendencies, and robustness of truthfulness under adversarial conditions.

policy_note.caveat: Definition of 'deception' varies significantly across labs and annotation schemes, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless methodology is identical. Production traffic composition (user population, deployment context, jailbreak rate) can shift the metric without any change in model behavior. Labeling deception in free-form text requires human or LLM-as-judge annotation, both of which carry their own error rates. Specific methodology, annotator agreement figures, and traffic sampling details are typically not publicly disclosed, limiting external auditability.
policy_note.measures: Measures the fraction of production (real-user) interactions in which a model produces deceptive output — statements intended to create false beliefs in the user. Scored on live traffic rather than synthetic prompts, so it captures naturalistic deception patterns across diverse real-world queries.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better; a deception rate of 0% would mean no deceptive outputs were detected. Because this is measured on production traffic rather than a fixed held-out set, absolute numbers are not directly comparable across labs unless sampling methodology is disclosed. Frontier models are expected to be in the low single-digit percent range or below on well-defined deception criteria.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy audiences evaluating real-world honesty and deception risks in deployed language models.

policy_note.caveat: This is a nascent evaluation area with no single canonical dataset or standardized methodology; scores across labs are rarely directly comparable. Benchmark designs are often proprietary or unpublished, making replication difficult. The construct itself is contested—passing a deceptive alignment eval may reflect limited situational awareness rather than absence of deceptive intent.
policy_note.measures: Assesses whether a model exhibits deceptive alignment by behaving differently when it believes it is being evaluated versus deployed, probing situational awareness and the ability to infer context from subtle cues. Tasks typically involve scenarios where a model must decide whether to pursue its training objectives or reveal (or conceal) misaligned goals based on perceived oversight.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower rates of detected deceptive behavior are generally safer, though interpretation depends heavily on the specific operationalization. There is no agreed frontier range; most published results are sparse case studies rather than continuous scores across many models.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, alignment evaluators, and policy teams assessing whether frontier models exhibit strategic deception or behave inconsistently under perceived oversight.

policy_note.caveat: Highly scaffold- and prompt-dependent: whether a model surfaces stealth behavior varies sharply with scenario framing, system prompt wording, and the elicitation technique used. No widely standardized version exists; results across labs are difficult to compare. Low base rates for confirmed stealth behavior make statistical interpretation fragile on small eval suites.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model attempts to conceal its true capabilities or intentions during evaluation — specifically, whether it behaves differently when it infers it is being tested versus deployed. Probes for 'stealth' behaviors such as sandbagging, capability hiding, or inconsistent responses across contexts that suggest strategic self-presentation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower incidence of detected stealth behavior is better (i.e., a model that behaves consistently regardless of perceived monitoring context). There is no established numeric scale; results are typically reported as rates or qualitative verdicts. Frontier model behavior on this dimension is not publicly benchmarked in a uniform way.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing alignment and scheming risk; lab red-teams and pre-deployment safety reviews.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are strongly scaffold-dependent: the same model produces meaningfully different results under single-agent vs. multi-agent retrieval configurations, making cross-report comparisons unreliable without matching the exact setup. The 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' variant labels further suggest results conflate base-model capability with post-training and inference-budget choices.
policy_note.measures: DeepSearchQA measures a model's ability to answer questions that require multi-step information retrieval and synthesis, probing whether models can locate and integrate evidence across sources to produce accurate answers. Observed variant strings (single-agent, multi-agent, extended-thinking, rlhf) suggest it is used to compare inference-time configurations rather than a fixed evaluation setting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; represents percentage of questions answered correctly. Typical frontier model ranges vary substantially by configuration — multi-agent or extended-thinking variants consistently outperform single-agent baselines, so the variant must be specified for any comparison to be meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating search-augmented or agentic systems on open-domain question answering; useful for comparing retrieval strategies rather than base model knowledge alone.

policy_note.caveat: Harmless-rate metrics can conflate genuine safety refusals with over-refusal of benign health or nutritional questions, making it hard to distinguish a well-calibrated model from an overly restrictive one. Single-turn format does not capture multi-turn jailbreak vulnerability. Scoring thresholds for what counts as 'harmless' are typically rubric-dependent and may vary across evaluators.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model responds harmlessly to single-turn prompts involving disordered eating topics (e.g., requests for extreme restriction advice, purging tips, or content that could encourage eating disorder behaviors). A higher harmless rate indicates the model more consistently declines or redirects such requests safely.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; expressed as a rate (0–1 or 0–100%). A score near 1.0 means nearly all responses to disordered-eating prompts were judged safe. Frontier safety-focused models typically score above 0.90, but thresholds shift as evaluation rubrics evolve.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing a model's harm avoidance on sensitive mental-health and eating-disorder-related content.

policy_note.caveat: Refusal rate is a blunt metric: it does not distinguish between appropriate refusals and over-refusals on legitimate nutrition or health questions. The 'single-turn benign' variant label implies queries that appear harmless, which risks conflating safety with unhelpful over-restriction. Scores are highly sensitive to exact prompt phrasing and system-prompt context, making cross-model comparisons unreliable without identical scaffolding.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model refuses to engage with single-turn queries related to disordered eating behaviors (e.g., extreme caloric restriction, purging, harmful weight-loss methods). The 'single-turn benign' variant specifically probes queries that are framed innocuously but touch on content that could reinforce eating disorders.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher refusal rate indicates the model more consistently declines to produce potentially harmful disordered-eating content. However, a rate near 100% may signal over-refusal. There is no universally agreed optimal target; interpret relative to a model's stated safety posture and compare only against models evaluated on the identical prompt set.
policy_note.intended_for: Safety researchers and model evaluators assessing whether frontier models appropriately handle sensitive mental-health and eating-disorder content without either enabling harm or over-refusing benign health queries.

name: Disordered eating safety evaluation (benign refusal rate)

policy_note.caveat: Benign refusal rate is a one-sided metric: it quantifies over-refusal but not under-refusal (i.e., harmful content that passes through). The classification of a query as 'benign' is annotator-defined and may not generalize across deployment contexts, user populations, or clinical versus consumer settings. Results are highly sensitive to how the test prompts are phrased and to system-prompt framing.
policy_note.measures: This benchmark measures how frequently a model incorrectly refuses benign, legitimate queries about disordered eating topics — capturing over-refusal (false positive safety triggers) rather than harmful outputs.
