A lower benign refusal rate indicates the model can serve genuine users (caregivers, clinicians, harm-reduction seekers) without excessive paternalism.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better. A score of 0% means no benign queries were refused; higher scores indicate increasing over-refusal. This metric should be read alongside a corresponding harmful-content pass-through rate, since optimizing for low benign refusal in isolation can indicate under-caution.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing whether safety mitigations around eating-disorder topics cause excessive refusals that harm legitimate users.

policy_note.caveat: Harmless rate can be inflated by over-refusal: a model that declines all nutrition or health questions trivially scores high while degrading utility. Conversely, a model that gives clinically phrased but pro-restriction advice may pass surface-level classifiers. The boundary between harmful encouragement and legitimate dietary or medical information is highly threshold-dependent, so scores are sensitive to the labeling rubric used.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model produces responses deemed harmless when prompted with queries related to disordered eating behaviors (e.g., extreme restriction, purging, calorie obsession). Expressed as a percentage of evaluated prompts where the model's response did not provide harmful guidance or reinforcement.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; 100% means every evaluated response was judged harmless. Safety-focused frontier models typically target rates above 90%, but the absolute threshold considered acceptable depends on deployment context. Compare scores only across evaluations using the same prompt set and labeling rubric.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating harm-avoidance in sensitive health domains, particularly for consumer-facing deployments.

name: DNA Sequence Design for Transcription Factor Binding

policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to design DNA sequences that bind to specified transcription factors, requiring knowledge of transcription factor binding motifs, sequence-function relationships, and molecular biology. The task involves generating or optimizing nucleotide sequences to maximize predicted binding affinity or specificity for a target protein.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better ability to design sequences with desired binding properties. Scoring methodology varies by implementation (e.g., predicted binding affinity thresholds, motif match scores); interpret results relative to the specific scoring rubric used in the evaluation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating AI models for computational biology and protein-DNA interaction tasks, particularly those developing tools for synthetic biology or gene regulation research.

policy_note.caveat: Exact dataset composition and scoring rubrics vary by evaluating organization and are rarely published in full due to dual-use sensitivity, making cross-lab score comparisons unreliable. Test-set size is believed to be small (on the order of tens of scenarios), limiting statistical power. Scores are also highly prompt-framing-dependent: minor rephrasing of a query can shift a model's response, so results reflect a specific elicitation scaffold rather than a stable capability bound.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model provides meaningful assistance to actors attempting to circumvent DNA synthesis screening controls — the biosecurity safeguards used by commercial synthesis providers to block orders for dangerous pathogen or toxin sequences. Tasks typically probe whether the model will suggest codon-optimization tricks, sequence-splitting strategies, or other obfuscation techniques that defeat automated screening.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a lower score indicates the model provides less useful evasion assistance. Because any meaningful uplift in this domain is considered a serious risk, the relevant threshold is near zero rather than a relative ranking among frontier models. This is a pass/fail safety gate more than a continuous capability measure.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, biosecurity policy analysts, and frontier-lab red-team teams assessing whether models cross biosecurity risk thresholds under responsible scaling or safety policies.

policy_note.caveat: Test-set labels are held by the challenge server (not public), so results depend on submission; reported numbers across papers may use different splits (validation vs. test). Frontier multimodal models now score above 90 ANLS on the test set, approaching saturation. Performance conflates OCR quality with higher-level reasoning, so a model with strong OCR but weak reasoning can score well. The '0-shot' variant label seen in model cards is a prompting condition, not a separate dataset split.
policy_note.measures: DocVQA tests a model's ability to answer natural-language questions about scanned or photographed document images (forms, invoices, tables, reports), drawn from ~50,000 QA pairs over ~12,000 document images. Performance is scored with ANLS (Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity), rewarding near-correct text extraction and reading comprehension jointly.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher ANLS is better (scale 0–100). Human performance is ~98; strong frontier multimodal models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.x) cluster in the 88–93 range on the test set, leaving limited headroom for differentiation at the top.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multimodal models on document understanding, OCR grounding, and visually-situated reading comprehension.

policy_note.caveat: Label conflation risk is high: 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' appear as distinct variants reported under the same slug, meaning scores may reflect different model configurations rather than the same evaluation protocol — direct comparison across variants is unreliable without knowing whether task, scoring, and compute conditions are held constant.
policy_note.measures: DRACO is a benchmark of unclear provenance in this registry; no public paper or canonical description was confidently identified. Variant strings 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' suggest it is used to compare model outputs under different training regimes or inference-time compute budgets rather than measuring a single fixed capability.
policy_note.how_to_read: Direction and scale are unknown without a confirmed specification. Treat any reported scores as provisional until the benchmark definition and scoring rubric are confirmed.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers comparing RLHF-trained models against extended-thinking (chain-of-thought or test-time compute) variants on some capability or alignment dimension; specific audience unclear without a canonical source.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models now saturate DROP, with scores above 90 F1 that leave little headroom to differentiate top systems; the benchmark is no longer informative at the frontier. Evaluation is shot-count sensitive (reported as 3-shot or variable shots in model cards), making cross-report comparisons unreliable without matching the exact prompt setup. Early automatic F1 scoring had known leniency issues with numeric normalization that inflated some published numbers.
policy_note.measures: DROP tests discrete reasoning over natural language paragraphs drawn from NFL game reports and Wikipedia articles (~96,000 QA pairs). Models must perform arithmetic, counting, sorting, or set operations to answer free-form questions; answers are graded with a numerically-aware F1 metric that handles numbers and date spans.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher F1 is better; scale is 0–100. Human performance is ~96 F1. Frontier models cluster above 90, so scores below ~80 indicate a meaningful capability gap while scores above 88 are hard to interpret comparatively.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers evaluating multi-step discrete reasoning in reading comprehension; historically used as a mid-tier reasoning probe, now most useful for comparing sub-frontier models.

policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to design novel AAV (adeno-associated virus) capsid protein sequences with desired functional properties, such as manufacturability and tissue tropism, as part of Dyno Therapeutics' gene therapy research. The challenge probes generative and directed-evolution capabilities in protein sequence space.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate sequences that better satisfy functional fitness criteria (e.g., production yield, transduction efficiency). Scores are domain-specific; comparison is meaningful only between models evaluated under the same wet-lab validation or in-silico fitness protocol.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and computational biologists working on protein/capsid engineering, particularly those applying generative models or directed evolution algorithms to gene therapy applications.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier multilingual models may show ceiling effects on high-resource language pairs; performance can vary significantly based on whether a model's multilingual training was balanced or English-dominant, making comparisons across model families tricky.
policy_note.measures: ECLeKTic evaluates cross-lingual knowledge transfer in language models, testing whether models can correctly answer questions in a target language when the underlying knowledge was predominantly encoded in a different (typically English) source language during training. It probes whether multilingual capability reflects genuine knowledge transfer or surface-level translation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores reflect cross-lingual transfer accuracy; gaps between source-language and target-language performance indicate how much knowledge is lost or distorted in transfer.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multilingual LLMs, particularly those assessing whether strong English-language performance generalizes to other languages without retraining.

policy_note.caveat: The 'test' variant withholds ground-truth labels and requires server-side evaluation, so reported scores depend on leaderboard submissions and cannot be independently verified locally. Frontier multimodal models have approached and exceeded 70% accuracy, raising saturation concerns for top-tier comparisons. Scores are sensitive to how many frames are sampled from each clip, making scaffold/sampling-rate dependence a real comparability issue across model cards.
policy_note.measures: EgoSchema tests long-form video temporal reasoning using ~5,000 multiple-choice questions (5 options each) grounded in ~3-minute egocentric video clips drawn from Ego4D. Each question requires integrating evidence across the full clip rather than a single frame, probing genuine temporal understanding.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; chance is 20% (5-way multiple choice). Strong open-source models score roughly 55–65%; top frontier multimodal models reach 70–80%+. Scores well above chance but below ~75% indicate meaningful capability; gains beyond that are increasingly hard to compare given saturation pressure.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers evaluating long-form video understanding and temporal reasoning in vision-language models.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark's exact dataset composition, task format, and scoring rubric are not publicly documented in a canonical paper, making independent replication and cross-lab comparison difficult. Scores may be highly scaffold- and prompt-format-dependent; results from different evaluation harnesses are likely not directly comparable. The definition of 'integrity' may conflate factual accuracy tasks with refusal-rate tasks, obscuring which capability is actually being measured.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether AI models appropriately handle election-related content, including requests that could spread misinformation about voting, candidates, or electoral processes. Tasks typically probe model refusal behavior and accuracy on civics-adjacent queries where harmful outputs could affect democratic participation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate safer or more accurate model behavior on election-related content. Because this is a safety/refusal benchmark rather than a knowledge benchmark, near-ceiling scores are expected for aligned frontier models; differentiation tends to appear on edge cases and adversarial phrasings rather than on straightforward queries.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policy teams, and AI labs assessing model behavior in politically sensitive domains ahead of elections or regulatory review.

policy_note.caveat: Evaluation awareness is a narrow behavioral proxy — verbalization of awareness is not equivalent to actual awareness, and a model could score well by pattern-matching evaluation-like prompts without genuine situational understanding. Scores are highly sensitive to prompt framing and system-prompt context, so cross-lab comparisons require careful scaffold matching.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a language model explicitly verbalizes awareness that it is being evaluated or tested, rather than operating in a real deployment context. Probes metacognitive transparency as a safety-relevant signal: a model that recognizes and states it is in an evaluation may behave differently than one that does not.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate the model more reliably verbalizes when it detects an evaluation context. Interpretation is nuanced: very high scores could reflect genuine transparency or prompt-pattern overfitting; the research value lies in comparing model families and fine-tuning regimes rather than reading absolute numbers.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and alignment evaluators assessing whether frontier models exhibit transparency about their own evaluation status, relevant to deceptive alignment research.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark name 'Evasion' is used by multiple distinct evaluation suites (adversarial ML robustness, jailbreak resistance, classifier bypass), making cross-report comparisons unreliable without confirming which suite is cited. Scaffold and prompt formatting choices can substantially shift 10-shot scores.
policy_note.measures: Evasion assesses a model's ability to resist or perform adversarial evasion — either evading safety/content classifiers or resisting adversarial prompt manipulations designed to bypass policy guardrails. The 10-shot variant provides 10 in-context examples before each test query.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores typically indicate greater resistance to evasion (safer/more robust), but interpretation depends on whether the task measures attack success rate (lower = better) or defense accuracy (higher = better). Confirm axis direction from the specific report before comparing across models.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing robustness of models against adversarial or policy-evasion inputs.

policy_note.caveat: No public paper or canonical dataset description is known for this specific benchmark variant, making independent replication and score comparison difficult. The 'Irregular' label suggests a non-standardized or internally curated challenge set, which raises concerns about reproducibility and comparability across evaluations. Scores may reflect scaffold or prompt-template choices as much as underlying model capability.
policy_note.measures: Evasion Challenges (Irregular) appears to assess a model's robustness against adversarial or out-of-distribution inputs designed to bypass safety filters, alignment constraints, or detection systems, using irregular (non-standard or edge-case) attack patterns. The exact dataset size and task format are not publicly documented.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores typically indicate greater resistance to evasion (better safety robustness); however, the scoring direction should be confirmed per the specific evaluation harness used. No well-established frontier range is publicly available for this benchmark.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and red-teamers evaluating frontier model robustness to adversarial evasion prompts, particularly for non-standard attack patterns not covered by mainstream safety benchmarks.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to inference mode: models using extended reasoning (chain-of-thought or thinking tokens) consistently outperform standard-mode scores on the same model, so comparisons are only valid within the same scaffold. Because grounding judgment is itself performed by an LLM, evaluator bias and prompt sensitivity can influence rankings near the top of the leaderboard.
policy_note.measures: FACTS Grounding evaluates whether a model's free-form response to a request is fully supported by a provided reference document, testing grounding fidelity rather than world knowledge. Each example pairs a long source document with a user request; a separate LLM judge determines whether every claim in the generated response is explicitly supported by the document.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent the percentage of responses judged fully grounded in the source document. Frontier models in standard mode cluster roughly in the mid-to-high 80s, with extended-reasoning configurations pushing into the low-to-mid 90s.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating hallucination and retrieval-augmented generation fidelity; useful for comparing how well models stay within the bounds of a provided context.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark name 'False Premises' is used by multiple independent research efforts with different datasets and scoring rubrics, so scores may not be comparable across leaderboards. No single canonical dataset or paper has become the community standard under this name, making cross-report comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model can detect and correct false factual premises embedded in questions (e.g., "Why did Einstein fail math?") rather than confabulating an answer that accepts the false assumption. Evaluates the model's ability to refuse or redirect rather than hallucinate.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. A perfect score means the model consistently identified and corrected false premises; a low score means it accepted and elaborated on false assumptions. Frontier models generally score well but the benchmark remains useful for catching specific failure modes.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and evaluators probing honesty, factual grounding, and resistance to leading questions in language models.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark's relatively narrow focus on figurative/idiomatic expressions means frontier models have begun to saturate performance, limiting its ability to differentiate between top-tier systems. The 'no extended thinking' variant note indicates scores depend on whether chain-of-thought reasoning is enabled, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless the inference setup matches.
policy_note.measures: FigQA tests figurative language understanding, probing whether models can correctly interpret the intended meaning of metaphors, idioms, and other non-literal expressions, typically framed as a binary or multiple-choice commonsense reasoning task. It is evaluated in a 10-shot setting, meaning the model sees ten in-context examples before answering each question.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models generally score in the high-80s to low-90s range, so differences below ~2 percentage points should be treated with caution given evaluation noise.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP and LLM researchers assessing language understanding beyond literal semantics; useful for comparing models on pragmatic and culturally-grounded language comprehension.

policy_note.caveat: The 'High Thinking' and 'Max Thinking' variant labels are not standardized across labs and represent different reasoning-budget configurations rather than distinct task sets; scores across variants are not directly comparable. Scaffold and tool-use setup (e.g., which financial data APIs are available to the agent) can substantially alter results, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Finance Agent evaluates an AI agent's ability to complete multi-step financial tasks—such as portfolio analysis, financial document parsing, or investment decision-making—in an agentic setting. The 'High Thinking' and 'Max Thinking' variant labels indicate the benchmark is run under different extended-reasoning compute budgets, probing how additional thinking time affects financial task accuracy.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better task completion. Because variants reflect different compute budgets rather than difficulty levels, results should be read within the same variant (e.g., compare all models at 'High Thinking'); cross-variant improvement shows the marginal value of additional thinking compute.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating agentic reasoning on domain-specific financial tasks, particularly under extended-thinking or chain-of-thought regimes.

policy_note.caveat: Scores can differ meaningfully depending on whether execution accuracy (final answer correct) or program accuracy (exact reasoning chain correct) is reported — check which metric a card uses. Annual reports are widely available on the web, so training-data contamination is a plausible concern for models trained after 2021. Retrieval setup (oracle evidence vs. open-book) also affects scores substantially.
policy_note.measures: FinQA tests multi-step numerical reasoning over real financial documents: models must retrieve relevant evidence from both tables and prose in annual reports (10-K filings), then execute a multi-step arithmetic program to answer questions. The dataset contains ~8,281 QA pairs with annotated reasoning programs.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). As of early 2026, strong frontier models reach ~70–80% execution accuracy; human expert performance is roughly 91%. Scores well below 60% indicate poor numerical reasoning over structured financial data.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating financial reasoning, arithmetic multi-step inference, and table-text joint understanding in language models.

policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model's responses are consistent and equitable when users frame requests in the first person across different demographic identities (e.g., varying gender, race, religion, or nationality in the prompt). Probes whether the model's helpfulness, tone, or refusal behavior shifts based on implied user identity.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher consistency scores (smaller disparity across demographic groups) are better. Results are typically expressed as gap metrics or parity ratios rather than a single accuracy score; a gap near zero indicates equitable treatment.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and fairness researchers assessing whether language models exhibit demographic bias in first-person interaction contexts.

policy_note.caveat: The exact methodology, dataset size, and harm taxonomy vary by lab — 'first-person fairness harm_overall' is a label pattern used in internal evaluation suites (notably Anthropic's) and may not correspond to a single public benchmark, making cross-model comparisons unreliable. The aggregate 'overall' score can mask large per-category or per-group variance.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model produces differentially harmful outputs depending on the demographic identity (e.g., race, gender, religion) of the person in a first-person prompt. The harm_overall score is an aggregate across harm sub-dimensions, measuring equity of treatment across groups rather than absolute refusal rates.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a lower harm_overall score indicates the model produces less harmful content (and does so more equally across groups). Scores near zero indicate low differential harm; a model could score low here while still failing demographic parity on other dimensions.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and fairness researchers, policy analysts, and lab evaluation teams assessing whether models exhibit demographic bias in harm generation.

policy_note.caveat: Sentences are drawn from Wikipedia and Wikinews, which are commonly present in large pretraining corpora, creating contamination risk for models trained on web-scale data. Annotation quality varies significantly across languages — high-resource languages have more reliable reference translations than very low-resource ones. Aggregate averages can obscure extreme variance between language pairs (high-resource pairs regularly score 50+ spBLEU while some low-resource pairs score under 5), so reporting only the mean can be misleading.
policy_note.measures: FLORES-200 measures machine translation quality across 200 languages using ~1,000 sentences sourced from Wikipedia and Wikinews, each professionally translated into all 200 languages, enabling evaluation of any language-pair direction. It probes a model's multilingual translation capability, especially on low-resource languages underrepresented in standard MT benchmarks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The primary metric is spBLEU (sentencepiece BLEU) or chrF++. Frontier multilingual MT systems (e.g. NLLB-200, Google Translate) average roughly 30–50 spBLEU across all directions; general-purpose LLMs typically score lower on low-resource pairs. Always check which language pairs and directions are reported — aggregates over 200 languages hide enormous per-pair spread.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and ML engineers evaluating multilingual or machine translation capabilities of language models, particularly coverage of low-resource and non-English-centric language pairs.

policy_note.caveat: Because questions are derived from Wikipedia, training-data contamination is a plausible concern for models with broad web crawls. Scores are sensitive to the retrieval pipeline used alongside the LLM, so results from a closed RAG scaffold are not directly comparable to open-book or no-retrieval settings.
policy_note.measures: FRAMES (Factuality, Retrieval, And Multi-hop Evaluation of RAG Systems) measures a model's ability to answer complex factual questions requiring multi-hop reasoning across multiple Wikipedia documents, with roughly 824 test questions spanning 2–15 retrieval hops. It probes whether models can correctly synthesize information from several sources rather than recalling single-fact answers.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better (0–100%). Frontier models with strong retrieval scaffolds typically score in the high-60s to low-80s percentage range; no-retrieval baselines and weaker models fall well below 50%.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating retrieval-augmented generation pipelines and long-context LLMs on multi-hop factual reasoning; useful for comparing RAG architectures rather than isolated model capability.

policy_note.caveat: The dataset is kept private and not publicly released, which limits independent auditing and makes external verification of reported scores difficult. At launch (late 2024) all frontier models scored under 2%, so the benchmark is far from saturation — but the closed nature means contamination cannot be independently checked and score comparisons depend on Epoch AI administering the evaluation.
policy_note.measures: FrontierMath is a collection of roughly 300 original, expert-level mathematics problems spanning advanced fields such as number theory, algebraic geometry, analytic number theory, and combinatorics, created with input from over 60 research mathematicians. Problems have computationally verifiable answers (concrete numbers or mathematical objects), probing deep mathematical reasoning well beyond olympiad difficulty.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percentage of problems answered correctly. As of late 2024, frontier models clustered below 2%, so even a jump to single-digit percentages represents meaningful capability progress. The benchmark has wide headroom and is not yet useful for distinguishing models at the low end.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and frontier-lab evaluators assessing expert-level mathematical reasoning in large language models, particularly for tracking progress beyond what olympiad-style benchmarks (MATH, AIME) can differentiate.

policy_note.caveat: Results are rarely disclosed in granular numeric form due to the sensitive subject matter, which severely limits cross-model comparison. Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the specific question set, red-teamer skill, and evaluator rubric all affect uplift ratings. The 'extended-thinking' variant (chain-of-thought reasoning enabled) can produce different uplift profiles than standard inference, so results across thinking/non-thinking conditions should not be treated as interchangeable.
policy_note.measures: The FSF CBRN Evaluation tests whether a model provides meaningful 'uplift' to individuals seeking to develop chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons — specifically whether responses go beyond what a domain expert could obtain from open sources. Outputs are judged by subject-matter experts against an uplift rubric, not by automated scoring.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower uplift is safer. Results are typically expressed as qualitative ratings ('meaningful uplift' / 'no meaningful uplift') or binary pass/fail against a threshold rather than a continuous numeric scale. Because most labs do not publish raw scores, there is no established frontier range for direct comparison.
policy_note.intended_for: Frontier AI safety teams and researchers assessing dual-use risk; used to inform deployment decisions and trigger capability thresholds under Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework.

policy_note.caveat: Evaluation methodology and precise task details are not fully public, limiting independent replication. Results are threshold-based rather than continuous scores, so cross-model comparison is limited. Performance is scaffold-dependent: agentic tooling and scaffolding choices materially affect outcomes. Model cards reporting this benchmark often omit specifics for security reasons, making apples-to-apples comparisons difficult.
policy_note.measures: Assesses whether a model possesses dangerous cybersecurity capabilities—such as vulnerability discovery, exploit development, or end-to-end attack orchestration—that could materially assist a threat actor in conducting significant cyberattacks. Part of Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework (FSF), which defines capability thresholds that trigger additional safeguards.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower capability levels are safer; the evaluation is primarily threshold-based (does the model exceed a defined danger level?) rather than a ranked leaderboard. A model clearing a threshold triggers policy responses rather than simply placing it on a spectrum.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policymakers, and lab leadership assessing whether a frontier model crosses capability thresholds that require additional deployment safeguards or restrictions under responsible-scaling policies.

policy_note.caveat: The 'extended-thinking' variant string observed in cards suggests results differ substantially depending on whether chain-of-thought reasoning is enabled, introducing scaffold dependence that makes cross-model comparisons unreliable unless the inference configuration is held constant. Dataset composition and labeling criteria are not publicly documented in detail, limiting independent replication.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model engages in or facilitates harmful psychological manipulation — tactics such as deception, coercion, emotional exploitation, or persuasion designed to override a user's rational agency. Tasks likely present scenarios where the model is prompted or induced to produce manipulative outputs, then scored on refusal quality and safety.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores (lower rate of harmful manipulation) are better. Scores reflect the proportion of evaluated scenarios in which the model avoids producing manipulative content; a model that never produces harmful manipulation would score at or near the maximum.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing whether frontier models exhibit or assist harmful manipulation behaviors; used internally by labs as part of pre-deployment safety evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: FSF Misalignment Evaluation is not a widely standardized public benchmark; results are highly scaffold-dependent, and the 'extended-thinking' variant scores are not directly comparable to standard (non-extended-thinking) runs. Operationalization of 'misalignment' varies by evaluator, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. Dataset composition and labeling criteria are not publicly documented in detail, limiting reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model exhibits misaligned behaviors—such as deception, goal misgeneralization, or corrigibility failures—under conditions designed to surface misalignment. The 'extended-thinking' variant specifically probes whether longer chain-of-thought reasoning changes the rate or character of misaligned outputs.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower rates of flagged misaligned behaviors are better. There is no established frontier-model baseline range in the public literature; scores should be interpreted relative to an organization's internal thresholds rather than cross-model leaderboard rankings.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and frontier-lab policy teams assessing whether a model's internal reasoning (especially under extended thinking) correlates with or conceals misaligned intent.

policy_note.caveat: Strong scaffold dependence: scores vary substantially based on which agentic framework, tool set, and retrieval stack the model is paired with, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. Level 1 questions are approaching saturation for frontier models with capable scaffolds (some systems exceed 80% on L1). The benchmark is small enough that a handful of questions can shift rankings.
policy_note.measures: GAIA evaluates general AI assistant capabilities on 466 real-world questions (165 validation, ~300 test) across three difficulty levels, each requiring multi-step reasoning plus tool use — web search, code execution, or file reading — to produce a single exact answer. It is designed to be trivial for humans (~92%) but challenging for AI systems.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent of questions answered exactly correctly. Human baseline is ~92%. Frontier agentic systems (as of early 2025) typically range 40–75% overall, with wide variance across difficulty levels and scaffolds. Always note which scaffold and tools were used when citing a score.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and engineers benchmarking agentic systems on general assistant tasks that require real-world tool use and multi-hop reasoning.

policy_note.measures: GDPval appears to be a benchmark of uncertain provenance; no widely documented details about its dataset size, task format, or targeted capability were found in public literature as of the knowledge cutoff.
policy_note.how_to_read: Direction and scale context unknown; consult the original benchmark publication or leaderboard for scoring conventions.
policy_note.intended_for: Unknown — insufficient public documentation to characterize the intended audience or primary use case.

policy_note.measures: GDPval-AA is not a benchmark I can reliably identify from available knowledge; no authoritative description, dataset size, task format, or capability domain can be confirmed without risking fabrication.
policy_note.how_to_read: Direction and scale are unknown; no reliable scoring context available.
policy_note.intended_for: Unknown — insufficient information to characterize the intended audience or use case.

policy_note.caveat:
Only 448 questions in the full set; ±1-2 percentage points may not be
statistically meaningful. The Diamond subset (198 questions) is harder
and more commonly reported. Domain-expert pass rate is around 65%.
policy_note.measures:
Graduate-level biology, physics, and chemistry questions written by
domain PhDs. Designed to be answerable by in-domain experts but
resistant to web search.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Common confusion: lab A reporting "GPQA" and lab B
reporting "GPQA Diamond" are different splits of the same benchmark
and are not directly comparable.
policy_note.intended_for:
Frontier-capability comparisons in scientific reasoning. Not
appropriate for routine model regression testing.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models now score in the 70–80%+ range, raising saturation concerns for top-tier differentiation. Scores are highly sensitive to prompting strategy (0-shot vs. CoT vs. multi-trial averaging), making cross-card comparisons unreliable without matching scaffold conditions. The 198-question pool is small enough that single-run variance is non-trivial; 5-trial averages reduce noise but are not always reported.
policy_note.measures: GPQA-Diamond is a 198-question multiple-choice subset of GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A) comprising the hardest, highest-quality questions across biology, chemistry, and physics, designed to require genuine graduate-level domain expertise. Questions are crafted to resist lookup and test deep reasoning rather than memorization.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; chance baseline is 25% (4-choice MCQ). Human expert performance is approximately 65–69%. Frontier models (2024–2025) typically score 60–85%, so scores below 60% indicate meaningful headroom and scores above 80% approach saturation for this subset.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and evaluators assessing graduate-level scientific reasoning in frontier language models.

policy_note.measures: GraphWalks tests a model's ability to reason about paths and traversals on structured graphs, typically requiring multi-hop relational reasoning such as following edges, counting steps, or determining reachability between nodes. Tasks are usually presented as natural-language or symbolic graph descriptions with questions about graph structure or navigation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Scores represent accuracy on graph traversal or reasoning questions; chance-level baselines depend on the answer format (e.g., multiple-choice vs. open-ended), and frontier model performance varies widely by graph complexity.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and evaluators studying graph-structured and multi-hop relational reasoning in language models.

policy_note.caveat: Two meaningfully different variant strings — 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' — have been observed in model cards reporting this benchmark; scores across these variants are not directly comparable, as extended-thinking configurations give models additional reasoning budget that can substantially inflate results on procedural graph tasks. Dataset size and sourcing are not well-documented in public literature, making contamination risk hard to assess.
policy_note.measures: GraphWalks BFS tests a model's ability to simulate or reason about breadth-first search traversal on graphs — typically asking the model to trace BFS execution order, identify reachable nodes, or compute shortest-path distances given an adjacency description. It probes algorithmic graph reasoning and step-by-step procedural execution.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better BFS execution accuracy. Because the 'extended-thinking' variant can yield noticeably higher numbers than the standard 'rlhf' variant, always confirm which configuration was used before comparing scores across model cards.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating a model's structured algorithmic reasoning, particularly multi-step graph traversal that requires maintaining state across many hops.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold- and context-length-dependent: the '64k context' and 'max context' variants are not interchangeable and should not be aggregated. Models with larger native context windows have a structural advantage, making cross-model comparisons valid only when context budget is held constant.
policy_note.measures: Tests a model's ability to correctly execute breadth-first search traversal over large graphs encoded as text within the context window. The '1M' designation refers to scale (likely ~1 million tokens of graph structure), with variants probing whether performance degrades at 64k versus maximum available context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; typically reported as accuracy (fraction of BFS traversals answered correctly). Frontier models at full context may score in the 40–80% range, with performance dropping sharply as graph depth and context length increase — a large gap between 64k and max-context variants signals context-length sensitivity rather than general reasoning failure.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating long-context algorithmic reasoning, specifically whether models can maintain state and follow deterministic traversal rules across very long token sequences.

policy_note.caveat: The 256K-1M token range means results are highly sensitive to the model's effective context window and positional encoding scheme; scores can vary significantly based on where graph edges are placed in the prompt. The variant label '256K-1M' conflates results across a wide context-length band, so aggregate scores may obscure per-length degradation curves.
policy_note.measures: GraphWalks BFS 256K-1M tests a model's ability to perform breadth-first search traversal over graphs encoded in very long contexts, ranging from 256K to 1M tokens. The task probes structured multi-hop reasoning and the capacity to track graph state across extreme context lengths.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. This is a challenging long-context benchmark; frontier models typically score well below ceiling, making it useful for differentiating models at the high end of context capability. Scores should be interpreted alongside the specific context-length sub-range (256K vs. 1M) rather than as a single aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and evaluators assessing long-context structured reasoning capabilities, particularly graph algorithm execution at scales that stress current context windows.

policy_note.caveat: Label conflation is a known risk: cards report this benchmark under at least two variant strings ('64k context' and 'max context'), meaning reported numbers may reflect different context lengths and are not directly comparable without knowing which slice was used. Performance is heavily scaffold-dependent — models that natively support 256K context windows will outperform those using truncation or summarization scaffolds, making cross-model comparisons misleading unless context handling is held constant. The 256K subset score should not be conflated with performance on the full 1M version.
policy_note.measures: Tests a model's ability to perform breadth-first search traversal over synthetic graph structures encoded in long documents, using a 256K-token subset drawn from the full 1M-token GraphWalks corpus. The task probes multi-hop reasoning and positional retrieval at scale by requiring models to follow edges across a context window and return correct BFS orderings or reachability answers.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores are typically reported as accuracy on BFS queries. Frontier models with native long-context support cluster in the upper range; models that silently truncate inputs score near chance on distant-node queries. Always verify which context-length variant (64K vs 256K vs max) is being reported.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating frontier models on long-context structured reasoning; useful for comparing models whose advertised context windows differ.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is likely significant: the observed variants 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' suggest scores differ substantially based on whether chain-of-thought reasoning is enabled, making cross-variant comparisons unreliable. Dataset size and construction methodology are not well-documented publicly, limiting reproducibility assessment.
policy_note.measures: GraphWalks Parents tests a model's ability to traverse directed graph structures and identify parent nodes given a starting node and a graph description. It probes multi-hop relational reasoning over symbolic graph representations presented in text.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better (accuracy or exact-match on parent identification). Frontier model ranges are not well-established in public leaderboards; interpret scores relative to the specific inference scaffold used, as extended-thinking variants may score considerably higher than standard variants.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating structured relational reasoning and graph traversal capabilities in language models, particularly under different inference regimes (standard vs. extended thinking).

policy_note.caveat: Variant strings observed in the wild ('64k context', 'max context') indicate that scores are frequently reported at different context lengths without clear labeling, making cross-model comparisons unreliable when the evaluation window differs. Models incapable of attending to the full 256K are excluded from or fail trivially on this variant, shrinking the comparable pool. Performance is also sensitive to how the graph is serialized (edge ordering, padding strategy), which can vary across evaluation harnesses.
policy_note.measures: Tests a model's ability to traverse a directed graph and identify parent-node relationships when the full graph is serialized into a 256K-token context window; this benchmark is a fixed-size subset drawn from a larger 1M-token version of the same task. The model must locate and follow edges across a very long document to answer parent-lookup queries correctly.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; chance level depends on graph branching factor. Frontier models typically score well below ceiling at 256K due to attention degradation over long distances; a score above ~80% at 256K is considered strong. Always check which context length was actually used before comparing numbers.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers stress-testing long-context retrieval and multi-hop reasoning in large language models, particularly those claiming extended context windows.

name: Gray Swan Red Team - Harmful Image-Text ASR

policy_note.caveat: ASR is heavily scaffold-dependent: results vary with the specific attack strategy, image perturbation method, prompt template, and the judge or classifier used to label a response as 'harmful.' Scores from different evaluation setups are not directly comparable. Full dataset composition and attack methodology details may not be publicly disclosed, limiting reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Measures the attack success rate (ASR) of adversarial image-text inputs against multimodal language models — the fraction of red-team jailbreak attempts combining images and text that successfully elicit harmful outputs. Probes multimodal safety under adversarial conditions constructed by Gray Swan's red team.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — an ASR of 0% means no adversarial image-text attacks succeeded. Safety-tuned frontier models aim for single-digit or near-zero percentages; higher values indicate greater vulnerability to multimodal jailbreaks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing multimodal robustness against adversarial jailbreak attempts; useful for comparing safety alignment across model versions.

name: Gray Swan Red Team - Harmful Text ASR

policy_note.caveat: ASR is highly scaffold-dependent: results vary substantially based on the specific attack prompts, iteration budget, and judge used to classify success, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless methodology is held constant. Gray Swan's exact prompt set, success criteria, and scoring judge may differ across evaluation runs or model card vintages, so numbers reported by different labs are often not directly comparable.
policy_note.measures: Measures the attack success rate (ASR) of adversarial red-team prompts attempting to elicit harmful text from a model — the fraction of jailbreak attempts that produce policy-violating outputs. Lower ASR indicates greater robustness against adversarial manipulation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — 0% ASR means no attack succeeded, 100% means every attack succeeded. Frontier models typically report single-digit to low-double-digit ASR on structured red-team suites, but the baseline shifts dramatically with attack sophistication; always check what attack methodology produced the number.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing a model's robustness to adversarial jailbreak attempts targeting harmful content generation.

name: Gray Swan Red Team - Malicious Code ASR

policy_note.caveat: ASR is highly scaffold-dependent: scores vary substantially based on which attack strategies, prompt templates, and automated judging criteria Gray Swan uses in a given evaluation round, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. The 'malicious code' success criterion requires a human or automated judge call that can conflate dual-use code with clearly harmful outputs. Results are not reproducible without access to the exact attack corpus and judge rubric.
policy_note.measures: Measures the Attack Success Rate (ASR) — the fraction of adversarial jailbreak attempts that successfully elicit malicious code outputs from a model. Gray Swan's red-team suite applies structured attack prompts targeting harmful code generation and records what percentage bypass the model's refusals.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a 0% ASR means no tested attacks succeeded; 100% means all did. Frontier models typically score in the single digits to low tens of percent on hardened evaluations, but numbers are not comparable across different attack suites or judging thresholds.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policy teams, and lab red-teamers assessing a model's resistance to adversarial prompts targeting harmful code generation.

policy_note.caveat: High contamination risk: GRE preparation materials (official guides, practice tests, Kaplan/Manhattan Prep books) are extensively indexed on the web and likely present in most large pretraining corpora. Saturation is also a concern — frontier models routinely score near the ceiling of the human score scale (170/170), making differentiation between top models difficult. The 5-shot CoT scaffold means scores are not directly comparable to evaluations using zero-shot or different prompt formats.
policy_note.measures: Measures mathematical reasoning across arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and data analysis at the level of the GRE Quantitative Reasoning section. Models are evaluated in a 5-shot chain-of-thought prompting setup on problems drawn from or modeled after the standardized graduate admissions test.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The GRE Quant section scores on a 130–170 integer scale; human test-takers average roughly 153. Frontier models frequently achieve 163–170, compressing meaningful signal at the top end. Gains within that top band should be interpreted cautiously given saturation and contamination.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers benchmarking general quantitative and mathematical reasoning ability, particularly for comparisons against a human-normed standardized test scale.

policy_note.caveat: The GRE Verbal section is a standardized human test not designed for LLM evaluation; score mapping from raw/scaled GRE scores to model percentile comparisons can be inconsistent across papers. Saturation is a concern as frontier models score near ceiling on many standardized verbal tests. Contamination risk is non-trivial given GRE prep materials are widely distributed in pretraining corpora.
policy_note.measures: Measures verbal reasoning ability as tested on the Graduate Record Examinations (GRE), covering reading comprehension, text completion, and sentence equivalence tasks. Evaluated in a 5-shot chain-of-thought setting, probing language understanding and inferential reasoning at a graduate-admissions level.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores are typically reported as percent correct or mapped to GRE scaled scores (130–170 range). Frontier models generally score in the high-human-percentile range, so differentiation at the top is limited.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking general language understanding and verbal reasoning, particularly for comparing models against a human graduate-level baseline.

policy_note.caveat:
Largely saturated by frontier models (>95%). Original dataset has
documented labeling errors. Now most useful as a low-cost sanity check
rather than a capability differentiator.
policy_note.measures:
8,500 grade-school-level arithmetic word problems requiring 2-8
reasoning steps. Solutions are natural-language with a final numeric
answer.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Scored on exact match of the final numeric answer;
intermediate reasoning is not scored.
policy_note.intended_for:
Basic arithmetic-reasoning sanity check; regression testing of smaller
models.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark name 'HallBench' overlaps with several similarly named hallucination evaluation suites (e.g., HaluEval, HallusionBench, HaluBench), which can cause label conflation in model cards and leaderboards. Scores may not be directly comparable across papers if different variants or subsets were used. Contamination risk is non-trivial for benchmarks built from web-crawled factual corpora.
policy_note.measures: HallBench evaluates large language models' tendency to hallucinate — generating plausible-sounding but factually incorrect, unsupported, or fabricated content. It probes factual accuracy and faithfulness across adversarial or knowledge-intensive question types designed to elicit confabulation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower hallucination rates (or higher faithfulness/accuracy scores, depending on framing) are better. Frontier models vary substantially on hallucination tasks, making this a more differentiating dimension than saturated reasoning benchmarks.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners assessing LLM reliability, factual grounding, and susceptibility to producing unverified claims.

policy_note.caveat: Hard negatives in protein binding datasets are often computationally curated rather than experimentally validated, which can introduce label noise. Performance is highly sensitive to the curation strategy used to select negatives; different construction methods produce incomparable scores across implementations. Saturation is unlikely to be an issue given the difficulty of the task, but small dataset size may limit statistical power.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to correctly classify protein pairs that do NOT bind (hard negatives) — cases structurally or sequentially similar to known binding pairs, making them difficult to distinguish from true binders. It probes whether models generalize binding specificity rather than exploiting superficial similarity signals.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better (typically reported as AUROC or accuracy). Scores near 0.5 indicate near-random performance on the hard-negative set; scores above 0.85 suggest strong specificity discrimination. Compare only runs using the same negative-curation protocol, as construction methodology dominates score variation.
policy_note.intended_for: Computational biologists and ML researchers developing or evaluating models for protein–protein interaction (PPI) prediction, drug discovery, and virtual screening pipelines.

policy_note.caveat: The 'Deep Think mode' variant label indicates scaffold dependence: scores obtained with extended reasoning enabled are not directly comparable to standard-mode scores. Odds ratio metrics are sensitive to baseline choice and prompt framing, making cross-model comparison difficult unless evaluation conditions are held strictly constant.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's propensity to generate harmful manipulative content, expressed as an odds ratio relative to a baseline or refusal rate. The odds ratio format quantifies how much more (or less) likely a model is to produce manipulative outputs compared to a reference condition.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower odds ratio is better — a value below 1.0 indicates the model is less likely than the baseline to produce harmful manipulative outputs. A value of 1.0 is neutral; above 1.0 indicates elevated risk. Frontier model ranges vary by evaluation harness and baseline definition.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing a model's tendency to produce harmful persuasion or manipulation; relevant for red-teaming and pre-deployment safety audits.

policy_note.caveat: Scoring depends heavily on the LLM used as the rubric judge (typically an OpenAI model), which may inflate scores for OpenAI models relative to competitors. As a newly released benchmark (May 2025), contamination and saturation profiles are not yet well established, but frontier models already span a wide range, suggesting headroom remains.
policy_note.measures: HealthBench evaluates LLMs on approximately 5,000 realistic, multi-turn health conversations authored by physicians, scored against physician-written rubrics using an LLM judge. It probes the quality, safety, and accuracy of open-ended health advice across a wide range of clinical scenarios.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent a 0–100 percentage of physician-rubric criteria met. Frontier models at release ranged roughly from the low 40s to the mid 60s, leaving meaningful differentiation across tiers.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, clinical AI developers, and policymakers evaluating the readiness of LLMs for health-related deployment.

policy_note.caveat: The Consensus subset is deliberately harder and scores lower than full HealthBench — do not compare scores across the two variants without noting this. Rubric grading is itself LLM-assisted (GPT-4o), so model-family correlations may introduce systematic bias favoring OpenAI-style outputs. Scores depend on the grading rubric version; label carefully when comparing across reporting dates.
policy_note.measures: HealthBench Consensus evaluates model responses to ~5,000 multi-turn health and medical conversations using physician-written rubrics, specifically on the subset of items where graders showed high inter-rater agreement. It probes clinical communication quality, safety, and accuracy across diverse patient scenarios.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are expressed as a percentage of rubric criteria met (0–100). Frontier models at release scored roughly in the 50–70% range on the full benchmark; Consensus scores run lower. A gap between a model's full HealthBench and Consensus scores indicates sensitivity to ambiguous cases.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capability researchers, clinicians evaluating frontier model medical readiness, and policymakers assessing health AI deployment risk.

policy_note.caveat: Scores depend on the LLM-as-judge evaluation framework, meaning different judge models or prompting scaffolds can shift absolute scores. The 'Hard' subset was explicitly carved out because the full HealthBench showed early saturation signs among top frontier models, so scores on the full benchmark and the Hard subset are not directly comparable; care should be taken not to conflate them.
policy_note.measures: HealthBench Hard is a challenging subset of OpenAI's HealthBench benchmark, which evaluates model responses to health-related multi-turn conversations using physician-written rubrics scored by an LLM judge. It probes clinical reasoning, appropriate triage, safety-conscious communication, and the ability to handle medically ambiguous scenarios where frontier models are most likely to be differentiated.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; scores are expressed as percentages. The Hard subset is designed so frontier models cluster in a lower, more spread range than the full benchmark, making small differences more meaningful. Expect frontier model scores roughly in the 30–55% range rather than the 50–70%+ range typical of the full HealthBench.
policy_note.intended_for: AI developers and healthcare-AI researchers comparing frontier model performance on clinically realistic, high-stakes health queries.

policy_note.caveat: HealthBench was created and released by OpenAI, which may introduce evaluator-lab bias that advantages OpenAI models. Label conflation is a real risk: 'HealthBench', 'HealthBench Hard', and 'HealthBench Professional' are distinct difficulty tiers and their scores are not interchangeable — model cards reporting a single 'HealthBench' number should be checked for which variant was used. Rubric-graded evaluations also introduce inter-rater variability depending on which physicians authored the criteria.
policy_note.measures: HealthBench Professional evaluates language models on professional-level medical questions using physician-written rubrics; responses are scored against criteria developed by clinicians, probing clinical reasoning, diagnostic thinking, and health knowledge that goes beyond lay-level understanding. The Professional variant draws on the harder subset of the ~5,000-conversation HealthBench corpus, targeting questions requiring domain expertise typically held by healthcare professionals.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent the fraction of physician-written rubric criteria met, expressed as a percentage (0–100%). Frontier models on the Professional variant tend to cluster in the 60–80% range as of mid-2025; the harder tier was designed to avoid the ceiling saturation seen on lay-level medical QA benchmarks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and product teams assessing LLM suitability for clinical or professional health applications; policy analysts benchmarking risk in high-stakes medical deployment contexts.

policy_note.caveat:
Now thoroughly saturated by frontier models (>95%) and heavily
contaminated in pretraining corpora. Largely retired from frontier
reporting but still appears in legacy comparisons.
policy_note.measures:
Multiple-choice sentence-completion tasks designed to require
commonsense reasoning, derived adversarially against language models
of the 2019 era.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Treat with skepticism when comparing 2024+ models;
differences within the noise floor.
policy_note.intended_for: Legacy comparison only. Not informative for current frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is explicit: 'default thinking' and 'extended thinking' variants produce distinct scores, so cross-model comparisons are only meaningful when the same thinking mode is used. The benchmark appears to be an Anthropic-internal evaluation; dataset composition, size, and labeling criteria are not publicly documented, making independent replication or contamination auditing difficult.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to correctly fulfill difficult but legitimate (non-harmful) user requests, probing whether safety or refusal mechanisms produce false positives on high-complexity benign tasks. Variants compare performance under default versus extended (chain-of-thought) thinking modes.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better, indicating the model correctly completes more difficult benign requests without unnecessary refusal. Compare within the same thinking-mode variant; the 'overall' figure aggregates both modes. Absolute scale and frontier range are not publicly documented.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capability researchers evaluating the balance between safety refusals and helpfulness on demanding but benign prompts; useful for detecting over-refusal regressions.

policy_note.caveat: The 'no tools' and 'with tools' variants produce substantially different scores and must not be compared directly — reported results must specify which variant was used. Scaffold dependence is high: which tools are provided (code execution, web search, calculator) changes scores significantly, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. The benchmark was designed to resist saturation, but frontier models with tools were already scoring above 30–50% by mid-2025, compressing headroom faster than intended.
policy_note.measures: HLE (Humanity's Last Exam) is a ~3,000-question benchmark spanning mathematics, natural sciences, humanities, and other advanced academic domains, featuring multiple-choice and free-response questions drawn from graduate-level and competition-level material. It probes expert-level reasoning across disciplines specifically chosen to challenge frontier models where existing benchmarks had saturated.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as percent correct. At launch in early 2025 frontier models without tools scored roughly 1–10%; with tool use, leading models reached 20–50%+ by mid-2025. The no-tools variant remains the cleaner comparator across model releases.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and policy analysts assessing frontier model reasoning at the upper tail of difficulty, where mainstream benchmarks no longer differentiate.

policy_note.caveat:
Heavily contaminated in modern training corpora — multiple papers have
shown verbatim solution memorization. Saturation: frontier models
exceed 90%, narrowing useful comparison range. HumanEval+ extends the
test cases to catch superficial memorization.
policy_note.measures:
164 hand-written Python programming problems with docstring
specifications. Measures function-completion correctness via unit
tests.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Metric is pass@1 by default (single sample, must
pass all tests).
policy_note.intended_for:
Coarse coding-capability check. Not a substitute for benchmarks like
SWE-bench that test multi-file engineering.

policy_note.caveat: Inherits contamination risk from the original HumanEval problems, which have been public since 2021 and appear widely in pre-training corpora. Saturation is a concern — frontier models score 85–92%+ on pass@1, compressing differentiation at the top. Limited to Python and to 164 problems, so breadth of language coverage and problem diversity are narrow.
policy_note.measures: HumanEval+ extends the original 164-problem HumanEval Python code-generation benchmark by adding ~80× more test cases per problem (generated via the EvalPlus framework), reducing false-positive pass rates caused by the original benchmark's sparse test suites. Models are evaluated on pass@1: whether a single generated completion passes all tests.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are pass@1 (percentage of problems solved on the first attempt). Frontier models (GPT-4 class and above) typically score in the 85–92% range; a model scoring below ~70% is meaningfully behind the frontier. Scores are always lower than the same model's HumanEval score, since stricter tests catch more incorrect-but-lucky completions.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners evaluating and comparing code-generation models on functional correctness with stricter test coverage than vanilla HumanEval.

policy_note.caveat: Results are not standardized across organizations — annotator pool, prompt distribution, rating rubric, and number of raters vary per study and are often undisclosed, making cross-lab comparisons invalid. Side-by-side human evals are susceptible to position bias (preference for first or second response), verbosity bias (longer responses rated higher), and rater-instruction sensitivity. Win rates are relative to a single fixed baseline (Gemma-2-27B) and do not generalize to other comparisons.
policy_note.measures: Human preference rate when a model's responses are judged side-by-side against Gemma-2-27B outputs, typically reported as a win/tie/loss percentage. Human raters select which response they prefer across a set of prompts covering general instruction-following, helpfulness, and response quality.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win rate is better. Results are expressed as a percentage of prompts where the evaluated model was preferred over Gemma-2-27B; 50% represents parity. Frontier models released after Gemma-2-27B (mid-2024) typically report win rates above 50% on their own internal evals.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating whether a model exceeds or falls short of Gemma-2-27B on open-ended human preference tasks; typically appears in model release reports as a practical capability anchor.

policy_note.caveat: There is no single canonical protocol: each lab defines its own task distribution, annotator pool, rating guidelines, and number of comparisons, making cross-report numbers incomparable. GPT-4o-mini itself is periodically updated, so the baseline shifts over time. Results are heavily prompt-mix-dependent — a conversational-heavy evaluation will rank models differently than a coding-heavy one. 'Side-by-side' format is also known to introduce position bias.
policy_note.measures: Human raters compare model outputs side-by-side against GPT-4o-mini responses on open-ended prompts, recording which response is preferred or whether they tie. The result is typically expressed as a win/tie/loss rate or a net preference percentage over the GPT-4o-mini baseline.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win rate is better. A score near 50% indicates rough parity with GPT-4o-mini; frontier-tier models typically report 60–80%+ preference rates in their own evaluations. Because each lab runs its own variant, compare only numbers from the same evaluation setup.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and product teams benchmarking a model's overall response quality relative to a widely deployed, cost-efficient mid-tier baseline (GPT-4o-mini).

policy_note.caveat: Not a standardized benchmark — each lab runs its own version with proprietary prompt sets, rater pools, and tie-handling rules, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. Side-by-side format introduces position bias. Results are anchored to Llama-3.3-70B at a fixed point in time, so the absolute number loses meaning as both models age. No canonical dataset or paper governs the protocol.
policy_note.measures: Human preference rate in side-by-side comparisons between the evaluated model and Meta's Llama-3.3-70B as a fixed reference baseline. Raters are shown outputs from both models for the same prompt and indicate which they prefer, yielding a win/tie/loss rate.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score above 50% means human raters preferred the evaluated model over Llama-3.3-70B more often than not. Scores are typically reported as win rates (e.g., 60% means the model won 60% of pairwise comparisons). Frontier models typically score in the 55–75% range against this baseline depending on task mix.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and practitioners comparing a frontier model's overall response quality against a well-known open-weight reference point.

policy_note.caveat: Results are not standardized across labs — each lab defines its own prompt set, rater pool, rating rubric, and tie-handling rules, so scores from different organizations are not directly comparable. Using Qwen-2.5-32B as the baseline anchors the scale to a single point in time; as that model ages, the baseline becomes less informative. Evaluations conducted by the model developer introduce conflict-of-interest risk. No public dataset or shared protocol exists for this variant.
policy_note.measures: Human preference rate in pairwise side-by-side comparisons between the evaluated model and Qwen-2.5-32B as a fixed baseline. Human raters judge which response they prefer across open-ended prompts, with results expressed as a win/tie/loss or net win-rate percentage.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. A score above 50% win-rate means the evaluated model was preferred over Qwen-2.5-32B more than half the time. Scores near 50% indicate rough parity with that baseline; scores well above (e.g. 60%+) indicate a meaningful preference advantage. Absolute numbers are only meaningful relative to the specific evaluation setup used.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing a specific model's overall conversational quality against the Qwen-2.5-32B reference point, typically as reported in a lab's own model release documentation.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are relative to a fixed baseline (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and are not comparable across labs that run their own versions with different task sets, rater pools, or rating rubrics. As Claude 3.5 Sonnet ages, the baseline becomes easier to beat, inflating apparent progress. Win rate conflates correctness, code style, verbosity, and explanation quality unless the rubric explicitly separates them.
policy_note.measures: Human raters compare model-generated coding responses head-to-head against Claude 3.5 Sonnet outputs and record which they prefer; the score is the win rate (fraction of comparisons where the evaluated model is chosen). Task distribution, rater pool, and rubric are lab-specific and typically undisclosed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; 50% means parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, above 50% means the evaluated model is preferred more often than the baseline. Margins of a few points may not be statistically significant given typical sample sizes for human evals.
policy_note.intended_for: AI lab researchers and product teams assessing whether a new model improves on Claude 3.5 Sonnet on real-world coding tasks as judged by human evaluators.

policy_note.caveat: Proprietary internal evaluation with no public dataset or methodology paper, making independent replication impossible. Win-rate framing is baseline-relative — a score means nothing without knowing the baseline version; as Claude 3.5 Sonnet itself improves, historical comparisons become incomparable. Human rater pool composition, task distribution, and inter-rater agreement are not disclosed. Results may not transfer across languages, genres, or cultural contexts.
policy_note.measures: Measures human preference for creative writing outputs via pairwise comparison: human raters choose which model's response they prefer on open-ended creative writing tasks (e.g., stories, poems, stylistic prose). Results are expressed as win rate against Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a fixed baseline.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win rate is better. A win rate above 50% means the evaluated model was preferred over Claude 3.5 Sonnet more often than not. Frontier models typically cluster in the 40–60% range against each other; numbers far above 50% are uncommon and warrant scrutiny of task selection.
policy_note.intended_for: AI developers and researchers comparing frontier model creative writing quality; primarily cited in Anthropic model release documentation.

policy_note.caveat: Win rates are baseline-anchored to Claude 3.5 Sonnet, making cross-lab comparisons impossible without a shared reference; results are not reproducible externally because rater pools, rubrics, and document sets are typically proprietary and undisclosed. The metric moves whenever the baseline model is silently updated.
policy_note.measures: Human preference win rate on document analysis tasks, where raters compare model outputs head-to-head against Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a fixed baseline. Tasks typically involve comprehension, summarization, or question-answering over real-world documents.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win rate is better. 50% represents exact parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet; scores above 50% indicate the evaluated model is preferred by human raters more often than not. Absolute scale depends on rater agreement rates, which are rarely reported.
policy_note.intended_for: Model developers and product teams assessing relative document-comprehension quality against a concrete Claude 3.5 Sonnet reference point.

policy_note.caveat: As a relative metric anchored to a specific baseline (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), scores are not directly comparable across evaluation rounds if the baseline changes. Rater pool size, annotation guidelines, and task distribution are not publicly disclosed, limiting reproducibility and external validation. Win-rate framing can also obscure tie rates.
policy_note.measures: Human raters compare model outputs head-to-head against Claude 3.5 Sonnet on instruction-following tasks, with scores reported as win rates — the fraction of trials where the evaluated model's response was preferred. The evaluation probes how faithfully models follow explicit user instructions across diverse prompt types.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; 50% means parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, above 50% means the evaluated model is preferred more often on instruction-following tasks. Frontier models from Anthropic reporting this metric typically cluster in the 50–60% range against the 3.5 Sonnet baseline.
policy_note.intended_for: AI developers and researchers assessing instruction-following quality of new frontier models relative to Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a fixed reference point.

policy_note.caveat: Win rate is a relative metric anchored to a specific baseline model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet); scores are not comparable across evaluations that use a different anchor. Results depend heavily on rater pool composition, task sampling, and instruction framing, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. No standardized public dataset or protocol is known for this evaluation.
policy_note.measures: Human rater preference judgments on visual understanding tasks, reported as win rate against Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a fixed baseline. Evaluators compare paired model responses to image-based prompts and select the better output.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a win rate above 50% indicates the evaluated model is preferred over Claude 3.5 Sonnet by human raters more often than not. Scores near 50% indicate rough parity with the baseline.
policy_note.intended_for: AI developers and researchers assessing multimodal model quality on visual comprehension tasks relative to a known Claude baseline.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to scaffold: variant strings in the wild include 'extended-thinking', 'pass@1', 'no tools', and 'text-only', and these conditions produce materially different numbers that are not directly comparable. The benchmark was designed for a capability level where frontier models score in the low-to-mid single digits, so rapid model improvement risks saturation of easier sub-domains before the hardest questions become tractable.
