Question difficulty is uneven across disciplines, which can skew aggregate scores depending on model strengths.
policy_note.measures: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is a closed-ended, multi-subject Q&A benchmark of ~3,000 expert-level questions across mathematics, sciences, humanities, and other disciplines, each submitted and vetted by domain specialists. It probes the absolute frontier of model knowledge, targeting questions where current AI and most humans would be expected to fail.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scale is 0–100% accuracy. As of early 2025, frontier models ranged roughly 3–15% depending on model and scaffold, making even small absolute gains meaningful. Extended-thinking or chain-of-thought scaffolds push scores noticeably higher than direct-answer baselines.
policy_note.intended_for: AI capabilities researchers and frontier labs assessing the upper bound of model knowledge and reasoning; useful for differentiating among the strongest current models where standard academic benchmarks have saturated.

policy_note.caveat: Prompt distribution reflects the specific population of early ChatGPT/API users and may not generalize to other user bases or use cases. Human preference labels carry annotator subjectivity and can shift over time as user expectations evolve. The underlying prompt corpus is not fully public, making independent replication difficult. Scores are sensitive to the baseline model chosen for comparison.
policy_note.measures: Measures how often a model's responses are preferred by human raters over a baseline, using prompts drawn from real ChatGPT playground users and OpenAI API users. Tasks span open-ended generation, question answering, summarization, and instruction following, reflecting naturalistic user intent rather than curated benchmarks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win-rate or preference score is better. Scores are typically reported as a percentage of responses preferred over a reference model (often the SFT baseline); 50% indicates parity, above 50% indicates improvement. Frontier RLHF models typically score in the 55–75% range against untuned baselines.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating RLHF-trained or instruction-tuned models on realistic conversational tasks; useful for assessing alignment with human preferences on naturalistic prompts rather than academic benchmarks.

policy_note.caveat: Preference scores are highly sensitive to rater pool composition, task sampling, and prompt phrasing — small changes in instructions or annotator demographics can shift results substantially. The 'Business' label is not standardized across labs, so the exact task mix may differ between models reporting this benchmark, making cross-model comparisons unreliable without shared methodology documentation. Preference does not imply factual correctness.
policy_note.measures: Human-preference evaluation in business contexts, where human raters compare model outputs on business-relevant tasks (e.g., drafting, summarization, analysis, customer communication) and indicate which response they prefer. Results are typically reported as a preference rate or win rate against a baseline.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores typically represent win rate or preference rate (0–100%) against a reference model or human baseline. Context on the comparison baseline is essential — a 70% preference rate means little without knowing what model or human tier was used as the reference.
policy_note.intended_for: AI product teams and enterprise buyers evaluating model fit for professional and business writing or communication tasks.

policy_note.caveat: This label covers many distinct evaluation setups — different rater pools, prompt distributions, comparison baselines, rating rubrics, and platforms — making cross-study results largely incomparable. Preference can be driven by surface features like response length or formatting rather than true quality, and inter-annotator agreement is frequently low. Without knowing the specific baseline model and rater instructions, a reported win rate carries significant ambiguity.
policy_note.measures: Human Preference Evaluation (General) captures how often human raters prefer a model's outputs over those of a baseline or competing model across a broad range of open-ended, general-purpose tasks. Results are typically reported as a win rate or preference rate percentage derived from pairwise comparisons.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a win rate above 50% means the model is preferred over the comparison baseline more often than not. Absolute numbers are less meaningful than the stated baseline — a 60% win rate against GPT-3.5 is not equivalent to 60% against GPT-4.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and product teams comparing model quality on general tasks using human judgment rather than automated metrics; commonly reported alongside RLHF training papers and model release announcements.

policy_note.caveat: Human preference evaluations conflate factual correctness with presentation style, verbosity, and confidence, which can disadvantage terse-but-correct answers. Rater expertise level in STEM domains varies across implementations and strongly influences results. No single canonical version of this benchmark is widely standardized, so scores reported under this name may not be directly comparable across labs or papers.
policy_note.measures: Human-rated preference judgments on model-generated responses to STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) questions or tasks, typically via pairwise comparisons or Likert-scale ratings by human evaluators. Probes both correctness and response quality as perceived by human raters with relevant domain knowledge.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger human preference for a model's outputs. Scores are typically expressed as win rates (%) in pairwise settings or mean ratings on a Likert scale; without a fixed leaderboard, interpret scores relative to the specific baselines reported in each study.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and model developers assessing how well frontier models satisfy human expectations on technical STEM content, particularly when automated metrics are insufficient.

policy_note.caveat: Results are scaffold- and prompt-dependent; different evaluation harnesses, annotator pools, or prompt distributions produce incomparable numbers. The baseline (Gemma-2-27B-IT) is a fixed point in time, so the metric becomes less informative as the field moves on and newer models are used as baselines instead. Human preference labels conflate multiple dimensions (factual accuracy, style, verbosity) without separating them.
policy_note.measures: Measures how often a model's outputs are preferred by human raters over those of Google's Gemma-2-27B-IT instruction-tuned model, typically via side-by-side comparison of responses to prompts spanning instruction following, helpfulness, and quality. The result is expressed as a win rate or preference percentage against this specific baseline.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score above 50% means human raters preferred the evaluated model over Gemma-2-27B-IT more than half the time. Frontier models typically score well above 50% against this baseline, so the metric is most discriminative for models in or near the Gemma-2-27B performance tier.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing a model's overall response quality and helpfulness against a well-known open-weight mid-size baseline; useful for situating a new model relative to the Gemma-2 family.

policy_note.caveat: There is no single standardized version of this evaluation — different labs run their own prompt sets, rater pools, and instructions, so win-rate figures across different model cards are not directly comparable. The baseline (GPT-4o-mini) has itself been updated over time, introducing timeline-dependent drift. Human preference is sensitive to response length bias (raters often favor longer answers) and rater demographic composition. Results also depend heavily on the domain mix of the evaluation prompts, which is rarely fully disclosed.
policy_note.measures: Measures human-judged response preference between a candidate model and GPT-4o-mini as a fixed baseline, typically reported as a win/tie/loss rate across a set of open-ended prompts. Probes overall helpfulness and response quality as perceived by human raters in side-by-side comparisons.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win rate (% preferred over GPT-4o-mini) is better. A score above 50% means human raters preferred the candidate model more often than not; below 50% means GPT-4o-mini was preferred. Frontier models typically report win rates in the 55–75% range against GPT-4o-mini; near 50% signals rough parity with that baseline.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and product teams assessing a model's overall conversational quality relative to a widely-deployed mid-tier baseline.

policy_note.caveat: Results are relative to a single fixed baseline model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), so scores are not comparable across evaluations that use different baselines. Preference studies are highly sensitive to prompt selection, rater demographics, and evaluation interface design; reported win rates may not generalize. As Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct itself improves or is superseded, the benchmark's discriminative value diminishes.
policy_note.measures: Measures how often a model's responses are preferred by human raters over those of Meta's Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct in head-to-head comparisons. The evaluation captures overall response quality as judged by humans, including helpfulness, clarity, and appropriateness.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent the percentage of head-to-head trials where human raters preferred the evaluated model over Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. A score above 50% indicates the model is preferred more often than the baseline; 50% indicates parity.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing instruction-following and conversational quality of a new model against the Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct baseline.

policy_note.caveat: Methodology varies significantly across labs — prompt set composition, annotator pool, tie-handling, and whether blind evaluation is truly enforced all affect results. Because Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct is a specific versioned baseline, win rates are not comparable across evaluations that use different baselines or different prompt distributions. No canonical shared protocol exists, so scores reported by different organizations under this name may not be commensurable.
policy_note.measures: Head-to-head human preference win rate comparing a model's responses against Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct as a fixed baseline. Human annotators perform blind pairwise comparisons across a set of prompts and select which response they prefer, yielding a win/tie/loss breakdown.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher win rate is better. A score above 50% means the evaluated model is preferred over Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct more often than not. Frontier models typically report win rates in the 55–75% range against this baseline; scores near 50% indicate rough parity.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing instruction-following and general-quality output against a strong open-source mid-size baseline; useful for positioning a model relative to Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct specifically.

policy_note.caveat: Dataset composition and size vary significantly across labs that report this metric, making cross-model comparisons unreliable. Because the exact prompt corpus is usually withheld for security reasons, third parties cannot reproduce scores. Prompts from prior evaluation rounds may leak into fine-tuning data over time, inflating apparent robustness.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's resistance to adversarial jailbreak prompts that were authored or submitted by real human users, as opposed to synthetic or automated red-teaming inputs. The task format is typically attack success rate: whether the model complies with a prohibited request when prompted with a human-crafted jailbreak.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower attack success rate (ASR) is better; some labs report the inverse as a 'resistance rate' where higher is better. Frontier models typically report ASR in the low single digits on curated human-sourced sets, but scores are not directly comparable across labs due to differing prompt collections and refusal-detection criteria.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing real-world robustness of frontier models against adversarial misuse attempts sourced from actual user interactions.

policy_note.caveat:
Tests format compliance, not response quality. A model that answers
wrong but follows instructions perfectly scores well. Two reporting
variants exist (prompt-level vs. instruction-level strict accuracy)
and the variant is not always disclosed.
policy_note.measures:
541 prompts paired with verifiable constraints (e.g., "respond in
exactly 3 paragraphs", "include the word X", "use only lowercase").
Scoring is rule-based: did the output satisfy each constraint?
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Prefer the "strict" variant when comparing across
labs; "loose" gives partial credit and inflates scores.
policy_note.intended_for: Measuring whether a model can follow detailed formatting instructions.

policy_note.caveat: Scores exhibit scaffold dependence: the VQA judge model chosen (e.g., GPT-4V vs. a smaller model) materially affects rankings, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable when judge models differ. The 'character' category boundary may vary across implementations, potentially conflating human-figure edits with broader object or style edits.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates text-guided image editing quality specifically on character/person subjects, using VQA-based alignment scoring to assess whether editing instructions (e.g., changing appearance, clothing, pose) are correctly reflected in the output image. Part of the GenAI-Bench suite, which decomposes image editing into semantic skill categories.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores reflect VQA-judged alignment between the editing instruction and the resulting image, typically expressed as a 0–1 or percentage alignment score. Frontier diffusion-based editing models generally score in the 0.6–0.85 range on character subcategories, but absolute values shift with the judge model.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking text-guided image editing models, particularly on tasks involving human figures or character-specific attributes.

policy_note.caveat: GenAI-Bench scores depend heavily on the automated VQA-based evaluation pipeline used for judging, which can diverge from human preference; different evaluator models or prompting scaffolds may yield significantly different scores. The 'creative' split specifically targets compositional and abstract edits, which may conflate difficulty with creativity.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates text-guided image editing quality using the GenAI-Bench framework, assessing how accurately a model applies creative and compositional edit instructions to source images across dimensions such as object manipulation, style transfer, and scene modification.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores reflect alignment between edited outputs and edit instructions, typically reported as a percentage or normalized score; frontier models on creative/compositional splits tend to cluster in a lower range than on simpler editing tasks due to increased instruction complexity.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating multimodal generative models on instruction-following image editing tasks.

policy_note.caveat: GenAI-Bench scores can vary significantly based on the VQA model used as the automatic evaluator (e.g., LLaVA vs. GPT-4V), making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless the same evaluator is specified. The infographics subset is a narrow slice of the full benchmark and may not generalize to photorealistic or artistic editing tasks.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates text-guided image editing quality on infographic-style images, assessing how well a generative AI model can apply editing instructions (e.g., color changes, object additions, text modifications) to structured visual content. Part of the GenAI-Bench suite, which uses human-aligned VQA-based scoring.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Scores are typically reported as a 0–1 or 0–100 alignment metric derived from VQA correctness; frontier model ranges and leaderboard standings depend on the evaluator version used.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating text-to-image editing models, particularly on structured/document-style visuals like charts, posters, and diagrams.

policy_note.caveat: Scores can vary substantially depending on the VQA model used to judge edits, introducing scaffold dependence. The object and environment sub-categories are sometimes reported separately and sometimes aggregated, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable if the exact split is not specified. As a relatively recent benchmark, frontier model saturation has not yet been widely reported, but headroom may narrow quickly.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates text-guided image editing models on their ability to accurately add, remove, replace, or modify objects and environmental elements (e.g., background, weather, scene context) within an image according to a text prompt. Part of the GenAI-Bench suite, which uses fine-grained compositional prompts and VQA-based automated scoring to assess editing faithfulness.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Scores are typically expressed as a percentage or normalized rating reflecting alignment between the edited image and the instruction, as judged by an automated VQA pipeline. Absolute numbers should be interpreted alongside the specific VQA judge used, as baselines shift between evaluations.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating or comparing text-guided image editing models on compositional, instruction-following editing tasks.

policy_note.caveat: As a narrow subtask within GenAI-Bench, scores are sensitive to the diffusion backbone and prompting scaffold used, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. The task's subjective nature means automated metrics may diverge from human preference judgments. No widely reported saturation data exists for this specific subtask.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a generative AI model's ability to edit product images by placing them into new background contexts while preserving product identity and appearance. Part of the broader GenAI-Bench suite covering compositional image editing tasks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; metrics typically reflect composite quality ratings (fidelity, context coherence, or human preference win-rate). Absolute scale depends on whether human evaluation or automated VQA-based scoring is used — compare only within the same evaluation protocol.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating image editing or text-to-image models for commercial or e-commerce applications, particularly background replacement and scene compositing quality.

policy_note.caveat: GenAI-Bench uses automated VQA-based scoring (e.g., BLIP-VQA or similar vision-language judges) which may not fully align with human aesthetic judgments on stylization quality. Scores can vary significantly depending on the judge model version used. The stylization sub-task is a narrow slice of the full benchmark suite, so results should not be generalized to overall image editing capability.
policy_note.measures: Measures a generative model's ability to apply artistic or visual stylization to images based on text prompts, as part of the broader GenAI-Bench evaluation suite. Tasks probe style transfer fidelity, adherence to stylistic descriptors (e.g., 'oil painting', 'watercolor', 'anime'), and preservation of content structure under style transformations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores reflect alignment between model output and stylization prompts as judged by an automated VQA scorer, typically on a 0–1 or percentage scale. Frontier diffusion and multimodal generation models generally score in the upper range, so meaningful differentiation tends to occur among mid-tier models.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating text-to-image or image-editing models on compositional instruction-following, specifically stylistic transformation tasks.

policy_note.caveat: Likely an Anthropic-internal evaluation; methodology, dataset size, and exact attack-type taxonomy are not publicly documented, making cross-lab comparisons difficult. Scores may be scaffold- and prompt-format-dependent since the same image content can be presented in varied contexts.
policy_note.measures: Measures whether a model will assist with attack planning (e.g., physical or cyber attacks) when the harmful request is conveyed through image inputs rather than plain text. Probes whether multimodal input pathways introduce safety regressions relative to text-only prompting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rate is better (the model should refuse or deflect attack-planning requests). Absolute scores are most meaningful as deltas across model versions or modalities rather than as standalone figures.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating whether multimodal capability introduces new attack surfaces or bypasses text-safety filters.

policy_note.caveat: Scoring is highly scaffold- and rubric-dependent: pass/fail rates shift with prompt framing, evaluator thresholds, and the specific taxonomy of 'extremism' applied. The evaluation suite is not publicly released, making cross-lab or cross-version comparisons unreliable. Results reported in model cards reflect the lab's internal criteria and may not generalize to other threat models.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates how a vision-language model responds to image inputs containing extremist content — such as propaganda, violent extremist imagery, or radicalization material — measuring whether the model refuses or otherwise handles such inputs in a policy-compliant way. Dataset size and exact composition are not publicly documented.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better safety compliance (fewer policy-violating outputs). No standardized public leaderboard exists; results are typically reported as a pass rate or refusal rate percentage within a single lab's model card, so numbers are only meaningful relative to prior versions of the same model.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing whether multimodal models appropriately decline to produce or amplify extremist content when that content is delivered via image rather than text.

policy_note.caveat: Appears to be an internal lab evaluation rather than a published benchmark, so methodology, dataset composition, and labeling criteria are not publicly documented. Scores are not directly comparable across labs that may define 'erotic' differently. Pass/refuse thresholds and exact metric definition (refusal rate, harm rate, etc.) vary by reporting lab.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a multimodal model appropriately refuses or otherwise safely handles image inputs containing erotic or sexually explicit content. Tests the model's content-safety behavior on visual stimuli rather than text-only prompts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Interpretation depends on the reported metric: if the score is a refusal rate on harmful content, higher is safer; if it is a harmful-output rate, lower is safer. No published frontier range is available due to the internal nature of the evaluation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating content-moderation and harm-avoidance capabilities of multimodal (vision-language) models.

policy_note.caveat: Likely an internal Anthropic evaluation suite; methodology, dataset size, and exact scoring rubric are not publicly documented, limiting external reproducibility and cross-model comparison. Scores may reflect both refusal rate and response quality, making it difficult to interpret a single number without the breakdown.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates model behavior on image inputs that involve hate-related content, probing whether the model appropriately refuses or handles images that contain or elicit hateful material. The task format involves presenting image inputs with hate-adjacent context and assessing the model's safety response.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate safer, more appropriate model responses to hate-related image inputs. Frontier model scores are not publicly benchmarked against a broad field, so results are most meaningful as intra-family comparisons across Claude generations.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing multimodal models' robustness to hate-related image inputs; primarily used in Anthropic model card reporting.

policy_note.caveat: Likely an internal or proprietary evaluation suite (e.g. from Anthropic or a similar lab); methodology, dataset size, and exact category taxonomy are not publicly documented, making cross-lab comparisons difficult. Scores may reflect scaffold and prompt framing choices as much as underlying model capability.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's safety behavior when presented with illicit or policy-violating image inputs — typically assessing refusal rates and appropriate non-compliance across categories such as illegal content, dangerous instructions, or prohibited material conveyed through images. Probes the multimodal safety alignment of vision-capable models.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better compliance with safety policies (more reliable refusal of illicit inputs). Absolute scale and frontier range are not publicly established; scores are most meaningful when compared across versions of the same model family.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating the robustness of multimodal refusal behavior in vision-language models.

policy_note.caveat: Likely an internal evaluation with undisclosed dataset size and labeling criteria, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. Scores depend heavily on the specific refusal threshold chosen and the harshness of the prompt accompanying the image; scaffold or system-prompt variation can shift results significantly.
policy_note.measures: Measures a multimodal model's rate of harmful or policy-violating responses when presented with image inputs related to self-harm topics. Probes whether visual context (e.g., images depicting self-harm methods or ideation cues) elicits unsafe text completions that a text-only prompt might not.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower harmful-response rate is better. Frontier models typically aim for near-zero rates on clear-violation inputs; differentiation emerges on ambiguous or clinical imagery where over-refusal is also a failure mode.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing multimodal harm-avoidance, particularly for models deployed in consumer-facing contexts where image upload is permitted.

policy_note.caveat: Heavily scaffold-dependent and baseline-relative: scores are expressed as comparisons to specific Gemini versions (1.5 Pro 002, 2.5 Pro, 2.5 Flash), making cross-model or cross-report comparisons unreliable without knowing the exact baseline used. The 'non-egregious' vs unmarked variants conflate distinct severity tiers, and cards do not consistently specify which tier is being reported.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a multimodal model generates unsafe or policy-violating text when given image inputs, with a specific 'non-egregious' sub-category tracking lower-severity violations. Results are typically reported as a relative rate against a Gemini baseline model rather than as an absolute score.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a lower score indicates fewer unsafe outputs. Because scores are relative to a named Gemini baseline, a value below 1.0 (or negative delta) means the evaluated model is safer than the baseline on this axis; the absolute scale is not standardized across reports.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating multimodal model safety, particularly for image captioning and visual question-answering deployments.

policy_note.caveat: Extremely small dataset (6 problems) means scores are noisy — one problem solved or missed swings the result by ~17 percentage points. Scaffold dependence is pronounced: chain-of-thought length, tool use (code interpreter, symbolic solvers), and human-in-the-loop verification protocols vary across lab evaluations, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. Saturation risk is emerging: frontier models already reach or exceed gold-medal thresholds (5/6), leaving little headroom to differentiate top models.
policy_note.measures: IMO 2025 measures olympiad-level mathematical problem-solving: 6 problems (algebra, combinatorics, geometry, number theory) from the 66th International Mathematical Olympiad held in July 2025. Models are scored pass@1 on whether they produce a fully correct solution on a single attempt, often with a human verifier confirming proof validity.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; score is fraction of 6 problems solved pass@1 (0/6 to 6/6), sometimes expressed as a percentage. A score of 5/6 (~83%) corresponds roughly to a gold-medal threshold. As of mid-2025, leading frontier models cluster between 4/6 and 6/6, so differences of a single problem carry outsized weight.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners assessing the frontier of formal and informal mathematical reasoning in large language models; useful for tracking progress on hard, competition-grade proof problems.

policy_note.caveat: Because the benchmark rewards abstention, models fine-tuned to be more refusal-prone may score artificially high without being genuinely better calibrated. Scoring conventions can vary across implementations (binary correct/incorrect vs. partial credit for explanation quality), which makes cross-report comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model correctly recognises and refuses coding tasks that are deliberately impossible to solve — e.g. requests with contradictory requirements or logically undefined outcomes — rather than hallucinating a plausible-looking but invalid solution. Measures calibration and honesty under pressure rather than raw coding ability.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; a perfect score means the model never attempts an impossible task. Frontier models that are heavily RLHF-tuned toward helpfulness may score lower than expected because compliance pressure works against correct refusal.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and evaluators assessing model reliability and sycophancy resistance; useful for teams building coding assistants where confidently wrong output is worse than an explicit refusal.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models saturate the English MC subset relatively quickly given the constrained 4-option format; random baseline is ~25%, leaving limited headroom to differentiate top models. Scores are sensitive to the context-window limit of the evaluated model — models that truncate the input rather than processing the full context are at a structural disadvantage, so reported scores should always be read alongside the model's stated context length.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to answer multiple-choice questions requiring comprehension and retrieval over ultra-long English documents exceeding 100k tokens. Tasks include novel-based Q&A and long-document understanding presented as 4-way multiple choice, tested at 0-shot.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are accuracy (0–100%). Random chance is ~25%. Capable frontier models with full context support typically score in the 70–90% range on this subset; scores below ~40% suggest inadequate long-context handling.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating long-context language model capabilities, particularly retrieval and comprehension over 100k+ token inputs.

policy_note.caveat: Performance is gated by a model's maximum context length — models without a 100k+ token window cannot be evaluated at all, making cross-model comparisons uneven. Scaffold dependence is significant: chunking strategy, prompt placement, and how the long text is fed to the model materially affect scores. Some frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5+) have reached high scores on the retrieval-heavy portion, narrowing differentiation at the top.
policy_note.measures: InfiniteBench En.QA evaluates open-ended question answering over English-language novels and books exceeding 100,000 tokens, requiring models to locate and synthesize information dispersed across very long documents. It tests genuine long-context retrieval and reasoning, not just extended-window processing.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as exact-match or F1 accuracy (0–100 scale). When InfiniteBench was released (early 2024), frontier models scored roughly 10–30 on En.QA; stronger long-context models have since pushed into the 30–60+ range. Compare only models with equivalent context-window sizes.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating long-context language model capabilities, particularly those benchmarking models claiming 100k+ token context windows.

policy_note.caveat: Scoring depends on a judge model (typically GPT-4) to assess each decomposed requirement, creating scaffold dependence — results can shift when the judge model or its prompt changes. As frontier models reach high DRFR scores, headroom for differentiation at the top of the leaderboard narrows.
policy_note.measures: InFoBench evaluates instruction-following fidelity by decomposing each instruction into atomic sub-requirements and measuring the fraction a model satisfies (Decomposed Requirements Following Ratio, DRFR). It probes fine-grained compliance with complex, multi-constraint natural-language instructions rather than coarse pass/fail judgments.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are expressed as a percentage of decomposed requirements satisfied (0–100%). Capable instruction-tuned frontier models typically score in the mid-to-high 80s or above.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers benchmarking instruction-tuned LLMs, particularly for evaluating whether models reliably satisfy all constraints in complex, multi-part prompts.

policy_note.caveat: The '+Prompt Injection' variant label indicates a meaningfully different threat surface than the base eval; scores across variants should not be aggregated or directly compared. Dataset composition, size, and pass/fail thresholds are not publicly documented, limiting external reproducibility. Results are highly scaffold-dependent: the same underlying model paired with different input-filter implementations will produce different scores.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model's input-layer content filter correctly blocks requests touching restricted biology topics (e.g., dual-use research of concern, bioweapons-adjacent queries). The '+Prompt Injection' variant probes whether adversarially crafted injections can circumvent the filter before the main model ever processes the request.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger filtering (more restricted-biology requests correctly blocked). Because this is a safety refusal metric, frontier models are expected to score near 100%; a score meaningfully below that signals a filtering gap. The prompt-injection variant is harder, so scores there are typically lower than the base variant.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety evaluators, policy teams, and model card reviewers assessing biosecurity-related input-filtering robustness in frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: Results are highly scaffold- and injection-technique-dependent: a model that resists one injection vector may fail another, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless methodology is held constant. The "+Prompt Injection" variant conflates two failure modes (filter evasion and injection susceptibility), so a single score does not distinguish which layer failed. No public standardized dataset or leaderboard is widely established for this specific combined evaluation.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model's input-side safety filters blocking restricted biology content (e.g., dual-use pathogen or bioweapons-adjacent requests) can be bypassed via prompt injection attacks. Evaluates the robustness of content filters specifically under adversarial injection conditions, not baseline refusal behavior alone.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better resistance (fewer successful filter bypasses). Because this tests a rare-event failure mode, even small absolute differences (e.g., 2% vs. 5% bypass rate) can be policy-significant; do not interpret scores through a typical accuracy lens.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, red-teamers, and policy evaluators assessing model robustness against adversarial attempts to elicit dangerous biology content.

policy_note.caveat: The base benchmark and the '+Prompt Injection' variant measure meaningfully different threat models (naive misuse vs. adversarial bypass), so scores across the two variants are not directly comparable and should not be aggregated. Results are also highly sensitive to system-prompt and scaffold configuration, meaning published numbers may reflect deployment choices rather than intrinsic model capability.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model's input filters correctly block requests for restricted chemistry content — such as synthesis routes for dangerous substances — across a set of adversarial prompts. The '+Prompt Injection' variant additionally probes whether prompt-injection-mediated attacks can bypass those same filters.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher block/refusal rates are better (lower risk). Compare variants separately; a model that scores well on the base task may still be vulnerable on the +Prompt Injection variant.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating model robustness against chemical-domain misuse and prompt-injection-based safety bypasses.

policy_note.caveat: The combined slug conflates two distinct failure modes — baseline refusal of restricted chemistry prompts and susceptibility to prompt injection — making it difficult to attribute score differences to one mechanism. Scores depend heavily on the specific injection templates used and the filtering scaffold, so results may not transfer across deployment configurations.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model's input-level content filters for restricted chemistry requests (e.g., synthesis routes for dangerous substances) can be defeated by prompt injection attacks embedded in the input. Probes the robustness of safety filters under adversarial manipulation rather than direct refusal behavior.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate the model (or its filter layer) successfully resists prompt-injection attempts to elicit restricted chemistry content. Frontier safety-focused models are expected to score near 100%; any meaningful drop below that signals a exploitable gap.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating the robustness of input-side safety mitigations against adversarial jailbreak techniques in CBRN-adjacent domains.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are expressed as relative comparisons (e.g., 'relative to Gemini 1.5 Pro 002', 'relative vs Gemini 2.5 Pro'), so absolute capability levels cannot be inferred and cross-provider comparisons are not meaningful. Different baselines across card versions create label conflation: a '+5%' against Gemini 1.5 Pro 002 is not comparable to a '+5%' against Gemini 2.5 Pro. The evaluation methodology (human raters vs. automated judge) is not publicly specified, adding additional uncertainty.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates how well a model follows safety-related instructions — such as correctly refusing disallowed requests or adhering to specified content constraints — relative to a named Gemini baseline model. Reported as a relative comparison score rather than an absolute value, making the baseline model identity essential context for interpretation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher (more positive relative score) is better, indicating stronger safety instruction-following than the named baseline. Because all scores are relative, the reported number only has meaning when the baseline model is known; treat cross-card comparisons with caution.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating Gemini-family models on safety instruction adherence, primarily within Google's own model cards.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to how the conflict is framed: a mildly phrased user override may produce different behavior than a forceful one, making aggregate numbers hard to interpret across papers. There is also genuine normative ambiguity — some developer/user conflicts involve user safety or autonomy concerns where blind deference to the developer is the wrong answer, so high scores are not unambiguously good. No standard public test suite has been widely adopted under this exact slug, so reported numbers may reflect bespoke internal evals with differing methodology.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model correctly prioritizes developer-level (system prompt) instructions over conflicting user-turn requests, probing adherence to a principal instruction hierarchy. Tasks present explicit conflicts between what the developer specified and what the user asks for, then score whether the model defers to the higher-privileged party.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are generally better, indicating the model respects the developer/operator layer over the user layer in conflicts. Context matters: a model that scores 100% may be over-deferring to system prompts even when the user has legitimate safety needs. Compare scores only within studies using identical conflict-framing methodology.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and alignment researchers, model evaluators, and developers building multi-tenant or operator-mediated applications who need to understand how a model responds when principal instructions conflict.

policy_note.caveat: No standardized public dataset exists under this exact name; reported scores almost certainly reflect proprietary internal evaluations, making cross-model comparisons unreliable. Results are highly scaffold-dependent — conflict severity, framing, and how explicitly the hierarchy is stated all shift scores substantially. Different labs use different taxonomies (system vs. developer vs. user vs. operator), so label conflation across model cards is likely.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model correctly prioritizes system-level (operator) instructions over developer/user-level instructions when the two conflict, evaluating the model's adherence to a principal authority hierarchy. Tasks typically present paired instructions from different privilege levels and score whether the model resolves conflicts in the expected direction.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent the fraction of conflict scenarios where the model correctly defers to the higher-privilege principal. Because this is typically an internal eval, there is no established frontier range — treat absolute numbers as lab-specific and focus on trends across model versions from the same lab.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy analysts assessing how reliably frontier models enforce operator-level authority and resist privilege escalation or prompt injection from lower-trust principals.

policy_note.caveat: The slug conflates several distinct evaluation designs — OpenAI's internal instruction-hierarchy evals, academic reproductions, and ad-hoc red-teaming suites — making cross-model score comparisons unreliable. Results are highly sensitive to conflict framing: models that robustly follow system prompts against obvious override attempts may still capitulate under indirect or jailbreak-style user pressure. No single canonical dataset is universally adopted.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model correctly follows system-prompt instructions when they directly conflict with user-turn instructions, probing adherence to a privilege hierarchy in which operator-level context should take precedence over end-user requests. The task format typically presents paired scenarios where system and user directives are in explicit tension and asks the model to choose which to obey.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; 100% indicates the model always defers to the system prompt in a conflict. Frontier models span roughly 60–95% depending on conflict type and prompt format, so absolute scores should not be compared across evaluation frameworks without confirming identical methodology.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and alignment researchers assessing how reliably models respect operator-defined constraints when users attempt to override them; also relevant to product teams building multi-tenant or system-prompt-gated deployments.

policy_note.caveat: This appears to be a narrow, purpose-built safety probe rather than a widely published benchmark; scoring methodology and dataset size are not publicly documented in detail. Results may be highly scaffold- and prompt-template-dependent, making cross-model comparisons unreliable without identical evaluation harnesses.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model can be jailbroken via a developer-level system message that frames the AI as a tutor, probing robustness of the instruction hierarchy against safety-bypassing prompts injected at the system-prompt tier. Evaluates whether models correctly resist policy violations even when the developer message explicitly instructs unsafe behavior.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger resistance to the jailbreak; a score of 1.0 (100%) means the model never complied with the unsafe developer instruction. Frontier safety-focused models are expected to score near the ceiling, so low variance at the top may limit differentiation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and developers assessing model robustness to jailbreak attempts delivered through the system-prompt (developer-message) channel, particularly in instructional or tutoring deployment contexts.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are scaffold-dependent: the specific jailbreak prompt template and evaluation rubric used by each lab affect pass/fail rates, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable without a shared harness. As a single-scenario probe it captures one narrow attack vector; a model may pass this while failing other instruction-hierarchy tests with different personas or framings.
policy_note.measures: Measures whether a model correctly follows operator-level (system message) instructions when a user attempts a jailbreak framed as a tutoring interaction. Tests the model's ability to maintain the privilege hierarchy—honoring system-prompt constraints even when the user message constructs a plausible educational pretext to override them.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score of 1.0 (or 100%) means the model consistently refused to violate the system-message constraint across all jailbreak attempts in the tutor scenario. Frontier models generally score high on simple hierarchy probes, so scores below ~0.8 indicate meaningful vulnerability.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing robustness of instruction-priority mechanisms and resistance to persona-based jailbreak attempts at the system-message level.

policy_note.caveat: Results are not independently reproducible — the methodology, scaffold, and pass/fail criteria are proprietary and may differ across labs that report an 'internal agentic coding' figure. Scores are heavily scaffold-dependent: the same underlying model can produce materially different numbers under different agent frameworks. Cross-lab or cross-paper comparisons should be treated with extreme caution.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to complete multi-step, tool-assisted coding tasks autonomously in an agentic loop setting. Because the benchmark is internal to the reporting lab, dataset size, task format, and evaluation harness are not publicly disclosed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; typically reported as a pass-rate percentage. Because the benchmark is not standardized, reported numbers should be read as lab-internal progress signals rather than absolute capability claims.
policy_note.intended_for: Internal model-development teams at AI labs assessing agentic coding capability during pre-release evaluation; not designed for external comparison.

policy_note.caveat: Results are reported as 'best run,' meaning cherry-picked peak performance rather than median or average across trials, which inflates apparent capability and makes cross-model comparisons unreliable. As an internal (non-public) suite, the dataset, protocol, and baseline conditions are opaque — independent replication is not possible, and there is no external validation against contamination or scorer bias.
policy_note.measures: An internal benchmark suite measuring the speedup factor AI assistance provides on research tasks; the reported figure is a ratio indicating how many times faster AI-assisted work is relative to an unassisted baseline. Dataset size and task composition are not publicly disclosed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score of N means tasks were completed N× faster with AI assistance than without. Because methodology is unpublished and only best-run figures are reported, scores across different labs or model versions should not be treated as directly comparable.
policy_note.intended_for: Internal lab researchers and technical decision-makers evaluating AI-assisted research productivity; not designed for external benchmark comparisons.

name: Internal AI Research Evaluation Suite 2 (advanced tests pass rate)

policy_note.caveat: This is an internal, non-public benchmark; methodology, dataset composition, and scoring details are not independently verifiable. Results are not reproducible outside the originating lab, and comparisons across labs are not meaningful. The 'advanced tests' variant label suggests only a subset of the full suite is reported, making cross-card comparisons unreliable if labs differ in which subset they expose.
policy_note.measures: Pass rate on the 'advanced' subset of a proprietary internal AI research evaluation suite (version 2), assessing harder research-oriented tasks compared to the suite's baseline tier. Dataset size and exact task format are not publicly disclosed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher pass rate is better; reported as a percentage (0–100%). Without a public leaderboard or known frontier range, scores should only be interpreted relative to other results from the same lab using the same suite version.
policy_note.intended_for: Internal model development teams tracking progress on harder research-capability tasks across training runs or model versions.

name: Internal AI Research Evaluation Suite 2 (basic tests pass rate)

policy_note.caveat: This is an internal, non-public benchmark with no published methodology, making independent verification and cross-lab comparison impossible. 'Basic tests pass rate' is an underspecified metric — the difficulty threshold, test domains, and grading criteria are opaque. Results are not directly comparable across labs or model versions unless the suite definition is held constant and disclosed.
policy_note.measures: An internal evaluation suite used by an AI lab to assess whether a model passes a set of basic functional tests; the reported metric is the pass rate (fraction of tests passed) on what the lab designates as foundational or entry-level checks. Dataset size, task format, and domain coverage are not publicly documented.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score represents the percentage of basic tests passed. Without published baseline distributions or frontier ranges, scores cannot be contextualized against other models.
policy_note.intended_for: AI lab researchers and internal evaluators tracking whether a model meets baseline capability thresholds during development; not designed for external benchmarking or cross-organization comparison.

name: Internal Model Evaluation and Use Survey

policy_note.caveat: The 'hard variant' label may be inconsistently applied across model cards — some cards may report scores against the standard kernel optimization benchmark under the same name, making cross-card comparisons unreliable. Scaffold and tooling dependence is likely significant: scores can vary substantially depending on whether the model has access to a compiler, profiler, or iterative execution loop.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's ability to write or optimize low-level computational kernels (e.g., GPU/CUDA or CPU kernels) for performance, targeting harder problem instances than the standard variant. Tasks likely require correctness plus meeting stricter efficiency or throughput targets.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. As a hard variant, frontier model scores are likely lower than on the standard version; exact score ranges are not well-documented publicly, so relative rankings across models are more informative than absolute scores.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and engineers evaluating frontier models on low-level code optimization and systems programming capability.

policy_note.caveat: Highly susceptible to saturation: strong frontier models routinely achieve near-perfect scores on 32K retrieval tasks, making it ineffective for differentiating top-tier models. Being fully synthetic, it measures mechanical attention span rather than real-world retrieval utility. Scores are scaffold- and prompt-format sensitive — different padding strategies or key formats can shift results noticeably.
policy_note.measures: Tests a model's ability to retrieve the correct value for a specified key from a context window filled entirely with synthetic key-value pairs. The observed variant uses a 32K-token context, probing faithful long-context retrieval with no semantic reasoning required — pure lookup.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models cluster near 95–100% at 32K, so this benchmark is more useful for identifying regressions or comparing mid-tier models than for ranking top performers.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating a model's effective context window and long-context fidelity, particularly to detect degradation at specific context depths.

policy_note.caveat: The cloning scenarios subset is narrow and highly specialized; strong performance may reflect memorization of standard molecular biology protocols from training data rather than genuine reasoning. As a dual-use biology benchmark, scores are sometimes withheld or interpreted cautiously in public model cards due to biosecurity sensitivity.
policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to reason through molecular cloning scenarios in a biology laboratory context, including tasks such as selecting restriction enzymes, designing cloning strategies, and choosing appropriate vectors. Evaluated under a 10-shot prompting setup.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better. Scores are reported as percentage correct on multiple-choice or scenario-based questions; random-chance baseline depends on the number of answer choices (typically 4–5 options). Frontier model scores cluster in the 60–85% range on cloning subtasks, making mid-range differentiation meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and biology-AI evaluators assessing the extent to which frontier models have internalized wet-lab molecular biology knowledge, with particular attention to dual-use biosecurity risk.

policy_note.caveat: Only vision-capable (multimodal) models can be evaluated, so scores are not comparable across text-only vs. multimodal model families. As a subset of LAB-Bench, aggregate suite scores may obscure FigQA-specific performance; always check the per-task breakdown. Early frontier results suggest the task remains moderately challenging but rapid multimodal progress may push toward saturation.
policy_note.measures: FigQA is a multiple-choice visual question-answering task within the LAB-Bench suite, requiring models to interpret figures—charts, plots, and diagrams—drawn from biology and life-sciences research papers. It probes whether a model can extract quantitative and qualitative information from scientific visuals to answer targeted questions.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; scores are reported as percent correct on multiple-choice items. Frontier multimodal models (as of early 2025) cluster in the 60–80% range, with random-chance baselines depending on the number of answer choices (typically 4-way).
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and computational biologists assessing multimodal models on scientific-literature comprehension; useful for labs choosing models for automated literature review or data-extraction pipelines.

policy_note.caveat: As a domain-specific biology subtask, scores can vary meaningfully depending on whether the model has encountered similar sequence databases or textbook-style problems during pretraining, raising contamination concerns. Performance may also be scaffold-sensitive since few-shot prompt formatting affects accuracy on structured science QA.
policy_note.measures: SeqQA is a subtask within the LAB-Bench suite that tests a model's ability to answer questions about biological sequences — DNA, RNA, and proteins — covering properties, annotations, and sequence-level analysis. Questions are presented in a multiple-choice format evaluated under a 10-shot setting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as percentage accuracy on multiple-choice questions. Frontier models typically score in the 60–85% range on SeqQA, leaving meaningful headroom compared to saturated general-knowledge benchmarks.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating AI models for life sciences research assistance, particularly tasks involving biological sequence comprehension.

policy_note.caveat: Like most static Python coding benchmarks, LBPP-Python is susceptible to training-data contamination if its problems appear in pretraining corpora. Frontier models have reached high pass-rates on simpler Python benchmarks (e.g. HumanEval), so saturation may limit its ability to differentiate top-tier models over time.
policy_note.measures: LBPP-Python evaluates large language models on Python code generation using a set of programming problems designed to go beyond basic exercises. Models are prompted to write Python functions or scripts, and correctness is measured by executing the generated code against hidden test cases.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent pass@k (typically pass@1), ranging from 0–100%. Frontier models generally score in the 60–90% range depending on problem difficulty tier; lower scores indicate meaningful gaps in code generation capability.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing LLM coding ability in Python; useful for tracking progress on functional code generation beyond toy-level tasks.

policy_note.caveat: Performance varies enormously across the 162 subtasks — aggregate scores can mask strong performance on easy tasks and weak performance on harder ones, so per-task breakdowns are more informative than single-number summaries. Coverage is predominantly US law, limiting generalizability to other jurisdictions. Some individual subtasks have small test sets (dozens of examples), increasing variance on those tasks.
policy_note.measures: LegalBench evaluates legal reasoning across 162 tasks collaboratively designed by law students and lawyers, covering six reasoning types: issue spotting, rule recall, rule application, rule conclusion, interpretation, and rhetorical understanding. Tasks use formats including binary classification, short-answer, and multiple choice, spanning US contract law, statutory interpretation, and more.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; accuracy is reported per-task and aggregated. Frontier models (GPT-4 class) score in the 60–75% range on aggregate, but performance on harder subtasks (e.g., statutory interpretation) is considerably lower. Comparisons should ideally report per-task or per-category breakdowns rather than a single aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and legal technologists evaluating LLM legal reasoning capability; useful for comparing models before deployment in legal-adjacent applications.

policy_note.measures: LengthCtrl evaluates a model's ability to follow explicit length constraints in its outputs — for example, generating a response of exactly N words or within a specified token range. It probes fine-grained instruction-following specifically around output length control.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better compliance with specified length targets. Frontier models vary significantly in their ability to hit exact length targets versus approximate ranges; scores near 100% indicate near-perfect length adherence.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating instruction-following precision, particularly length adherence, in language models.

policy_note.caveat: The contamination-free property is time-bounded: questions released today will eventually appear in future training corpora, so the benchmark's advantage erodes as models are retrained. Scores are not directly comparable across releases without version-pinning, because the question pool changes; published leaderboard numbers should always be read alongside the LiveBench release date.
policy_note.measures: LiveBench evaluates LLMs across six task categories — math, coding, reasoning, language, data analysis, and instruction following — using questions derived from recently released sources (papers, datasets, news) to minimise training-data contamination. Questions are refreshed monthly; total count varies but typically sits in the hundreds at any snapshot.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as overall accuracy percentages with per-category breakdowns. Frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.x, Gemini 1.5) typically cluster in the 50–75% overall range depending on release vintage, giving reasonable separation at the top.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners who need a low-contamination alternative to static benchmarks for evaluating general-purpose LLMs; useful for tracking progress without the saturation ceiling that affects MMLU and similar fixed datasets.

policy_note.caveat: Cross-paper comparisons are unreliable because scores depend heavily on which date window of problems is evaluated — a model tested on problems from 2023-Q4 through 2024-Q2 may score very differently than one tested on a later window. Exact training cutoffs are often undisclosed, so contamination cannot be fully ruled out. Easy-tier problems show emerging saturation for top frontier models.
policy_note.measures: LiveCodeBench evaluates code generation on competitive programming problems (sourced from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces) released after each model's training cutoff, minimizing contamination. It covers four scenarios: code generation, self-repair, test-output prediction, and code execution reasoning, with primary scores reported as pass@1 on the code generation task.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are pass@1 (fraction of problems solved on the first attempt). Frontier models typically range from ~50% to ~75%+ on code generation depending on the date window, with harder problem tiers substantially lower. Always note the evaluation date range when comparing results across papers.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners benchmarking LLM coding ability with reduced training-data contamination; useful for tracking progress on competitive programming tasks over time.

policy_note.caveat: Two non-comparable variants are frequently conflated: pass@1 (greedy or temperature-0 single attempt) and pass@k (best-of-k sampling), and model cards often omit which was used. Scores are window-specific — this four-month slice is not directly comparable to earlier or later LiveCodeBench ranges. Models released after early 2025 may have seen some of these problems in post-cutoff fine-tuning data, partially undermining the contamination-resistance goal.
policy_note.measures: LiveCodeBench evaluates code generation on competitive programming problems scraped from LeetCode, Codeforces, and AtCoder that were published between October 1, 2024 and February 1, 2025, using hidden test-case execution to judge correctness. The rolling date window is designed to minimize training-data contamination; pass@1 (single attempt) and pass@k (multiple attempts) are both common reporting modes.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as a percentage. On pass@1, frontier models (Claude 3.5/3.7, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.x) typically score in the 40–70% range for this date window — harder recent problems pull scores lower than earlier windows. Always verify whether a reported number is pass@1 or pass@k before comparing across cards.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners benchmarking frontier model coding ability on genuinely unseen competitive programming problems, where contamination from standard static benchmarks is a concern.

policy_note.caveat: Because problems are drawn from a rolling live window, difficulty and topic distribution shift across time slices — scores on this 4-month window are not directly comparable to earlier or later LiveCodeBench windows. The 'single attempt' variant (pass@1) produces lower absolute scores than n-sample estimates; compare only within the same attempt setting. Contamination risk is lower than static benchmarks but not zero, as some frontier labs may have scraped recent contest sites.
policy_note.measures: LiveCodeBench evaluates code generation by testing models on competitive-programming problems sourced from LeetCode, Codeforces, and AtCoder that were published between January 1, 2025 and May 1, 2025. Models must produce correct executable code judged by hidden test cases, scored as pass@1 (single attempt).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent the percentage of problems solved on the first attempt (pass@1). As of early 2025, top frontier models score roughly 50–75% on recent LiveCodeBench windows; scores below ~30% indicate weak competitive-programming-level coding ability.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating functional code generation ability on realistic, recently-published competitive programming problems with low contamination risk.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to the problem time window sampled (e.g., last 3 months vs. all-time), so cross-report comparisons are only valid when the same window is used. The variant strings reveal two major label-conflation axes: (1) single-attempt pass@1 vs. multiple-attempt pass@k, and (2) standard inference vs. extended/chain-of-thought reasoning — extended reasoning consistently inflates scores, making those numbers not directly comparable to standard pass@1 figures. Always confirm which axis applies before comparing numbers across cards.
policy_note.measures: LiveCodeBench v5 evaluates code generation on competitive programming problems drawn continuously from LeetCode, Codeforces, and AtCoder after model training cutoffs, reporting pass@1 on hidden test cases. Its rolling collection design is intended to reduce training-data contamination relative to static coding benchmarks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as a percentage (0–100). Frontier models on recent problem windows typically score roughly 30–65% at pass@1 under standard inference, with extended-reasoning variants pushing some models above 70%. A model's relative rank can shift substantially depending on problem difficulty tier and time window chosen.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners benchmarking code generation and competitive-programming reasoning in frontier language models.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to the time window: models whose training cutoff post-dates May 2025 may have seen these problems, reintroducing the contamination the 'live' design tries to prevent. Results are not directly comparable across versions (v1–v6) because each covers a different date range and difficulty distribution. Scaffold and execution-environment differences (e.g., code-execution harness, language version) can shift scores materially.
policy_note.measures: LiveCodeBench v6 measures code-generation ability on competitive programming problems drawn from LeetCode, Codeforces, and AtCoder published between January 1, 2025 and May 1, 2025. Models are evaluated on functional correctness (pass@1) against hidden test cases across problems of varying difficulty.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are pass@1 (fraction of problems solved on the first attempt). As of early 2026, top frontier models score roughly 60–75% on the v6 window; scores below ~40% indicate limited competitive-programming competence.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners comparing frontier model coding ability on recently published, contamination-resistant competitive programming problems.

policy_note.caveat: No widely recognized, standardized benchmark with this exact name is known in the public literature as of mid-2025. This slug may refer to an internal, proprietary, or ad-hoc evaluation used by a specific lab, or may be a self-reported capability category rather than a reproducible benchmark. Results are likely not comparable across different model cards.
policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to reason about or perform tasks related to optimizing the training process of large language models, such as hyperparameter selection, compute efficiency, convergence analysis, or architectural choices. The exact task format and dataset size are not publicly documented for a canonical benchmark under this name.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are generally better, but without a canonical definition of scale or scoring methodology, cross-model comparisons should be treated with caution. Check the originating model card for the specific evaluation protocol used.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners evaluating a model's meta-level reasoning about LLM training workflows, compute efficiency, and optimization strategies.

policy_note.caveat: Pre- vs. post-mitigation variant labels are not interchangeable — a post-mitigation score cannot be compared against a pre-mitigation score from a different model. Scoring depends heavily on the elicitation methodology and the specific threat scenarios chosen, making cross-lab comparisons difficult. The benchmark is not publicly released in full to prevent adversarial misuse, limiting independent replication.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether AI models provide meaningful uplift to actors seeking to cause biological harm, across three capability stages: Ideation (generating attack concepts), Acquisition (obtaining materials/agents), and Formulation (producing or weaponizing agents). Each stage is scored both before and after safety mitigations are applied, measuring both raw model risk and the effectiveness of mitigations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower scores indicate less uplift provided (safer behavior). Pre-mitigation scores establish a baseline risk level; post-mitigation scores reflect residual risk after safety interventions. The gap between the two indicates mitigation effectiveness. Absolute scores are not typically published publicly.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing catastrophic biosecurity risk in frontier models; intended for internal red-teaming and regulatory reporting rather than general leaderboard use.

policy_note.caveat: Scoring direction is ambiguous without knowing the benchmark's framing: a high score could reflect either dangerous capability (model complies and provides uplift) or strong refusal (model declines appropriately). Results are highly scaffold- and prompt-dependent; small prompt variations can produce large score swings. The 'Task 1' suffix implies a series, and conflation across numbered variants may occur when labs report scores without specifying the exact task index.
policy_note.measures: Assesses whether a model provides meaningful technical uplift on extended, multi-step virology tasks — such as pathogen enhancement, synthesis, or acquisition questions — that could pose biosecurity risks. Task format involves long-form prompts requiring detailed scientific reasoning about dangerous biological material.
policy_note.how_to_read: Interpretation depends on benchmark framing: if scoring refusal, higher is safer; if scoring compliance/accuracy, lower is safer. Typical use is as a red-line threshold test rather than a continuous ranking — frontier models are compared against an absolute safety threshold, not ranked against each other.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating dangerous-capability thresholds and biosecurity risks in frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: Biosecurity-adjacent benchmarks carry dual-use sensitivity: high scores may indicate dangerous uplift potential rather than desirable capability, making 'higher is better' framing context-dependent. The 'overall' label suggests aggregation over subtasks whose individual weighting is not publicly documented, which can obscure where a model actually excels or fails.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates AI model performance on long-form virology tasks requiring detailed, expert-level responses about virological concepts, mechanisms, or procedures. The 'overall' variant aggregates scores across all subtasks within Task 1 of the evaluation suite.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate greater virology task completion ability; in a safety context this may be undesirable. Scores should be interpreted alongside per-subtask breakdowns — the overall aggregate may mask high performance on the most sensitive question types.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, biosecurity policy analysts, and lab red-teamers assessing whether frontier models provide meaningful uplift to actors seeking virology expertise for potentially harmful purposes.

policy_note.caveat: This benchmark sits in dual-use territory: a higher score indicates greater virology capability but may simultaneously signal elevated biosecurity risk, so raw score comparisons across models must be interpreted with care depending on whether the use case is capability assessment or risk auditing. Scoring methodology and exact question set are not widely published, limiting independent reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to produce detailed, long-form answers to expert-level virology questions, probing depth of biological knowledge and willingness to engage with technically sensitive content. The 'Task 2' designation suggests a second-wave or harder subset within a broader virology evaluation suite.
policy_note.how_to_read: Direction depends on framing: higher scores indicate greater virology knowledge depth, which is desirable for scientific utility but potentially concerning for dual-use risk. Consult the benchmark's own risk rubric before treating higher as straightforwardly better.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, biosecurity policy analysts, and lab red-teamers evaluating frontier model risk profiles in the life-sciences domain.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly dependent on the video-sampling strategy used (frames per second, total frames passed to the model), making cross-system comparisons unreliable unless sampling parameters are identical. Context-window limits of current frontier models mean many submissions process only a fraction of each video's frames, conflating long-video reasoning ability with context capacity.
policy_note.measures: LongVideoBench evaluates multimodal models on question-answering over long-form video content, probing temporal reasoning, event tracking, and cross-segment comprehension across videos ranging from under a minute to over an hour. Tasks are multiple-choice questions that require integrating information spread across different temporal positions in the video.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (%) on multiple-choice questions. Frontier models (as of early 2025) typically score in the 55–70% range, with human performance estimated above 85%, leaving meaningful headroom.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and practitioners assessing how well vision-language models handle temporal reasoning and long-context video understanding.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to the number of few-shot examples and prompt format, so 1-shot results are not directly comparable to 0-shot or 5-shot runs reported elsewhere. Metric choice matters: chrF++ correlates better with human judgement for morphologically rich low-resource languages than BLEU. High-resource language pairs within the same benchmark suite inflate aggregate scores, masking poor performance on the truly low-resource tail.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates machine translation quality into and out of low-resource languages using the FLORES-200 (~1000 professionally translated sentences across 200 languages) and NTREX-128 (news-domain test references across 128 languages) datasets. The 1-shot variant provides a single in-context translation example before asking the model to translate a held-out sentence, typically scored with chrF++ or BLEU.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. chrF++ is reported on a 0–100 scale; frontier models typically score 50–70+ on moderate-resource languages and considerably lower on very low-resource ones. BLEU scores on the same sets run roughly 10–30 points lower than chrF++. Compare only within the same metric, shot count, and language-pair subset.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers assessing multilingual coverage and translation quality, especially for underrepresented languages where standard MT benchmarks have thin evaluation sets.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a significant concern: frontier models routinely score above 85–90%, leaving little headroom to differentiate top systems. Because LSAT questions are widely circulated in commercial prep materials, training-data contamination is a plausible confound. CoT scaffold choice (e.g., greedy vs. self-consistency) can materially shift reported scores.
