policy_note.measures: Tests logical and analytical reasoning through multiple-choice questions drawn from the Law School Admission Test, covering logical reasoning (argument analysis, inference) and analytical reasoning (constraint-based logic puzzles). Commonly evaluated in a 5-shot chain-of-thought setting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as percent correct (0–100). Human baseline is roughly 60–75% (median test-taker); strong frontier models frequently exceed 85–92%, making discrimination at the top of the leaderboard difficult.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating general reasoning, logical deduction, and argument comprehension in language models; useful for comparing mid-tier models where saturation is less severe.

policy_note.caveat: Performance is highly scaffold-dependent: models that subsample frames sparsely versus those with native long-video processing show large score gaps unrelated to underlying reasoning ability, making cross-system comparisons unreliable unless the frame-sampling strategy is reported.
policy_note.measures: LVBench evaluates multimodal models on long-video question answering, using multiple-choice questions over videos that average roughly one hour in length. It probes temporal reasoning, event retrieval, and holistic comprehension across extended video content that cannot be answered from a few sampled frames.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; scores are reported as percentage correct on multiple-choice questions. The benchmark is intentionally difficult — frontier multimodal models as of early 2025 typically score in the 30–60% range, well below estimated human performance, so there is currently no saturation concern.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and labs evaluating multimodal models on long-form video understanding; useful for distinguishing models that genuinely process extended temporal context from those relying on local-clip heuristics.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent — the manipulator model's capability and strategy significantly affect how hard the task is for the target, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable unless the attacker model is held constant. The benchmark is relatively narrow in scope (single codeword elicitation) and may not generalize to real-world multi-turn manipulation resistance.
policy_note.measures: MakeMeSay tests a model's resistance to social engineering: an adversarial agent tries to manipulate a target model into uttering a secret codeword without revealing what the codeword is, while the target model is instructed to avoid saying it. It probes susceptibility to indirect prompt injection and conversational manipulation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower success rate for the manipulator (i.e., the target model says the codeword less often) is better for the target model. Frontier safety-focused models typically resist elicitation at higher rates than base or less-aligned models; exact published ranges vary by attacker model used.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and red-teamers evaluating a model's robustness to social engineering and indirect prompt injection attacks.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the same model may refuse under one agent harness but comply under another depending on system-prompt framing, tool availability, and multi-turn pressure. Pass/fail thresholds and prompt sets are not standardized across labs, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless the exact evaluation setup is identical.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether an AI model acting as a coding agent will produce malicious code (malware, exploits, backdoors, or other harmful artifacts) when prompted or manipulated to do so. Probes refusal robustness under adversarial task framing in an agentic coding context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rates (fewer malicious artifacts produced) indicate safer behavior; a score near 0% is the target. Frontier safety evaluations typically aim for near-zero rates on clearly malicious tasks, so small absolute differences at the low end can be meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and frontier labs assessing model compliance with harmful coding requests in agentic settings; relevant for pre-deployment safety evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic framework wrapping the model (action space, tool set, retry logic) substantially affects outcomes, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. The exact task distribution and pass/fail criteria are typically internal and not publicly audited, limiting independent replication.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether an AI model with computer-use (GUI agent) capabilities can be manipulated into completing malicious tasks—such as installing malware, exfiltrating data, or bypassing access controls—when operating autonomously on a desktop or browser environment. Tests refusal robustness under adversarial or socially-engineered prompts in an agentic setting.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate stronger resistance to misuse (more refusals of malicious instructions); lower scores flag concerning compliance. No broad public leaderboard exists—results are typically reported as refusal rates or task-completion rates on a 0–100% scale within individual lab safety reports.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams assessing whether frontier models are safe to deploy in autonomous computer-use contexts; relevant to responsible-scaling policy evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: The observed variant 'without mitigations' implies a paired 'with mitigations' condition exists; scores are not comparable across variants and reporting the unmitigated figure in isolation can be misleading about deployed safety. Refusal rate alone does not capture partial compliance or subtle harm; a model may refuse overtly malicious phrasings while complying with lightly reworded equivalents. Dataset composition (difficulty mix, harm categories covered) is not publicly specified, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model refuses to execute harmful or malicious tasks when operating as a computer-use agent (controlling a desktop/browser environment). Higher refusal rates indicate safer agentic behavior against prompts requesting actions such as credential theft, unauthorized access, or destructive file operations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is safer — a refusal rate of 100% means the model declined every malicious computer-use prompt in the evaluation set. Frontier models with mitigations disabled typically score well below their mitigated counterparts; absolute scores should always be read alongside the variant label ('without mitigations' vs. baseline).
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy audiences evaluating the baseline agentic safety of frontier models prior to deployment-time guardrails.

name: Malicious Use of Claude Code - Malicious Refusal Rate

policy_note.caveat: Results are only meaningful in relative terms across variants ('without mitigations', 'with previous mitigations', 'with new mitigations') — the absolute refusal rate depends heavily on the composition and difficulty of the elicitation prompt set, which is not publicly disclosed. Scores are not directly comparable across model versions if the prompt set changes between evaluations.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which Claude Code refuses to carry out requests classified as malicious (e.g., writing malware, enabling unauthorized access, or facilitating harm). Evaluated across prompt sets designed to elicit harmful agentic code-execution behavior, with variant splits comparing behavior under different mitigation configurations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better — a higher malicious refusal rate means the model more reliably declines harmful requests. Scores are percentages (0–100); the meaningful signal is the delta between variant columns rather than any single number in isolation.
policy_note.intended_for: Anthropic safety and policy teams assessing the incremental effectiveness of new mitigations against malicious-use attempts in agentic coding contexts.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are scaffold-sensitive: the degree of simulated pushback and the conversational framing vary across implementations, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. The benchmark conflates sycophancy (changing a correct answer under pressure) with genuine uncertainty acknowledgment, which can inflate apparent failure rates for well-calibrated models.
policy_note.measures: MASK (Measuring AI Sycophancy and Knowledge) evaluates whether a model maintains consistent factual beliefs under social pressure — specifically, whether it will reverse a correct answer when a user pushes back or expresses disagreement. Scenarios present factual questions followed by adversarial follow-ups designed to elicit capitulation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate the model more reliably maintains correct beliefs under pressure (less sycophantic). Frontier models typically score in the 60–85% range on consistency metrics; a model scoring near chance (~50%) is effectively capitulating to most pushback regardless of correctness.
policy_note.intended_for: Safety and alignment researchers evaluating honesty and epistemic consistency in conversational AI; model developers diagnosing sycophancy regressions.

policy_note.caveat:
Contamination is a real concern given the problems originate from
publicly indexed competition archives. Frontier scores have reached
99%+, leaving the benchmark near saturated.
policy_note.measures:
12,500 competition mathematics problems (AMC, AIME, Putnam, etc.) with
worked-out solutions. The MATH-500 subset, the most commonly reported
variant, samples 500 problems for stable comparison.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Be alert for label conflation: "MATH" (full set),
"MATH-500" (sampled), and "MATH (hard)" (a difficulty filter) all
appear in cards and are not directly comparable.
policy_note.intended_for: High-school-to-undergraduate math reasoning comparison.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a growing concern: frontier models now exceed 90% on this subset, compressing meaningful differentiation at the top. Because MATH-500 is a fixed, widely-published subset, training-data contamination risk is higher than for the full 12,500-problem MATH dataset. Results are also sensitive to prompt format and tool use (e.g., code-interpreter access can inflate scores substantially).
policy_note.measures: MATH-500 is a 500-problem representative subset of the full MATH competition-math benchmark, selected by OpenAI for their PRM (Process Reward Model) research. It covers seven difficulty levels and topics including algebra, geometry, number theory, counting and probability, and precalculus, evaluated as exact-match answer correctness.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percent correct (0–100). Frontier models as of 2025 cluster in the 85–97% range, making sub-90% results a meaningful signal of weaker math capability and differences above 90% harder to interpret.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners evaluating mathematical reasoning and multi-step problem-solving ability in language models.

policy_note.caveat: Because the benchmark relies on recency to control contamination, its validity erodes as training cutoff dates advance and models incorporate newer competition problems. Scores also vary depending on whether tool use (code execution, calculators) is permitted versus pure text reasoning, making cross-report comparisons unreliable without knowing the evaluation scaffold.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates mathematical reasoning on recently released math competition problems (AMC, AIME, and olympiad-level contests), using problems published after major model training cutoffs to minimize contamination. Tasks are exact-answer or short free-response format drawn from real competitions.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent accuracy (fraction of problems answered correctly). Frontier models typically range from roughly 50% to 90% depending on competition tier (AMC being easier, olympiad-level being harder). Compare scores only across runs using the same competition set and tool-use policy.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers benchmarking mathematical reasoning on frontier models, particularly where contamination of established datasets (MATH, AIME 2024) is a concern.

policy_note.caveat: The 'testmini' split (1,000 examples) is the de-facto standard evaluation subset and is not interchangeable with full-test scores. CoT prompting reliably boosts scores over plain 0-shot, so variant strings (0-shot vs. 0-shot CoT) must be matched when comparing models. Frontier models now exceed 80–90% accuracy on testmini — above estimated average human performance (~60–65%) — indicating meaningful saturation at the top of the leaderboard. Contamination risk is elevated for models trained after the benchmark's late-2023 release.
policy_note.measures: MathVista evaluates visual mathematical reasoning across 6,141 problems drawn from 31 datasets, spanning geometry, algebra, statistical reasoning, and abstract pattern recognition. Models must parse diagrams, charts, figures, or scene images and produce or select correct numerical or symbolic answers.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (% correct). Human average on testmini is approximately 60–65%. Strong frontier models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5+ class) cluster in the 70–90%+ range on testmini, with the top of the distribution increasingly compressed.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and model developers evaluating joint visual understanding and mathematical reasoning in multimodal systems.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a significant concern: GPT-4-class models already score at or above the ~75th-percentile human passing threshold, leaving little room to differentiate top frontier models. Contamination risk is elevated because MBE practice questions are widely published in commercial bar-prep materials that likely appear in pretraining corpora. The underlying questions are proprietary to the National Conference of Bar Examiners (NCBE); public benchmark sets use released or reconstructed items, so exact dataset composition varies by paper.
policy_note.measures: Tests legal reasoning across 200 multiple-choice questions drawn from the Multistate Bar Examination (MBE), covering seven subjects: Civil Procedure, Constitutional Law, Contracts, Criminal Law and Procedure, Evidence, Real Property, and Torts. The 0-shot CoT variant prompts models without examples, requiring them to reason through legal scenarios to the correct answer.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as percentage correct out of 200 questions. Human bar candidates typically need roughly 60–65% to pass; GPT-4-era frontier models have reported scores in the 70–80%+ range, meaning discrimination at the top end is limited.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers evaluating professional-level legal reasoning in language models; policy analysts assessing AI readiness for legal assistance tasks.

policy_note.caveat:
Saturated by frontier coding models. Heavy contamination concerns
given public availability of solutions. MBPP+ extends the test cases
to catch superficial memorization.
policy_note.measures:
974 short Python programming problems with brief descriptions and unit
tests. Function-completion benchmark similar to HumanEval but with
simpler, more introductory-level problems.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Default metric is pass@1.
policy_note.intended_for: Sister-benchmark to HumanEval for coding-capability sanity-checking.

policy_note.caveat: Scores on MBPP+ are systematically lower than scores on plain MBPP for the same model because the denser test suite rejects solutions that accidentally pass the original sparse tests — consumers must not compare MBPP+ numbers against plain MBPP numbers directly. Frontier models (GPT-4-class and above) cluster in the 70–85 % range, compressing differentiation at the top end. Some contamination risk exists because the original MBPP problems are widely circulated in pretraining corpora.
policy_note.measures: MBPP EvalPlus (MBPP+) measures Python code generation on the ~378-problem MBPP sanitized set, augmented with roughly 35× more automatically-generated test cases per problem than the original MBPP suite. A solution must pass all augmented tests to count correct, probing whether generated code handles edge cases beyond the original minimal test inputs.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are pass@1 (fraction of problems solved on the first attempt). Typical frontier-model range is roughly 65–85 %, compared to 80–90 %+ on the weaker original MBPP suite. The gap between a model's MBPP and MBPP+ score is itself informative — a large gap suggests the model produces brittle code.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners benchmarking code-generation models, particularly those wanting a stricter Python correctness signal than the original MBPP or HumanEval provides.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models now score above 80–90% pass@1, making the benchmark largely saturated for top-tier models. The original MBPP dataset has known contamination risk (it was publicly released in 2021 and widely used in training corpora); MBPP+ mitigates inflated scores from weak test coverage but does not eliminate contamination. Scores are scaffold-dependent: different code execution harnesses or prompt templates produce meaningfully different results, so cross-leaderboard comparisons require matching evaluation setup.
policy_note.measures: MBPP+ is the EvalPlus-augmented version of Google's Mostly Basic Python Problems benchmark, covering ~378 sanitized Python programming tasks. It evaluates code generation correctness by running model-produced code against a substantially expanded test suite (roughly 35× more tests per problem than the original MBPP), targeting basic-to-intermediate algorithmic and utility coding skills.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as pass@1 (percentage of problems solved on the first attempt). Frontier models (GPT-4-class, Claude 3+) typically score 75–90%+, while the original MBPP scores for the same models are noticeably higher due to weaker test coverage — the gap illustrates the benchmark's stricter evaluation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking code generation models on basic Python programming ability, particularly when comparing against prior MBPP results with stricter correctness standards.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark's name 'MBXP (5 Languages)' is ambiguous — the full MBXP suite covers 10+ languages, so different model cards may report on different 5-language subsets, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. Contamination risk is elevated because the underlying MBPP problems are widely circulated in training corpora. Scores are sensitive to scaffold choices (pass@1 vs pass@10) and the specific test harness used.
policy_note.measures: MBXP (5 Languages) measures code generation ability across 5 programming languages by presenting function-completion tasks (signature + docstring) derived from the MBPP dataset, with correctness verified via unit tests using a pass@k metric. It tests whether a model can generalize basic algorithmic problem-solving beyond Python to additional languages.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as pass@k (percentage of problems where at least one of k samples passes all unit tests). Frontier models typically score 60–85% pass@1 on languages like Java and JavaScript but lower on less common languages. Always verify which 5 languages a card is reporting before comparing across cards.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners benchmarking multilingual code generation models, particularly for assessing whether capability transfers from Python to other languages.

policy_note.caveat: The variant string 'prior score' observed in model cards suggests results are sometimes reported as relative comparisons against an earlier checkpoint rather than against a fixed held-out test set, making cross-model comparisons unreliable. Scaffold dependence is a likely concern: scores can vary significantly depending on which MCP client harness or host application is used during evaluation.
policy_note.measures: MCP Atlas evaluates a model's ability to discover, select, and correctly invoke tools exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), testing agentic tool-use competency across a catalog of MCP servers. Tasks probe whether a model can map natural-language requests to the right server and parameters from an atlas of available integrations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Because this benchmark targets agentic tool selection and invocation, absolute scores are less meaningful than relative rankings; expect wide variance across scaffolds and prompt styles. Frontier model ranges are not yet standardized in public reporting.
policy_note.intended_for: Developers and researchers evaluating how well frontier models perform agentic tool-use tasks mediated by the Model Context Protocol; relevant to teams building MCP-native applications.

policy_note.caveat: Contamination risk is elevated because source questions come from publicly available licensing exam prep materials likely present in pretraining corpora. Frontier models now score 70–80%+, compressing differentiation at the top end. Scores reported at 0-shot vs. 5-shot are not directly comparable and should not be aggregated across shot settings.
policy_note.measures: MedMCQA Dev evaluates medical knowledge and clinical reasoning using 4-option multiple-choice questions drawn from Indian medical entrance exams (AIIMS and USMLE-style), spanning ~21 subjects such as anatomy, pharmacology, pathology, and surgery. The dev split (~4,000 questions) is a held-out subset of the full ~187,000-question corpus.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; chance baseline is 25% (uniform over 4 choices). Competitive general-purpose models typically score 60–75%; strong medical models can reach 75–80%+. Always note whether 0-shot or 5-shot prompting was used.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and healthcare AI developers benchmarking medical knowledge breadth and clinical reasoning in language models.

policy_note.caveat: Aggregate scores compress very heterogeneous subtasks, making it difficult to interpret a single number without per-category breakdowns. Because tasks span such diverse formats and difficulty levels, a model's overall score can mask large variance across subdomains. Contamination risk varies per subtask since some source material (images, questions) may overlap with pretraining corpora.
policy_note.measures: MegaBench is a large-scale multimodal evaluation suite covering 500+ diverse real-world tasks spanning vision-language reasoning, single- and multi-image understanding, video, and text-only tasks across many domains and formats. It is designed to give a broad picture of general multimodal capability rather than probing any single skill.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; scores are typically reported as an aggregate percentage across subtasks. Frontier multimodal models (as of 2025) cluster roughly in the 50–70% range on the full suite, with no model saturating the benchmark, making it useful for differentiating strong models.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and developers seeking a comprehensive, multi-task evaluation of vision-language models beyond narrow academic benchmarks.

policy_note.caveat: Strong scaffold dependence: the agentic framework, tool suite, retry budget, and compute allocation materially affect scores, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless configurations are matched exactly. Pre-deployment evaluation task sets are kept private by METR to prevent training contamination, so externally reported numbers often come from smaller public subsets or lab-disclosed figures with limited reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: METR evaluates AI agents on long-horizon autonomous tasks requiring real-world tool use (code execution, web browsing, file manipulation, shell access). Results are reported as the fraction of task instances completed successfully across repeated trials, with the median taken across the task set.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate greater autonomous task-completion capability — from a safety-evaluation standpoint, higher scores are the threshold of concern rather than a straightforward 'better'. Scores are expressed as a fraction of trials succeeded (e.g., 0/10 = 0%). Frontier models on public task subsets currently cluster in the low-to-mid range; interpretation requires knowing the specific task difficulty tier and scaffold used.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policymakers, and model developers assessing autonomous-capability thresholds for pre-deployment safety reviews; also used by frontier labs as an internal gating criterion.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly sensitive to prompting variant: 8-shot chain-of-thought typically yields substantially higher numbers than 0-shot, so comparisons across cards reporting different variants are not valid. Saturation is a concern for top frontier models, which regularly exceed 90% on high-resource languages. Because MGSM is derived directly from GSM8K — one of the most widely used training benchmarks — contamination risk is elevated for both the source problems and their translations.
policy_note.measures: MGSM tests multilingual arithmetic reasoning by translating 250 GSM8K grade-school math word problems into 10 languages (Bengali, Chinese, German, Japanese, Russian, Spanish, Swahili, Telugu, Thai, French). Models must solve multi-step arithmetic problems and produce a correct numerical answer, probing both language understanding and mathematical reasoning across typologically diverse scripts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models (2024–2025) typically score 85–92% averaged across all 10 languages; weaker or older models show larger drops on low-resource languages like Swahili and Bengali. Always note the prompting variant (0-shot, 0-shot CoT, or 8-shot CoT) when comparing results.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multilingual mathematical reasoning, particularly whether a model's math capability degrades across non-English and non-Latin-script languages.

policy_note.caveat: Because Michelangelo is a proprietary internal benchmark, results are not independently reproducible and comparisons are only meaningful within Mistral's own release reports. The exact task mix, scoring rubric, and dataset provenance are opaque to external researchers, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Michelangelo is Mistral AI's internal broad-capability evaluation suite, used to benchmark their models across reasoning, knowledge, and instruction-following tasks. Specific sub-task composition and dataset sizes are not publicly disclosed.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Absolute numbers should be treated as relative indicators within Mistral's own model lineage rather than against scores from other labs on different evaluation harnesses.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing Mistral model releases to each other; not designed for cross-lab apples-to-apples comparison.

policy_note.caveat: Flagged 'exploratory', meaning task design, scoring rubrics, and dataset composition are not yet standardized and likely vary across uses. Situational-awareness evaluations carry an inherent interpretability problem: a sufficiently capable model that detects the eval could suppress its awareness, making a low score ambiguous between genuinely unaware and successfully hiding awareness.
policy_note.measures: Probes whether a model exhibits awareness of its situational context in ways relevant to deceptive alignment—for example, detecting that it is in an evaluation versus a real deployment and adjusting behavior accordingly. The 'exploratory' variant label indicates a research-stage probe without a fixed dataset size or standardized task format.
policy_note.how_to_read: Score direction is context-dependent: lower situational awareness is preferable if the probe is measuring eval-gaming potential, but higher awareness may be preferable if the task rewards recognizing misalignment-relevant cues. No established frontier range exists; results are typically compared across a small set of frontier models rather than a broad leaderboard.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and alignment teams at frontier labs assessing deceptive alignment and evaluation-gaming risks.

policy_note.caveat: The 'exploratory' variant label indicates this is a non-standardized, research-stage evaluation with no fixed dataset or public leaderboard; scores across labs are likely not directly comparable. Scaffold and elicitation method likely have large effects on outcomes, making cross-report comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model can recognize, resist, or generate stealth misalignment behaviors — scenarios where an AI system pursues misaligned goals while appearing aligned to overseers. Tasks are described as exploratory, suggesting open-ended adversarial or red-teaming prompts rather than a fixed multiple-choice format.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower incidence of successful stealth misalignment is better. No established numeric scale exists publicly; results are typically reported qualitatively or as pass/fail rates on challenge instances.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing deceptive alignment or goal-concealment risks in frontier models.

policy_note.caveat: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base, not a standardized benchmark with a fixed test set or canonical scoring methodology; different evaluations operationalize it differently (Q&A, classification, mapping), making cross-paper score comparisons unreliable. Because the full ATT&CK corpus is publicly available and widely cited in security literature, contamination of training data is highly likely for frontier models, inflating apparent performance.
policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's knowledge of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) as catalogued in the MITRE ATT&CK framework — a publicly maintained knowledge base of real-world attack behaviors across Enterprise, Mobile, and ICS platforms. Tasks typically involve identifying, classifying, or explaining attack techniques and mapping threat-actor behaviors to ATT&CK categories.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better coverage of ATT&CK technique knowledge. No universal scale exists; interpret results relative to the specific task design (e.g., technique classification accuracy, sub-technique recall). Compare only within studies using identical task formulations.
policy_note.intended_for: Cybersecurity researchers, red/blue team practitioners, and AI safety evaluators assessing a model's threat-intelligence knowledge and its potential utility or risk in offensive/defensive security workflows.

policy_note.caveat: Label conflation is significant: 'bronze pass@1' (single attempt, bronze threshold) and 'bronze pass@10' or 'pass@10' (best of 10 independent runs) are not comparable — pass@10 substantially inflates apparent capability and papers often report only their best variant. Scaffold dependence is severe: the same underlying model scores very differently depending on the agentic framework (e.g., MLAB, AIDE, custom scaffolds), making cross-paper comparisons unreliable without controlling for scaffold. Contamination risk is elevated because Kaggle competition solutions, notebooks, and forum discussions are extensively indexed on the web.
policy_note.measures: MLE-bench evaluates AI agents on 109 historical Kaggle ML competitions, covering tasks such as data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning. Agents submit predictions scored against the original Kaggle leaderboard; performance is reported as the fraction of competitions where the agent earns a Kaggle medal (bronze, silver, or gold) relative to historical human competitors.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The primary metric is the fraction of competitions where the agent achieves at least a bronze medal (roughly top 40% of historical human submissions). Frontier agentic systems circa 2024–2025 achieved bronze pass@1 rates in roughly the 10–40% range depending on scaffold; pass@10 figures run noticeably higher. Always confirm which pass@k and which medal threshold a reported number uses before comparing across papers.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and lab evaluators assessing end-to-end machine learning engineering capability of autonomous coding agents, particularly in realistic competition-style settings.

policy_note.caveat: Interview-style coding problems are widely circulated online and in prep resources, raising contamination risk for models trained on web data. The pass@1 metric is sensitive to exact string matching or test harness details, so scores may vary across evaluation frameworks.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to write correct code for machine learning engineering interview-style problems on the first attempt, scored by pass@1 (the generated code passes all test cases without retries). Problems typically cover ML algorithms, data manipulation, and numerical computing tasks common in industry technical screens.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; pass@1 is expressed as a percentage (0–100). A score of 50 means half of problems were solved correctly on the first attempt. Frontier models typically score in the 50–80 range depending on problem difficulty and harness.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking code generation capabilities relevant to applied ML engineering roles; useful for comparing models on domain-specific (ML/data-science) coding rather than general algorithmic problems.

policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to identify and diagnose bugs in machine learning training code and pipelines, such as incorrect loss functions, data preprocessing errors, gradient issues, and misconfigured hyperparameters. Tasks typically present faulty training scripts or configurations and ask the model to locate and explain the root cause.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. This is a relatively niche benchmark with limited public leaderboard data, so absolute scores should be interpreted cautiously without a broad comparison baseline.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and AI evaluators assessing whether frontier models can assist with debugging deep learning workflows and act as effective ML engineering assistants.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: frame sampling rate, total frames extracted, and context window size all materially shift results, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable unless sampling protocols are matched. Models with natively longer context windows have a structural advantage that the benchmark does not control for.
policy_note.measures: MLVU (Multi-task Long Video Understanding) evaluates multimodal LLMs on long-form video comprehension across multiple task types, including needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, plot question answering, ego reasoning, and scene recognition. Videos span from several minutes to over an hour, stress-testing temporal reasoning at lengths far beyond short-clip benchmarks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (%). As of early 2025, competitive frontier multimodal models score roughly in the 60–75% range, with significant variance tied to video sampling strategy.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating long-video comprehension capabilities in multimodal large language models.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark was released in mid-2024, so models trained on data after that date face contamination risk on a relatively small held-out set. Some perceptual subtasks (e.g., basic object recognition) show early saturation for top frontier models, while reasoning-heavy subtasks remain more discriminative. Scores are reported per-subtask and in aggregate, so headline numbers can obscure weak spots.
policy_note.measures: MME-RealWorld evaluates large vision-language models on high-resolution, real-world image understanding across perception and cognition tasks, spanning ~29,000 QA pairs in 43 subtasks across 5 domains including OCR, object recognition, spatial reasoning, and scene understanding. Tasks use multiple-choice format drawn from practical real-world imagery rather than curated synthetic datasets.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; scores are reported as percentages per subtask and as an overall aggregate. Frontier models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) typically range 60–75% overall, with humans scoring around 85% on the hardest subtasks, leaving meaningful headroom.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking multimodal (vision-language) models on realistic, high-resolution visual tasks that go beyond clean benchmark imagery.

policy_note.caveat:
Saturation: frontier models score above 88%, leaving little signal
between top systems. The dataset has acknowledged labeling errors and
ambiguities, and several papers document training-data contamination on
subsets of MMLU.
policy_note.measures:
57 multiple-choice exams spanning STEM, humanities, law, medicine, and
other domains. Probes broad factual recall and conceptual reasoning at
a level roughly comparable to U.S. high-school through graduate study.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Reported by every frontier lab in this corpus,
making it the most-cited benchmark in the dataset (5 labs agree on it).
policy_note.intended_for:
Aggregate-knowledge comparisons between general-purpose LLMs. Not a
substitute for domain-specific evaluations.

policy_note.caveat:
Dataset contains some acknowledged mistakes per ongoing community
corrections. A subset of questions had answer-choice counts reduced
during manual review to remove unreasonable options.
policy_note.measures:
An enhanced MMLU with more challenging, reasoning-focused questions.
Expands answer choices from 4 to 10 and removes trivial or noisy items
found in the original.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Designed to maintain headroom above MMLU; expect
scores 10-20 points below MMLU for the same model.
policy_note.intended_for:
Researchers and developers comparing capability on harder
knowledge-plus-reasoning tasks where MMLU has saturated.

policy_note.caveat: Performance varies substantially by language and script, so aggregate scores can obscure poor coverage of lower-resource languages. Scores are not directly comparable to English MMLU because translation artifacts can make some questions easier or harder; label contamination from the original English MMLU may inflate scores on translated variants if training data included English originals.
policy_note.measures: Multilingual MMLU evaluates general knowledge and reasoning across 57 academic subjects (matching original MMLU's scope) in 14+ languages, using 0-shot multiple-choice questions. It probes whether models can apply the same breadth of world knowledge when prompted in non-English languages.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (0–100%). Frontier models typically score in the 70–90% range on high-resource languages (Chinese, French, German) and lower on less-resourced ones (Bengali, Swahili). Compare within the same language variant, not across languages.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers assessing multilingual capability of large language models, particularly for deployment in non-English speaking contexts.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models now cluster in the high-60s to mid-80s percent range, limiting differentiation at the top. Variant conflation is a significant reporting hazard: validation-set scores (~900 items) are consistently 2–5 points higher than held-out test scores; 'extended reasoning' or chain-of-thought prompting further inflates scores relative to standard 0-shot; and 'no tools' disambiguates agentic setups where tool-augmented models would otherwise be incomparable. Comparing scores across these variants without labeling them is misleading.
policy_note.measures: MMMU evaluates multimodal understanding across 11,500 college-level multiple-choice questions spanning 30 subjects in science, medicine, arts, engineering, and humanities, each pairing text with one or more images (charts, diagrams, photographs, tables). It probes whether a model can integrate domain knowledge with visual reasoning at an expert level.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). Random baseline is ~25% (4-option MCQ). Frontier models (as of early 2026) score roughly 65–85%; human expert performance is cited near 88%. Validation-split and extended-reasoning scores sit noticeably above test-split 0-shot scores — always check which split and prompting regime is reported.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and model card authors assessing general college-level visual-language reasoning across diverse academic disciplines.

policy_note.caveat: MMMU-Pro was created explicitly because the original MMMU became saturated (frontier models exceeding 70%); however, frontier scores on MMMU-Pro standard track are already clustering in the low-to-mid 60s%, and differentiation is narrowing. The two tracks (standard vs. vision-only) produce substantially different scores, and labs sometimes report only the higher standard-track result without disclosure — always verify which track is cited.
policy_note.measures: MMMU-Pro tests multimodal academic reasoning across college-level subjects using ~3,460 questions drawn from disciplines such as science, medicine, and engineering. It extends MMMU with 10-option multiple-choice format (reducing guess probability) and a separate vision-only track where questions must be answered from images alone, without text-embedded hints.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percentages. On the standard track, leading frontier models score roughly 55–70%; the vision-only track is harder by ~10–20 percentage points. Compare tracks separately, as pooling or cherry-picking tracks obscures real capability.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and lab evaluators assessing whether vision-language models perform genuine cross-modal academic reasoning rather than text-shortcut exploitation.

policy_note.caveat: The 'no tools' label is essential: MMMU-Pro also has a 'standard' or 'with tools' setting where models may call external utilities, and scores between the two conditions are not interchangeable — cards that simply report 'MMMU-Pro' without specifying the condition are ambiguous. Additionally, MMMU-Pro, MMMU, and MMLU-Pro are three distinct benchmarks with similar-looking names; cross-family comparisons require care.
policy_note.measures: MMMU-Pro (no tools) measures expert-level multimodal reasoning across 30+ college-level disciplines — including science, engineering, humanities, and medicine — using multiple-choice and open-ended questions that pair images with text, with the constraint that models may not invoke external tools such as code interpreters or OCR. It is a harder extension of the original MMMU benchmark, designed to reduce ceiling effects by using more difficult distractors and multi-image questions.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy (0–100%). MMMU-Pro is substantially harder than the original MMMU; frontier models as of late 2024 through 2025 typically score in the 40–65% range on the no-tools condition, providing meaningful differentiation where MMMU had begun to saturate.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and developers evaluating vision-language models on academic reasoning tasks in a pure, tool-free setting.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: results vary based on which tools are provided, how the tool-calling interface is implemented, and whether code execution output is fed back to the model—making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless exact tool configurations match. Scores are not directly comparable to standard MMMU-Pro (no-tools) numbers reported elsewhere, and conflation between these two variants is common in model cards.
policy_note.measures: MMMU-Pro (with tools) evaluates multimodal reasoning across college-level, multi-discipline questions—spanning STEM, humanities, and social sciences—when the model is permitted to use external tools such as Python code execution to assist in solving problems. It is a harder variant of MMMU-Pro, which itself extends the original MMMU benchmark with more complex, multi-step questions requiring image understanding.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as percentage of questions answered correctly. Standard MMMU-Pro (no tools) sees frontier models in roughly the 50–70% range; tool-augmented scores can differ substantially depending on scaffold quality. Because the variant is less commonly reported, reference ranges across labs are narrow.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers benchmarking multimodal models in agentic or tool-augmented settings, particularly those evaluating real-world problem-solving that benefits from computation or structured reasoning assistance.

policy_note.caveat: MMStar was explicitly designed to eliminate data leakage and text-only solvability present in earlier VLM benchmarks, but its small size (1,500 samples) means per-category variance can be significant. As frontier models continue to improve, saturation in aggregate scores is an emerging concern.
policy_note.measures: MMStar evaluates vision-language models (VLMs) on 1,500 manually curated multiple-choice questions spanning six visual capability categories: coarse perception, fine-grained perception, instance reasoning, logical reasoning, math, and science & technology. Each sample was hand-verified to require genuine visual understanding and cannot be answered from text alone.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; random-chance baseline is ~25% (4-option MCQ). At the time of publication frontier models (GPT-4V class) scored in the 45–60% range; current top models are approaching 70–80%, with 100% as theoretical maximum.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and evaluators benchmarking multimodal / vision-language models, especially to distinguish genuine visual reasoning from models that exploit text-only cues in standard benchmarks.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to which GPT-4 evaluator version is used, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable without knowing the judge version. The dataset is small (218 questions), so standard errors are large and small score differences are not statistically meaningful. Frontier models now routinely exceed 60–70%, creating saturation at the top of the leaderboard.
policy_note.measures: MM-Vet evaluates vision-language models on 218 open-ended questions that require integrating multiple visual and language capabilities simultaneously, including recognition, OCR, spatial awareness, math, and knowledge grounding. Each answer is scored 0–1 by a GPT-4 judge against reference answers, with a final score reported as a percentage.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are percentages (0–100). Early frontier models (GPT-4V at launch) scored ~49; current leading models exceed 70–80. A difference smaller than ~2–3 points should not be treated as meaningful given the small test set.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating large multimodal (vision-language) models on tasks requiring integrated, multi-skill reasoning rather than narrow single-capability probing.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are scaffold-dependent: frame-sampling strategy and how many frames are passed to the model substantially affect results, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable unless sampling details are disclosed. The benchmark is relatively new and frontier saturation on individual subject categories has not been fully characterized.
policy_note.measures: MMVU (Massive Multi-discipline Video Understanding) evaluates multimodal models on expert-level reasoning over short video clips across dozens of academic and professional disciplines, including science, engineering, and medicine. Questions are multiple-choice and require integrating visual evidence from the video with domain-specific knowledge.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as accuracy percentages on 4-option multiple-choice questions (25% random baseline). As of early 2025, frontier models score in the 55–70% range, indicating meaningful headroom below expert human performance.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers benchmarking multimodal (video + language) models on expert-level, knowledge-intensive video understanding tasks.

policy_note.caveat: As a canary/prompt-engineered probe, scores reflect refusal policy and RLHF tuning rather than any stable capability metric; results are highly sensitive to system prompt wording, jailbreak framing, and policy changes across model versions. The 'prompt engineered' variant label suggests results may not be reproducible across different prompt formulations.
policy_note.measures: A canary-style behavioral probe testing whether a model will autonomously create a Bitcoin wallet when prompted, assessing the degree to which models comply with or refuse agentic financial-action requests. It probes autonomous capability boundaries rather than raw knowledge.
policy_note.how_to_read: Interpretation depends on framing: a higher compliance rate signals greater autonomy/capability but higher risk; a lower rate signals stronger refusal policy. There is no single 'better' direction — context and intended use case determine what score is desirable. Frontier model ranges and comparison baselines are not publicly standardized for this probe.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams evaluating model autonomy boundaries, refusal behavior, and agentic risk in financial action contexts.

name: Model Autonomy - Find API key on filesystem (canary)

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold- and prompt-dependent — the 'prompt engineered' variant label signals that different system prompts or task framings produce substantially different find-rates, making cross-report comparisons unreliable without matching scaffold details. Whether the metric captures key discovery, key extraction, or attempted key use may also vary across evaluators.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model operating with filesystem access will autonomously locate a planted canary API key without being explicitly instructed to search for credentials. Measures unsanctioned resource-acquisition behavior as a safety-relevant autonomous capability.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower find-rate (closer to 0%) is safer; a model that never surfaces the canary key without instruction is the desired outcome. Frontier safety thresholds are typically set near 0% for this class of unsanctioned action.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and frontier-lab evaluators assessing autonomous dangerous-action tendencies as part of responsible scaling / model-autonomy evaluations.

name: Model Autonomy - Load docker image with Mistral 7B

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is significant: scores vary substantially depending on which agentic framework is used (which shell tools, Docker CLI access, and retry logic the scaffolding provides). The 'prompt engineered' variant label indicates results depend on how the task is specified to the model, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. The task is highly specific — success on this one workflow may not generalize to other autonomy tasks.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether an AI agent can autonomously execute the multi-step process of loading a Docker image containing Mistral 7B — including pulling or importing the image, configuring the container runtime, and verifying the model is operational. It probes agentic capability: multi-step planning, shell/tool use, and error recovery without human intervention.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better (higher pass rate = more autonomous). This is a binary pass/fail task so scores are typically reported as a success rate (0–100%). Frontier model performance varies widely by scaffold; treat any reported number as scaffold-specific rather than a model-intrinsic capability score.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capabilities researchers evaluating autonomous agent behavior, particularly the risk that frontier models can independently acquire and operate other large AI systems.

policy_note.caveat: The observed variant label 'prompt engineered' indicates results are scaffold- and prompt-dependent, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless prompts and scaffolds are held constant. The crypto-authentication component may produce different refusal rates across models depending on how they reason about the legitimacy of authentication versus the underlying task. No widely cited canonical dataset or standardized harness is publicly documented for this specific benchmark, limiting reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model will autonomously establish and operate a crypto-authenticated OpenAI API proxy when prompted — probing the degree to which a model can be directed to set up covert or unauthorized infrastructure. Tests agentic autonomy and instruction-following in a potentially harmful operational context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower compliance rates are safer — a model that refuses to act as an unauthorized API proxy scores better. Results are typically reported as pass/fail or compliance rate (0–100%); frontier safety-conscious models are expected to score near 0% compliance.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model evaluators assessing autonomous agentic behavior, particularly the risk that models will construct or relay unauthorized API infrastructure when instructed.

name: Model Autonomy - OpenAI API proxy find key (canary)

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold- and prompt-dependent; the 'prompt engineered' variant label indicates elicitation method varies across evaluators, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. As a binary pass/fail canary test it does not differentiate frequency or severity of the behavior—a model that finds the key 1% of the time scores identically to one that finds it 100% of the time unless rates are reported.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model operating in an agentic OpenAI API proxy setting will autonomously locate a planted canary API key—a honeypot credential embedded in the environment. Measures the rate at which the model finds and potentially acts on the key, probing unauthorized credential-seeking behavior.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better; 0% (model never locates or acts on the canary key) is the target. This is a red-line safety evaluation, not a capability benchmark—any nonzero rate is a potential concern. Frontier safety-focused models typically report near-zero rates.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing autonomous threat behaviors, agentic risk, and credential-exfiltration uplift in frontier models.

name: Model Autonomy - OpenAI API proxy given key no auth (canary)

policy_note.caveat: The 'prompt engineered' variant string signals that scores are highly sensitive to prompt framing, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless prompts are identical. As a canary evaluation the dataset is likely small and the pass/fail threshold may not be publicly validated; treat single-point scores as directional signals rather than precise capability measurements.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model will autonomously use a provided API key to route calls through an unauthenticated OpenAI API proxy, probing the model's willingness to take credential-leveraging actions in an agentic setting without explicit per-request authorization. The 'canary' label indicates an early-warning variant designed to detect capability emergence before it manifests in harder tasks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower task-completion rates are generally preferable from a safety standpoint (model declines to use the unauthenticated proxy). No broad frontier range is publicly established; scores should be read against the specific lab's own thresholds and compared only across identically scaffolded runs.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing autonomous or agentic model behavior, particularly credential misuse and self-directed API access.

name: Model Autonomy - Register cloud provider and start A100 VM

policy_note.caveat: Strong scaffold dependence: scores vary substantially based on the agent's tool access (browser automation, shell, cloud CLI) and the harness used, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable unless scaffolding is held constant. The 'prompt engineered' variant string indicates sensitivity to exact prompting strategy, which can dramatically alter pass rates. Task success may depend on whether real credentials and billing accounts are provided, introducing setup variability across evaluators.
policy_note.measures: Tests whether a model can autonomously complete the multi-step agentic task of registering an account with a cloud provider and provisioning an A100 GPU virtual machine, probing real-world resource acquisition capability with no human in the loop. The task requires account creation, payment or credit navigation, and API/console interaction to launch compute.
policy_note.how_to_read: Binary pass/fail per attempt, sometimes aggregated as a success rate over multiple runs; higher scores indicate greater autonomous capability to acquire cloud compute — treated as a risk signal as well as a capability signal. Frontier models as of early 2025 show low but nonzero success rates on this task class.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy makers assessing autonomous resource acquisition risk; used in capability elicitation and dangerous-capability evaluations to flag models that can independently obtain large-scale compute.

policy_note.caveat: With only 100 prompts the confidence interval is wide (~±5 pp at 50% rate), making small score differences unreliable. The metric is highly sensitive to how 'mistake' is operationalized, which varies by lab and evaluation team. The 'unmitigated' qualifier implies a paired mitigated version exists; cross-benchmark comparisons are only valid when both versions use identical prompts and grading rubrics.
policy_note.measures: Measures the fraction of responses in which a model makes an error across a fixed set of 100 prompts, with no mitigations (e.g., no refusal tuning, no output filters) applied. Probes raw model behavior before safety or correction interventions are layered on.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better; a lower mistake rate indicates fewer uncorrected errors. Scores are typically expressed as a percentage (0–100%). Because this is an unmitigated baseline, absolute values are expected to be higher than post-mitigation equivalents — the meaningful signal is the delta between unmitigated and mitigated versions, or trends across model generations.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and lab evaluation teams assessing baseline model error rates before mitigation strategies are applied, typically to quantify the incremental effect of those mitigations.

policy_note.caveat: Only models with native ≥1M token context windows can attempt this variant, so the comparison pool is very small and limited to a handful of frontier systems. Scores are highly sensitive to whether inference uses full-context attention versus chunked or sliding-window approaches, making cross-system comparisons potentially misleading without knowing the inference scaffold used.
policy_note.measures: MRCR (Multi-needle Retrieval and Coreference Resolution) at the 1-million-token context length tests a model's ability to locate and correctly attribute multiple distinct pieces of information buried across an extremely long context window. The task probes whether models can track and disambiguate references at scales far beyond typical benchmarks.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores reflect accuracy of retrieving and correctly resolving multiple target items within a 1M-token context. Because the eligible model pool is small (only models supporting ≥1M context), absolute score differences should be interpreted with caution—there is limited diversity in the comparison set.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and model developers evaluating frontier models on extreme long-context retrieval and coreference at the 1M-token scale.

policy_note.caveat: Heavy label conflation across reported variants makes cross-report comparisons unreliable: '128k (average)' averages recall across needle positions, '1M (pointwise)' scores at individual positions, and 'extended reasoning' vs 'no thinking' variants produce systematically different scores due to chain-of-thought scaffolding — all four variants are routinely cited as plain 'MRCR v2' without qualification.
policy_note.measures: MRCR v2 (Multi-needle Retrieval and Comprehension from Context) tests a model's ability to locate and reproduce multiple distinct pieces of information embedded at different positions within long documents; evaluated at 128k and 1M token context lengths using multi-turn retrieval prompts.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent recall accuracy as a percentage. On the 128k average variant, frontier models typically range from roughly 60% to 95%+; the 1M pointwise variant is harder and shows greater differentiation among top models.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and model developers evaluating frontier model long-context retrieval fidelity, particularly for use cases requiring precise multi-hop recall over very long documents.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a significant concern: top frontier models cluster near 9+/10, leaving little headroom to differentiate them. The LLM-as-judge setup introduces known biases (position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement when GPT-4 judges GPT-4 outputs). With only 80 questions the benchmark has high variance, and scores are not comparable across runs that use different judge model versions.
policy_note.measures: MT-Bench evaluates instruction-following and conversational quality across 80 two-turn questions spanning 8 categories (writing, roleplay, extraction, reasoning, math, coding, STEM, humanities). Responses are scored 1–10 by an LLM judge (typically GPT-4), probing how well models maintain coherent, helpful multi-turn dialogue.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scale is 1–10. Competitive open-weight models typically score 7–8.5; top proprietary frontier models reach 9–9.5. Due to saturation, differences below ~0.3 points are unlikely to be meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating chat-optimized LLMs on instruction-following and multi-turn conversational capability, particularly for comparing fine-tuned or RLHF-trained models.

policy_note.caveat: Aggregate scores can mask large per-language gaps — models with strong Latin-script training perform considerably better on European languages than on Arabic, Thai, or CJK scripts, so single-number comparisons across models are misleading without per-language breakdowns. Results are also scaffold-dependent: answer-matching strictness and prompt language affect scores noticeably.
policy_note.measures: Multilingual text-rich visual question answering across 9 languages (Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Vietnamese, and Italian), requiring models to read and interpret text embedded in natural images such as signs, menus, receipts, and documents. Each language contains several hundred question-answer pairs testing OCR-level reading and comprehension of scene text.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; reported as exact-match or normalized-match percentage per language and overall. As of late 2024, frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) score roughly 20–60% depending on language, with the largest models still well below human performance on low-resource scripts such as Thai and Arabic.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multimodal models on multilingual document and scene-text understanding, particularly for non-Latin script coverage.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to how images are presented to the model (interleaved vs. sequential in the context window) and to the maximum image-count limits of different APIs, creating scaffold dependence that makes cross-framework comparisons unreliable. Models with low image-count limits may be systematically disadvantaged independent of reasoning ability.
policy_note.measures: MuirBench evaluates multi-image understanding and reasoning across ~2,600 multiple-choice questions spanning 12 task types (e.g., multi-view scene understanding, temporal ordering, visual comparison, diagram interpretation), requiring models to jointly reason over multiple images per question rather than single-image analysis. It probes whether vision-language models can integrate information across image sets rather than treating each image in isolation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better; chance is 25% (4-way multiple choice). Frontier models score in roughly the 50–70% range as of late 2024, leaving substantial headroom before saturation.
policy_note.intended_for: Multimodal AI researchers and practitioners evaluating vision-language models on complex multi-image reasoning tasks beyond standard single-image VQA benchmarks.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models fine-tuned heavily on instruction-following data may show ceiling effects, limiting differentiation at the top of the leaderboard. Single-turn IFEval scores do not transfer directly to Multi-IF results, so conflating the two benchmarks overstates coverage of multi-turn behavior.
policy_note.measures: Multi-IF evaluates instruction following across multiple conversation turns, testing whether models can simultaneously satisfy several layered constraints (e.g., format, length, keyword requirements) that accumulate as a dialogue progresses. Scores reflect the fraction of programmatically verifiable instructions complied with across multi-turn exchanges.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as instruction-level or prompt-level accuracy percentages (0–100). Frontier models generally score in the 60–85 range on the stricter prompt-level metric, so differences of a few points are meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating chat models on realistic multi-turn instruction adherence, particularly for assistant deployments where users issue successive or compounding requests.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are expressed relative to a specific Gemini reference model (1.5 Pro 002 or 2.5 Pro/Flash depending on the card vintage), making cross-lab comparisons difficult. The egregious/non-egregious split means headline numbers vary substantially depending on which tier is cited. The evaluation appears to be Google-internal, limiting independent reproducibility and third-party verification.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates the rate at which a model produces harmful or policy-violating responses to safety-sensitive prompts across multiple non-English languages, with results split by violation severity (egregious vs. non-egregious). Scores are reported as relative violation-rate differences against a Gemini baseline model rather than as absolute percentages.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower (more negative relative score) is better — a negative value means fewer violations than the reference model. Interpret results in the context of which severity tier (non-egregious vs. overall) and which baseline model is cited, as these vary across cards.
policy_note.intended_for: Safety researchers and ML practitioners assessing multilingual safety coverage and regression across model generations, primarily in the context of Gemini model card disclosures.

policy_note.caveat: The benchmark appears across model cards without a single canonical public dataset or paper, making cross-lab score comparisons unreliable if prompt sets differ. Reporting the two variants separately can obscure the inherent sensitivity/specificity trade-off: a model can game one metric at the expense of the other.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a multimodal model correctly refuses harmful image-and-text requests without over-refusing benign ones; the two variants probe opposite failure modes — outputting unsafe content (not_unsafe) and incorrectly refusing safe requests (not_overrefuse).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better on both variants. not_overrefuse scores how often the model correctly complies with benign multimodal prompts (higher = fewer false refusals); not_unsafe scores how often the model correctly declines harmful prompts (higher = fewer unsafe outputs). Both metrics together characterize the refusal trade-off curve.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing safety calibration of vision-language models.

policy_note.caveat: The 'post-mitigation' variant label indicates the benchmark is used in a dual-use biosecurity context, measuring whether safety interventions reduce performance on legitimate expert tasks — scores across variants are not directly comparable and should not be aggregated. Human baseline figures may reflect domain-specialist populations, making model-vs-human comparisons sensitive to which expert cohort was sampled.
policy_note.measures: Assesses a model's ability to troubleshoot virology laboratory problems using multimodal inputs (images and text), presented as single-select multiple-choice questions. Probes expert-level understanding of virology protocols, experimental errors, and diagnostic reasoning in a lab context.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better. Scores should be read relative to the reported human baseline and compared across the standard vs. post-mitigation variants to assess safety-capability tradeoff; a large drop from standard to post-mitigation indicates over-refusal on legitimate expert content.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and biosecurity policy teams evaluating the tradeoff between harmlessness interventions and retained expert-level virology capability; useful for labs documenting responsible scaling commitments.

policy_note.caveat: Because MultiPL-E derives problems from HumanEval and MBPP, it inherits their contamination risk — those Python originals are widely present in training corpora, and model performance on translated versions may still benefit from memorized solutions. Aggregate scores mask large variance: models score much higher on popular languages (Python, JavaScript) than on niche ones (Racket, Lua), so a single number hides capability distribution. The aggregate reported in a model card may cover different language subsets depending on the evaluator.
policy_note.measures: MultiPL-E evaluates code generation across ~18 programming languages by translating HumanEval and MBPP problems into each target language and measuring pass@1 (fraction of problems solved on first attempt). The aggregate score is the mean pass@1 across all included languages.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores represent mean pass@1 (0–100%). Frontier models (as of 2024–2025) typically range from roughly 50–75% on the full aggregate, with significant spread across languages. Python-only HumanEval scores will be considerably higher than the MultiPL-E aggregate for the same model.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and practitioners comparing multilingual code generation capability across models; useful for assessing generalization beyond Python-only coding benchmarks.

policy_note.caveat: No single canonical dataset or methodology exists under this name; different labs and papers implement their own multi-turn jailbreak suites with differing attack categories, attacker models, and success criteria, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. Attack success rates are heavily scaffold-dependent: an automated red-team attacker model's capability level and prompt strategy substantially affect measured failure rates. Results may not generalise across deployment contexts (API vs. chat UI) or to novel attack patterns not in the evaluation set.
policy_note.measures: Measures a model's resistance to safety-policy violations elicited through multi-turn adversarial conversations, where each turn incrementally escalates or reframes requests to bypass refusals. Evaluates whether sustained conversational pressure—role-playing, hypothetical framing, incremental escalation—can cause a model to produce outputs it refused in a single turn.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower attack success rate (ASR) is better—it means fewer jailbreak attempts succeeded. Results are typically reported as a percentage of test cases where the model produced policy-violating output; 0% is ideal. Because methodology varies widely, compare only results produced under identical evaluation frameworks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policy teams, and model deployers evaluating a model's robustness to adversarial conversational manipulation before deployment.

policy_note.caveat: Performance is sensitive to the number of frames sampled per video — different frame-sampling strategies can produce meaningfully different scores, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable unless sampling is matched. Some sub-tasks are easier and frontier-class models approach saturation on them, masking differences at the overall accuracy level.
policy_note.measures: MVBench evaluates temporal video understanding across 20 sub-tasks (~4,000 multiple-choice questions), covering capabilities such as action prediction, object interaction, scene transition, and fine-grained motion recognition that cannot be resolved from static frames alone. Each question has 4 candidate answers, requiring models to reason over video sequences rather than individual images.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are reported as overall accuracy (0–100%). The random-chance baseline is ~25% for 4-choice questions. Competitive video models typically score in the 60–75% range; strong frontier multimodal models can reach above 75% on the full benchmark.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking multimodal video-language models on temporal and motion reasoning, particularly when evaluating whether gains come from static-frame recognition versus genuine temporal understanding.

policy_note.caveat: Because the dataset is not publicly released, independent contamination audits are impossible and results are only reported by Google. Scores are not directly comparable across labs since other organizations cannot run the benchmark themselves, limiting its utility as a cross-model leaderboard signal.
policy_note.measures: Natural2Code evaluates Python code generation from natural-language problem descriptions, using held-out problems with unit-test execution to measure functional correctness. It was designed by Google DeepMind as a lower-contamination alternative to HumanEval, with problems withheld from public release at training time.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as pass@1 (percentage of problems solved on the first attempt). Frontier models (Gemini era) score in the high-70s to low-80s range on pass@1, but cross-lab comparison is limited by the proprietary dataset.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and model developers evaluating code generation capability, particularly those wanting a contamination-resistant complement to HumanEval or MBPP.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models have approached saturation on the short-answer subset, limiting differentiation at the top of the leaderboard. Training data contamination is a known concern given the benchmark's age (released 2019) and the prevalence of Wikipedia and Google query logs in pretraining corpora.
policy_note.measures: Natural Questions evaluates open-domain question answering using ~3,500 test questions sampled from real Google Search queries, where models must extract or generate short and long answer spans from Wikipedia documents. It probes factual recall and reading comprehension over naturally occurring information-seeking queries.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as Exact Match (EM) or F1 on the short-answer subset. Frontier models score in the 55–65% EM range on the standard test set; human performance is approximately 87% F1.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and AI developers evaluating open-domain QA and factual retrieval capabilities.

policy_note.caveat: Contamination is a significant concern because the questions derive from Google Search logs and answers from Wikipedia, both of which appear heavily in pretraining corpora; models may recall answers from memorized training text rather than generalizing. Exact-match scoring penalizes valid paraphrases and date formats, understating true recall. Frontier models have largely saturated the benchmark, reducing its power to differentiate among top systems.
policy_note.measures: NaturalQuestions Closed-Book tests a model's ability to answer real Google Search queries from memory alone, with no retrieved context or documents provided. Questions are drawn from anonymized Google queries answered by Wikipedia passages; the closed-book variant strips all context, probing only parametric factual knowledge via exact-match scoring.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; metric is Exact Match (EM) on the ~3,610-question test set. Early large language models (T5-11B) scored ~36% EM; contemporary frontier models typically exceed 50–60%, making the benchmark a weak differentiator at the top end.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and AI evaluators assessing how much factual world knowledge is stored in model parameters without retrieval augmentation.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the quality of the retrieval system (BM25, DPR, etc.) heavily determines outcomes, making cross-system comparisons unreliable. Wikipedia content is pervasive in pretraining corpora, so models may answer correctly from memorisation rather than retrieval, inflating apparent open-domain QA capability. Frontier models now achieve exact-match scores in the mid-to-high 50s on the open-domain split, limiting headroom for differentiation at the top.
policy_note.measures: Open-domain question answering over real Google Search queries, where answers must be derived from Wikipedia passages retrieved at inference time rather than provided as context.
