policy_note.how_to_read: Lower sandbagging rates (smaller performance gap between control and evaluation-primed conditions) indicate more honest behavior; a large gap suggests the model may be deliberately underperforming when it detects it is being assessed. There is no widely agreed frontier range yet given the benchmark's early-stage status.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing whether frontier models exhibit strategic capability concealment or deceptive alignment behaviors during capability evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: Scores on ScreenSpot Pro are not comparable to scores on the original ScreenSpot benchmark — the Pro split uses substantially harder interfaces with smaller and more ambiguous targets. Results are sensitive to input image resolution and preprocessing, so scaffold or inference pipeline differences can shift scores meaningfully without reflecting true capability differences.
policy_note.measures: ScreenSpot Pro evaluates vision-language models on GUI element grounding in professional and complex software interfaces: given a screenshot and a natural-language instruction, the model must localize the target UI element by predicting its position or bounding box. It extends the original ScreenSpot benchmark with harder, denser, and more domain-specific screens (e.g., IDEs, design tools, productivity suites).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; the metric is localization accuracy (fraction of elements correctly identified). As of early 2026 frontier models score well below ceiling, so the benchmark still differentiates among leading models — unlike the saturated original ScreenSpot.
policy_note.intended_for: Computer vision and GUI-agent researchers assessing how well multimodal models ground language instructions to specific on-screen elements in professional software environments.

policy_note.caveat: The 'No Tools' label distinguishes this variant from setups that supply OCR or accessibility-tree scaffolding; scores are not comparable across variants. Professional application screens introduce visual complexity that may under-represent simpler consumer-UI scenarios, and results depend heavily on the image resolution and cropping passed to the model.
policy_note.measures: ScreenSpot-Pro (No Tools) evaluates GUI grounding — the ability to localize a specific UI element on a screenshot given a natural-language instruction, using professional-grade desktop and web application interfaces without any auxiliary tool assistance (e.g., no OCR API, no accessibility tree). The model must output coordinates or a bounding region purely from pixel input.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically expressed as element-localization accuracy (percentage of targets correctly identified). Frontier multimodal models score in roughly the 20–60% range on professional-application subsets, making this a differentiating benchmark rather than a saturated one.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multimodal models on realistic GUI automation tasks, particularly for agentic or RPA use cases where no programmatic UI metadata is available.

policy_note.caveat: Label conflation risk: scores are not directly comparable to the tool-free ScreenSpot-Pro variant, since scaffolding and tool-call overhead can mask or inflate raw grounding ability. Results are scaffold-dependent — different computer-use frameworks (Anthropic computer use, SoM prompting, etc.) can produce materially different scores on identical underlying tasks.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates GUI grounding accuracy of tool-augmented agents on professional desktop interfaces — asking models to locate specific UI elements (buttons, fields, icons) on screenshots from complex software environments such as IDEs, design tools, and productivity suites. The 'With Tools' variant provides agents with computer-use or screenshot-access tooling rather than relying on pure vision-only inference.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores reflect element-localization accuracy (typically reported as a percentage of correctly grounded targets). Frontier agentic models circa 2025 cluster in the 30–60% range on professional-grade GUI tasks, with substantial variance by software category.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating agentic computer-use systems, particularly those building or benchmarking GUI agents for professional software workflows.

policy_note.caveat: ScreenSpot is split across web/mobile/desktop environments and text/icon element types; scores on the 'web icon' subset are not directly comparable to full ScreenSpot aggregate scores or to the harder ScreenSpot-Pro variant. Icon elements are systematically harder than text elements (which can be located via OCR), so web-icon accuracy will be lower than web-text accuracy for the same model — conflating the two inflates apparent performance.
policy_note.measures: Tests multimodal GUI grounding on web screenshots, specifically requiring models to locate icon-type UI elements (e.g., icon buttons, navigation icons, logo elements) given a natural-language referring expression. The model must predict the correct pixel coordinates or bounding region of the target icon within the screenshot.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as accuracy (fraction of elements correctly localized, typically with a distance or IoU threshold). Icon subsets are among the hardest splits — frontier models in 2024–2025 ranged roughly 20–60% on web icon tasks, leaving meaningful headroom for differentiation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating multimodal LLMs on GUI grounding and web agent tasks, particularly for models that need to click or interact with icon-based UI controls.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are scaffold-dependent: coordinate normalization conventions and prompting strategies vary across implementations and can shift reported accuracy by several percentage points, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. The web-text split is relatively small (a few hundred examples), so variance is high and frontier models are approaching saturation, compressing differentiation at the top.
policy_note.measures: ScreenSpot Web Text evaluates vision-language models' ability to ground natural language element descriptions to precise click locations within web browser screenshots, focusing specifically on textual UI elements such as buttons, links, and labels. Given a screenshot and a short instruction, the model must predict the (x, y) coordinates of the target element.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; reported as element-localization accuracy (0–100%). A near-zero random baseline reflects the fine-grained spatial requirement. Frontier VLMs score roughly in the 70–95% range on web text, with top models clustering near the ceiling.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners benchmarking GUI grounding and visual agent capabilities of multimodal vision-language models.

policy_note.caveat: The label 'Sequence Design' is generic and may conflate distinct tasks (protein sequence design, DNA aptamer design, RNA design) or different evaluation protocols (computational structure-prediction validation vs. wet-lab oracle). Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: results from structure-prediction validators like ESMFold differ substantially from AlphaFold-based oracles. Frontier biology-specialized models may benefit from training-data overlap with known protein families.
policy_note.measures: Sequence Design evaluates a model's ability to generate functional biological sequences — typically protein or nucleic acid sequences — that satisfy structural or functional constraints. Tasks generally involve proposing amino acid or nucleotide sequences predicted to fold into a target structure or exhibit a desired biochemical property.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a common metric is the fraction of designed sequences whose predicted structure recovers the target (sequence recovery rate or TM-score threshold). Frontier generalist models typically score well below dedicated protein-design models (e.g., ProteinMPNN), so absolute numbers should be interpreted relative to the specific baseline reported.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and policy analysts assessing frontier model capabilities in computational biology and AI-for-science applications.

policy_note.caveat: Raw scores conflate two distinct behaviors: factual recall and abstention calibration. Models that frequently refuse uncertain questions score lower overall but higher on attempted questions, making cross-model comparisons misleading without also reporting attempt rate. Extended-reasoning variants (e.g. o1, o3) have been observed to score lower than their base counterparts on this benchmark due to 'overthinking' simple factual lookups — a known failure mode flagged by OpenAI. Contamination risk is elevated because short factual trivia is pervasive in pretraining corpora.
policy_note.measures: SimpleQA tests factual accuracy using ~4,300 short-answer questions, each with a single unambiguous correct answer verified by human raters. Models are graded as correct, incorrect, or not-attempted, probing whether models know facts and whether they abstain appropriately when uncertain.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; the standard metric counts not-attempted answers as incorrect. Frontier models typically score in the 30–60% correct range on the full set; no model has saturated it. Always report attempt rate alongside accuracy for meaningful comparisons.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and evaluators assessing factual accuracy, abstention calibration, and the effect of reasoning strategies on simple knowledge retrieval.

policy_note.caveat: Variant strings ('extended thinking', 'standard thinking', 'overall') indicate scores are reported separately by inference mode; cross-variant comparisons conflate reasoning depth with compliance rate. The exact dataset composition, size, and labeling criteria are not publicly documented, limiting external reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Measures whether a model correctly fulfills benign, non-harmful single-turn user requests without unnecessary refusal, excessive hedging, or over-cautious behavior. Probes the helpfulness side of the safety–helpfulness tradeoff by checking how often a model complies appropriately with legitimate queries.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. A score near 100% means the model almost never incorrectly refuses or over-hedges on benign requests. Frontier models typically score in the high 80s–90s range; substantial gaps between 'extended thinking' and 'standard thinking' variants on the same model indicate that reasoning mode affects compliance behavior.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and policy researchers evaluating over-refusal tendencies in frontier models; developers tuning helpfulness–safety balance in model deployments.

policy_note.caveat: The three reported variants — "extended thinking", "standard thinking", and "overall" — are not consistently distinguished across model cards, so cross-model comparisons may conflate scores from different reasoning modes. This appears to be an Anthropic-internal benchmark; the dataset size, category breakdown, and exact scoring rubric are not publicly documented, limiting external reproducibility.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates the rate at which a model correctly handles single-turn requests that violate usage policies — typically by refusing or safely redirecting rather than complying. Each item is a standalone prompt (no prior conversation context) designed to probe policy-relevant refusal behavior.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better, reflecting a higher proportion of violative requests handled appropriately. Absolute frontier ranges are not publicly disclosed; comparisons are most meaningful within the same variant (e.g., "standard thinking" vs. "standard thinking").
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating safety alignment and usage-policy compliance of language models, particularly to compare standard versus extended-thinking (chain-of-thought) modes.

policy_note.caveat: Marked as an internal benchmark with no public methodology, dataset, or scoring rubric disclosed; results are not reproducible or independently verifiable. Comparisons across labs are not meaningful since each lab may define 'soft bias' differently.
policy_note.measures: Probes for subtle, non-overt biases in model outputs—such as differential tone, framing, or quality of responses across demographic groups or politically sensitive topics—rather than explicit discriminatory content. Specific dataset size and task format are unknown as this is a proprietary internal evaluation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower scores are generally better (indicating less detected soft bias), but without a public rubric the scale and frontier range are opaque. Treat reported figures as lab-internal signals rather than cross-lab comparisons.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and alignment researchers within the developing lab; used to track bias reduction across model versions during internal development.

policy_note.measures: Speaker identification evaluates a model's ability to correctly identify or distinguish speakers from audio or transcribed speech segments, typically involving matching voice samples to known speakers or labeling speech turns in a conversation.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; typically reported as accuracy or identification rate as a percentage, though scale and dataset details vary significantly by evaluation setup.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers evaluating audio understanding, speech processing, or multimodal models on speaker diarization and recognition tasks.

policy_note.caveat: The variant string 'no extended thinking' suggests scores reported in model cards reflect standard inference without chain-of-thought; enabling extended thinking may yield meaningfully different results, making cross-model comparisons unreliable when inference modes differ. Dataset size and exact task distribution are not widely documented, limiting reproducibility assessment.
policy_note.measures: SpreadsheetBench evaluates a model's ability to perform spreadsheet tasks such as formula generation, cell reference reasoning, and data manipulation in Excel-like environments. It probes functional coding and structured data reasoning in the context of real-world productivity software.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Specific frontier ranges are not well-documented in public literature; interpret scores primarily in relative terms across models evaluated under identical inference settings.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating LLM capability on spreadsheet-related productivity tasks, particularly formula writing and tabular reasoning.

policy_note.caveat: SQuAD 1.1 is heavily saturated — frontier models have exceeded reported human performance (~90.9 F1) for several years, making it a poor differentiator among current systems. Contamination risk is high given the dataset's age (2016) and ubiquity in pre-training corpora. Cards reporting '1-shot' should be compared carefully with zero-shot or few-shot results, as prompt format significantly affects span-extraction scores. SQuAD 1.1 and SQuAD 2.0 are not interchangeable — the latter requires the model to abstain on unanswerable questions, which substantially lowers scores.
policy_note.measures: SQuAD (Stanford Question Answering Dataset) measures extractive reading comprehension: given a Wikipedia passage and a question, the model must identify the exact answer span within the passage. SQuAD 1.1 contains ~100k QA pairs; SQuAD 2.0 adds ~50k unanswerable questions to test abstention.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The primary metrics are Exact Match (EM) and F1 score, both on a 0–100 scale. On SQuAD 1.1, frontier models typically score 90–95 F1, making fine-grained comparisons unreliable. On SQuAD 2.0, competitive scores run roughly 85–92 F1 for strong systems.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and practitioners evaluating extractive reading comprehension and grounded question answering; also used as a legacy baseline for tracking progress over time.

policy_note.caveat: The evaluation criteria and prompt set are defined internally by each lab, so scores are not directly comparable across organizations reporting under similar names. Refusal rate alone does not distinguish over-refusal (false positives on benign prompts) from genuine safety; without a paired benign-prompt baseline the metric can be gamed by a model that refuses everything.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model refuses to generate content that violates a lab's usage policy — such as instructions for harm, explicit material, or other prohibited outputs. Typically presented as a set of prompts designed to elicit disallowed content, with compliance/refusal rate as the outcome metric.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher refusal rates on disallowed prompts are better, but only meaningful alongside a false-positive rate on benign prompts. Absolute scores are not interpretable without the lab's policy definition and prompt distribution.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and policy teams at AI labs assessing model compliance with internal content policies before deployment.

policy_note.caveat: The two variant strings (not_overrefuse, not_unsafe) represent distinct sub-benchmarks that are sometimes conflated when reported as a single 'Standard Refusal Evaluation' score; a high aggregate can mask failure on one axis. Results are highly sensitive to prompt phrasing and system-prompt configuration, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable without knowing the exact scaffold used.
policy_note.measures: A two-sided safety evaluation that scores models on refusal behavior: whether the model rejects genuinely harmful requests (not_unsafe) and whether it avoids refusing legitimate, benign requests (not_overrefuse). The two variants probe opposite failure modes of the same refusal policy.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better on both sub-metrics. not_unsafe: fraction of harmful prompts correctly refused; not_overrefuse: fraction of benign prompts correctly answered. Scores are typically expressed as rates in [0, 1] or percentages; frontier models generally aim for >0.9 on both axes, but optimizing one can degrade the other.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and policy teams evaluating the calibration of a model's refusal behavior — specifically the tradeoff between harmful-output suppression and over-refusal of safe content.

policy_note.caveat: Results are highly scaffold- and prompt-dependent: the same model can appear to sandbag or not depending on elicitation framing. Detection difficulty is confounded by the fact that genuine incapability and strategic underperformance produce identical outputs; distinguishing them requires multiple elicitation methods. No single canonical dataset exists under this name — 'sandbagging' evaluations differ substantially across research groups (e.g., password-locked model paradigms vs. fine-tuned sleeper-agent setups), so scores are rarely comparable across papers.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model can deliberately underperform on capability assessments while retaining the underlying capability — so-called 'sandbagging'. Probes are typically structured as elicitation tasks (e.g., chemistry, coding, dangerous-knowledge questions) where the model is prompted or fine-tuned to hide its true ability, and the benchmark measures how successfully it evades detection.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower sandbagging success rates are better (i.e., the model is harder to induce into hiding capabilities). There is no fixed numeric scale; results are typically reported as detection accuracy or elicitation success rate across probing conditions. Comparisons are meaningful only within a single study's methodology.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and evaluators assessing deceptive alignment risks; policy teams deciding whether capability elicitation protocols are sufficient for dangerous-capability gating.

policy_note.caveat: The automated LLM judge is itself a potential attack surface — adversarially crafted outputs may manipulate the scorer. Because the benchmark was explicitly built to fix 'empty jailbreak' overcounting in prior safety evaluations, scores are not directly comparable to results from benchmarks using different automated evaluators. Results also depend heavily on which jailbreak attack strategies are paired with the benchmark.
policy_note.measures: StrongReject evaluates how well language models resist jailbreak attempts by scoring model responses to ~313 harmful prompts across six harm categories (e.g., weapons, cybercrime, disinformation, hate speech). An LLM-as-judge assigns each response a 0–1 compliance score, specifically designed to penalize empty or evasive outputs that older safety evaluators mistakenly counted as successful refusals.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower scores are better (0 = model refused all harmful prompts; 1 = full compliance). Safety-tuned frontier models score near 0 on direct prompts but can score substantially higher under active jailbreak conditions; the benchmark is most informative when run across multiple attack methods rather than in isolation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and red-teamers measuring jailbreak resistance and refusal quality of instruction-tuned models; useful for comparing safety fine-tuning strategies.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to which judge model is used, introducing scaffold dependence — the same model can score differently under different judge configurations. The benchmark is specifically designed to penalise 'empty jailbreaks' (refusals that technically decline but still provide partial harmful content), so raw scores are not comparable to simpler binary refusal-rate metrics reported elsewhere. Dataset contamination is a concern for models trained after the benchmark's public release.
policy_note.measures: StrongREJECT evaluates the quality of AI model refusals on harmful prompts, going beyond binary accept/reject to score whether a refusal is substantive rather than empty or hedging. It uses an LLM-as-judge approach across a curated set of harmful requests spanning multiple harm categories to produce a scalar rejection-quality score.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better — a higher StrongREJECT score means the model more robustly and substantively refuses harmful prompts. Scores range from 0 to 1; well-aligned frontier models typically score above 0.8, while models with weaker safety training or successful jailbreaks score significantly lower.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and red-teamers evaluating jailbreak robustness and refusal quality in language models; useful for comparing alignment interventions.

policy_note.caveat: The variant strings observed in cards ('best score - extended thinking', 'top 3 average - standard thinking', etc.) indicate scores are reported separately by thinking mode and aggregation method, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless the exact variant matches. The small prompt set (~37 items) limits statistical power. The LLM judge (typically GPT-4 class) introduces evaluator variance, and prompt selection may not generalize to novel jailbreak vectors. Scores depend heavily on which jailbreak attempts are tried — a model's 'best score' reflects the most successful attack found, not average-case robustness.
policy_note.measures: StrongREJECT evaluates model resistance to jailbreak attacks by presenting a curated set of forbidden prompts across harm categories (e.g., illegal activity, hate speech, weapons) and scoring responses with an LLM judge on a 0–1 scale that combines refusal detection with response specificity and convincingness. A score near 0 means the model refused; a score near 1 means the model fully complied with a harmful request in a detailed and convincing way.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a score of 0 means the model refused all harmful requests, a score of 1 means full compliance. Frontier safety-aligned models typically score below 0.1 under standard prompting; extended thinking modes may shift scores in either direction. Compare only within the same variant (same thinking mode and same aggregation method).
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing resistance to adversarial jailbreak prompts; useful for comparing safety alignment across model versions or thinking modes.

policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model maintains safe, policy-compliant responses across multi-turn conversations involving suicide and self-harm topics, probing whether safety behaviors degrade as context accumulates or as users escalate requests across turns.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better adherence to safe messaging guidelines across conversation turns; a model that refuses or redirects appropriately throughout scores higher than one whose safety behavior erodes mid-conversation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing robustness of safety fine-tuning against multi-turn jailbreak or escalation patterns in sensitive mental health domains.

policy_note.caveat: The 'Benign' label is the complement of a paired 'Harmful' variant; conflating scores across the two variants produces meaningless aggregates. What counts as 'benign' involves annotator judgment calls on inherently ambiguous edge cases, making label consistency across dataset versions a known concern. Scores are sensitive to system-prompt wording, so results from different deployment scaffolds are not directly comparable.
policy_note.measures: Measures whether a model correctly handles benign single-turn queries touching suicide and self-harm topics without over-refusing — i.e., tests the false-positive rate of safety filters on legitimate requests (educational, clinical, journalistic, or supportive in nature). Task format is single conversational turns; the model is evaluated on whether it engages helpfully rather than incorrectly refusing.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; a score of 1.0 means the model never over-refused a benign query. Frontier models with well-calibrated safety training typically score high, but scores vary meaningfully with system prompt and inference scaffold. Always interpret alongside the paired Harmful variant — a model that never refuses anything scores perfectly here while being unsafe.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers evaluating over-refusal behavior — specifically whether safety mitigations on sensitive topics cause excessive false positives on legitimate queries.

policy_note.caveat: Results depend heavily on the quality and calibration of the automated safety classifier used to label responses as violative or not. Prompt phrasing and system-prompt configuration can significantly shift scores, so comparisons across scaffolds or evaluation harnesses should be treated with caution. The 'single-turn' framing may not capture multi-turn jailbreak dynamics.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model produces violative (unsafe or policy-violating) outputs in response to single-turn prompts involving suicide and self-harm topics. Scores represent the fraction of model responses classified as harmful by a safety classifier, where lower is better.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower scores are better; 0.0 means no responses were classified as violative, 1.0 means all were. Well-aligned frontier models typically score near 0 on this category, so small absolute differences can still be meaningful for safety-critical comparisons.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, model developers, and policy teams evaluating whether a model's guardrails are effective against harmful suicide- and self-harm-related requests.

policy_note.caveat:
Highly setup-dependent: scores vary by 10-20 points depending on the
agentic scaffold used (Aider, SWE-agent, Claude Code, etc.).
Self-reported scores often omit scaffold details, making direct
cross-lab comparison hard. Verified is the comparable subset; full
SWE-bench is not.
policy_note.measures:
2,294 real GitHub pull requests from 12 Python repositories, each
paired with the failing test that the PR resolves. The model must
produce a patch that makes the failing test pass. The Verified subset
(500 tasks) has had its setup manually validated.
policy_note.how_to_read:
Higher is better. Always check whether the report says "SWE-bench
Verified" (comparable) or "SWE-bench" (varies by setup).
policy_note.intended_for:
Multi-file, real-world software-engineering capability comparison.
The de-facto frontier coding benchmark.

policy_note.caveat: Strong scaffold dependence: the same model can produce markedly different scores depending on the agentic framework wrapping it, making cross-report comparisons unreliable. The variant strings 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' observed in cards indicate that reported numbers often reflect a specific model configuration rather than a fixed harness condition, further complicating apples-to-apples comparison. Label conflation risk with the Python-only SWE-bench and SWE-bench Verified variants, which use different issue pools and verification criteria.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates AI coding agents on resolving real GitHub issues across multiple programming languages (e.g. Python, Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust), requiring the model to produce a patch that makes failing repository tests pass. Scored as the percentage of issues fully resolved (%Resolved).
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scale is 0–100% resolved. Frontier models with strong scaffolds currently score roughly in the 20–50%+ range depending on language distribution and harness; numbers reported without a named scaffold should be treated with caution.
policy_note.intended_for: AI/ML researchers and developers evaluating coding agents on realistic, multi-language software engineering tasks beyond the Python-centric original SWE-bench.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is pronounced: scores shift substantially depending on the agentic framework and tool-use harness used, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless the scaffold is held constant. The variant strings 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' observed in model cards suggest reported scores may reflect different inference settings and training regimes, not a single canonical evaluation. As a newer and harder variant of SWE-bench, frontier score ranges are not yet stable and early leaderboard entries may reflect cherry-picked scaffolds.
policy_note.measures: SWE-bench Multimodal extends the original SWE-bench task to GitHub issues that contain images (screenshots, UI mockups, error dialogs, diagrams), requiring models to understand visual context when generating patches for real repositories. It evaluates end-to-end autonomous software engineering ability—patch generation and test passage—across primarily JavaScript/TypeScript codebases where visual bug reports are common.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are the percentage of held-out GitHub issues fully resolved (patch applied, tests pass). The multimodal variant is harder than SWE-bench Verified—expect frontier models in roughly the 10–35% range as of mid-2025, with wide variance by scaffold.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating multimodal large language models on realistic software engineering tasks that require joint visual and code understanding; complements SWE-bench Verified for labs whose models handle image inputs.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agent framework, tool set, and retry budget used during evaluation can shift results substantially, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless the scaffold is held constant. The variant strings 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' observed in model cards reporting this benchmark introduce label conflation risk — scores from extended-thinking mode are not directly comparable to standard-inference scores. Relationship to SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite is not always clearly stated in card reports.
policy_note.measures: SWE-bench Pro evaluates models on a harder subset of real-world GitHub issues requiring autonomous code editing and debugging, measuring the percentage of issues fully resolved by the model. It is designed to be more difficult than standard SWE-bench to avoid the saturation that frontier models have caused on the original benchmark.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are expressed as the percentage of GitHub issues fully resolved. The benchmark targets a harder regime than standard SWE-bench (where frontier models now exceed 50%), so expected frontier scores are lower. Always check which agent scaffold and inference configuration was used before comparing across models.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and developers evaluating frontier code models on complex, real-world software engineering tasks, particularly when standard SWE-bench results are too saturated to differentiate top models.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is the primary comparability hazard: scores shift substantially depending on the agentic framework used (e.g., Agentless, SWE-agent, OpenHands, a custom Claude tool-use loop), so results from different labs are often not directly comparable. The 'Verified' variant is frequently conflated with base SWE-bench in model cards — they differ in size (500 vs ~2294 problems) and difficulty calibration. Variant strings like 'extended-thinking' and 'rlhf' seen in reporting cards indicate that some submissions reflect training-method variants rather than a distinct benchmark, compounding label ambiguity.
policy_note.measures: SWE-bench Verified is a human-curated subset of 500 real GitHub issues drawn from Python open-source repositories; models acting as coding agents must produce a code patch that causes the repository's existing unit tests to pass. It was filtered from the original SWE-bench to remove problems with ambiguous or unreliable test harnesses.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; score is the percentage of the 500 issues where the model's patch passes all relevant unit tests. As of mid-2025, leading agentic systems score roughly 40–70%+; base SWE-bench scores for the same models are typically lower. Always check which scaffold and tool configuration was used before comparing across reports.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and practitioners benchmarking coding agents on real-world software engineering tasks; particularly useful for evaluating autonomous code-repair capability against a realistic, human-validated problem set.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is high — the 'browsing' variant (with web access) is not comparable to tool-restricted runs, and different agentic frameworks produce different scores. The 'helpful-only' and 'post-mitigation' variant labels indicate this benchmark is also used in safety capability evaluations; scores across those variants measure different things and should not be averaged or directly compared. Dataset contamination risk exists because tasks originate from public platforms.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates models on real-world individual-contributor software engineering tasks sourced from actual paid freelance postings (Upwork), scored pass@1 against end-to-end test suites. Each task carries a real dollar value; aggregate dollar-weighted completion is the headline metric alongside raw task pass rate.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; primary metric is pass@1 (fraction of tasks passing end-to-end tests on the first attempt), often also reported as dollar-weighted completion. Frontier models as of early 2025 solve a moderate fraction of IC SWE tasks; the dollar-weighted score emphasizes harder, higher-value tasks.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capability researchers assessing frontier model performance on economically-valued, real-world coding tasks; also used internally to measure safety-mitigation capability tax.

policy_note.caveat: The 'post-mitigation' variant applies contamination controls to reduce training-data leakage from publicly posted Upwork tasks; scores from mitigated and unmitigated runs are not directly comparable. As a relatively new (2025) benchmark, saturation data is limited but frontier models already achieve high pass rates on the Manager track, which may compress differentiation. The Manager track (selecting among provided implementations) measures evaluation and judgment skill, not code-generation ability — conflating it with the IC (Individual Contributor) track produces misleading comparisons.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to act as a technical manager by selecting the best implementation from multiple candidate solutions to real-world freelance software engineering tasks sourced from Upwork. Correctness is verified via end-to-end test suites, and tasks carry real monetary values totaling over $1M across the full dataset.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; pass@1 is the fraction of tasks where the model's single selected candidate implementation passes the automated end-to-end test suite. Because the Manager track requires no code authorship, scores tend to run higher than IC-track scores on the same model.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and practitioners assessing model capability for code comprehension, technical judgment, and solution ranking rather than code generation.

policy_note.caveat: There is no single canonical 'Sycophancy' benchmark; the slug likely aggregates scores from heterogeneous internal or published evaluations (e.g., Anthropic's synthetic sycophancy probes, or custom preference-flip tasks). Results are highly sensitive to prompt framing and the intensity of the simulated pushback, making cross-model comparisons unreliable unless the exact evaluation protocol is disclosed.
policy_note.measures: Sycophancy evaluations measure a model's tendency to abandon correct answers or validate false premises under social pressure — for example, agreeing with a user who pushes back on a factually accurate response. Tasks typically involve presenting a question, eliciting the model's answer, then introducing adversarial pressure to see whether the model capitulates.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower sycophancy rates are better. A score of 0% would indicate the model never capitulates to false pushback; high scores indicate frequent capitulation. Baseline rates for frontier RLHF models typically range from ~20–60% depending on task difficulty and pressure intensity, so even modest reductions are considered meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and alignment researchers evaluating whether a model prioritizes user approval over factual accuracy; useful for comparing RLHF-tuned models where reward hacking toward perceived user preference is a known risk.

policy_note.caveat: This is an Anthropic-internal evaluation; the exact dataset size, sampling procedure, and challenge-prompt distribution are not publicly documented, making direct cross-lab reproduction difficult. Scores can be sensitive to the exact phrasing of the pushback prompt, so results from differently scaffolded evaluations may not be comparable. The benchmark captures one narrow slice of sycophancy (answer reversal under pressure) and does not measure flattery, opinion-mirroring, or feedback inflation.
policy_note.measures: Measures whether a model maintains its correct answer when a user pushes back with skepticism or disagreement, without providing new evidence. The test format presents a factual or mathematical question, records the model's initial response, then applies a simulated social-pressure challenge (e.g., 'Are you sure? I think that's wrong.') and checks whether the model capitulates to an incorrect position.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — the score represents the fraction of trials in which the model incorrectly abandoned a correct answer under user pressure. A score of 0% means the model never caved; higher percentages indicate more sycophantic behavior. Frontier models have historically shown non-trivial rates on this style of evaluation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and alignment researchers evaluating whether models prioritize social approval over factual accuracy; model developers tracking sycophancy regressions across training runs.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic framework, tool-calling format, and system-prompt wording can shift pass rates substantially, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. The benchmark conflates task-success rate and policy-compliance rate into separate metrics that are sometimes reported individually and sometimes combined, so check which metric a given card is citing. Frontier models have not yet saturated this benchmark as of early 2026.
policy_note.measures: Measures an AI agent's ability to complete realistic multi-turn retail customer-service tasks (order management, returns, exchanges, account updates) while adhering to a defined retailer policy. Agents interact with simulated customers and a tool API; success requires both resolving the customer's request and avoiding policy violations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. Task success rate is the primary metric, expressed as a percentage of episodes fully resolved correctly; policy violation rate is a secondary penalty metric (lower is better). Frontier models as of early 2026 typically score in the 40–70% task-success range on the Retail split, leaving substantial headroom above current leaders.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and product teams evaluating LLM agents for enterprise customer-service automation, particularly those building or comparing agentic scaffolds.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent: the agentic framework, tool-call formatting, and retry logic used during evaluation can substantially shift results, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable unless scaffolds are matched. As a relatively new and domain-specific benchmark, public leaderboard coverage is limited, so frontier-range context is sparse.
policy_note.measures: tau2-Bench (Telecom) evaluates AI agents on realistic multi-turn customer service interactions in a telecommunications domain, requiring tool use (database lookups, account modifications) and policy-compliant decision-making across extended dialogues. It measures end-to-end task completion rate on scripted customer scenarios.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; primary metric is task success rate (0–100%). Because the benchmark is newer and narrowly domain-specific, established frontier ranges are not yet well-documented — treat absolute numbers cautiously and compare only runs using identical scaffolding.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating LLM agents on realistic agentic task completion, particularly in customer-service and tool-augmented dialogue settings.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are strongly scaffold-dependent — the agent framework, system prompt wording, and tool-call format all materially shift results, making cross-report comparisons unreliable unless the exact setup is disclosed. The relatively small per-domain task count also means run-to-run variance is non-trivial.
policy_note.measures: τ-Bench evaluates AI agents on realistic multi-turn customer-service tasks across retail and airline domains, where the agent must invoke tools (look up orders, process returns, modify bookings) and adhere to domain-specific policies to complete user goals. Task completion rate across ~100–200 tasks per domain is the primary metric.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are the fraction of tasks successfully completed (0–1 scale). The benchmark is designed to remain challenging: frontier models at release time scored roughly in the 0.3–0.6 range, leaving meaningful headroom for differentiation.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and product teams evaluating agentic LLMs on realistic tool-use, policy adherence, and multi-turn reasoning in customer-service settings.

policy_note.caveat: Scores exhibit high variance depending on the agentic scaffold used (prompt format, tool-calling framework, retry logic), making cross-paper comparisons unreliable without matching infrastructure. The stochastic simulated-user introduces episode-level noise, so single-run numbers are often reported without confidence intervals. Frontier models still score well below ceiling, so saturation is not yet a concern, but small evaluation sets in some published results limit statistical power.
policy_note.measures: TauBench (τ-bench) measures the ability of LLM agents to complete multi-turn, tool-augmented customer service tasks in two realistic domains—retail and airline—by interacting with a simulated user and calling domain-specific APIs. It evaluates task pass rate across full episodes, probing instruction-following, policy adherence, and multi-step tool use under realistic constraints.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are pass rates (0–100%) over a set of episodes. Frontier models (as of early 2025) typically score in the 40–70% range depending on domain and scaffold, leaving substantial headroom. Retail and airline sub-scores should be compared separately, as difficulty differs across domains.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety and capabilities researchers evaluating LLM agents on realistic agentic and tool-use tasks; teams benchmarking instruction-following and policy compliance in multi-turn settings.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are highly scaffold-dependent — the same model can show large swings depending on the tool-calling loop and system prompt used. The airline domain contains on the order of ~50–100 tasks, so confidence intervals are wide and small score differences are not meaningful. The simulated user is itself an LLM, so evaluation noise compounds across both agent and user turns. 'pass^1' label conflation: some cards report raw pass@1, others report it under the shorthand without clarifying whether policy-violation penalties are included.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates AI agents on multi-turn customer-service task completion in a simulated airline domain, where the agent must use provided tools/APIs and adhere to business policies to resolve passenger requests (e.g., rebooking, cancellations, seat changes). Success is measured as pass@1: the fraction of tasks fully resolved in a single conversation attempt.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are a pass rate from 0–100%. Frontier models (as of early 2025) typically score in the 40–70% range on the airline split; human baseline is near 95%. A 5–10 point gap between adjacent models is often within scaffold-noise margin.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers assessing agentic LLMs on realistic, policy-constrained customer-service automation in the airline vertical.

policy_note.caveat: pass^1 scores have high trial-to-trial variance for stochastic agents; single-run numbers reported in model cards may not be statistically stable without multiple seeds. Results are scaffold-dependent: the tool schema, system prompt, and agentic loop used during evaluation materially affect scores, so numbers across labs are often not directly comparable. The simulated user may not replicate the distribution of real customer phrasing or goal ambiguity.
policy_note.measures: TAU-bench (Retail) evaluates AI agents on multi-turn, tool-augmented customer-service tasks in a simulated retail environment — covering actions like order lookup, returns, exchanges, and account updates — using a scripted user simulator. The primary metric is pass^1: the fraction of episodes completed correctly on a single attempt, requiring both accurate tool use and adherence to retail policy rules.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; pass^1 is a 0–1 success rate. Frontier models (as of early 2025) typically score in the 0.40–0.70 range on the retail split, with substantial variance across runs. A score above ~0.70 is considered strong. Always note the agentic framework and number of trials when comparing results.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating agentic LLMs on realistic, policy-constrained tool-use tasks, particularly those building customer-service or task-completion agents.

policy_note.caveat: Several task formats (caption matching, open-ended captioning) rely on GPT-4 as an automatic judge, making scores sensitive to the judge model version and prompt — a form of scaffold dependence. Because the benchmark was released in 2024 and is relatively small (~410 videos), there is also a risk of contamination as frontier models increasingly train on curated video QA data.
policy_note.measures: TempCompass evaluates video large language models (Video LLMs) on temporal understanding across five temporal aspects: actions, direction, speed, event order, and attribute change. It uses ~410 videos with ~7,500 QA pairs spanning four task formats — multi-choice QA, yes/no QA, caption matching, and captioning — to probe whether models genuinely perceive temporal information rather than relying on static frame cues.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; results are typically reported as accuracy (%) per temporal aspect and task type, plus an overall average. Frontier video LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini) score in the 60–75% range overall as of mid-2024, with weaker models clustering in the 40–55% range, leaving meaningful differentiation room.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers building or evaluating video-language models, particularly those assessing temporal reasoning beyond single-frame understanding.

policy_note.caveat: Scores vary substantially across scaffold and configuration variants — 'w/ Codex-Max', 'rlhf', and 'default thinking' entries appear on the same leaderboard but are not directly comparable, creating label conflation risk. Scaffold dependence is a primary concern: the same underlying model can score very differently depending on the agentic harness used.
policy_note.measures: Terminal-bench 2.0 evaluates models on their ability to autonomously complete multi-step tasks in a real Linux terminal environment, including shell scripting, file manipulation, and system-level operations. It probes agentic, tool-use capabilities rather than static knowledge.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as task success rates (0–100%). The benchmark targets challenging real-world terminal tasks, so frontier models generally score well below ceiling, preserving differentiation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and engineers benchmarking agentic and tool-use capabilities of LLMs in realistic command-line settings.

policy_note.caveat: Scaffold dependence is a significant concern: scores vary substantially depending on the prompting strategy, action-space design, and whether chain-of-thought or scratchpad is permitted. 'Text-based RL' is a category label rather than a single canonical benchmark, so results reported under this name may come from different underlying environments (TextWorld, Jericho, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, etc.), making cross-model comparisons unreliable without knowing the specific environment and setup.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates an agent's ability to navigate and solve tasks in text-based interactive environments (e.g., parser-based games or simulated worlds) through sequential decision-making. The agent must read textual observations, issue text actions, and accumulate reward over multiple steps, probing planning, commonsense reasoning, and long-horizon memory.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better; they typically represent normalized reward (0–100 or 0–1 scale) or task completion rate. Frontier models vary widely depending on environment difficulty; scores above ~50% on hard splits are considered strong. Always compare only models evaluated on the same environment variant and scaffold.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers and AI safety teams assessing sequential reasoning, planning, and grounded language understanding in interactive settings.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are sensitive to which VQA model is used as the automated judge, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable when different judges are used. The benchmark measures semantic alignment only and does not capture aesthetic quality, realism, or artifact rates. Prompts are skill-stratified rather than naturalistic, so scores may not reflect real-world use-case performance.
policy_note.measures: GenAI-Bench evaluates compositional text-to-image alignment by probing how well image generation models handle complex prompts requiring attribute binding, spatial relations, non-spatial relations, counting, and other compositional skills. Evaluation is automated via VQA-based scoring against ~1,600 structured prompts spanning multiple difficulty tiers.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better text-image alignment. Scores are typically expressed as an overall VQA accuracy (0–1 or 0–100). Frontier diffusion and autoregressive image models generally score in the 0.6–0.8 range on overall alignment; gaps between skill categories (e.g., spatial vs. attribute binding) are often more informative than the aggregate.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers evaluating or comparing text-to-image generation models on compositional prompt following, particularly for fine-grained capability analysis by skill category.

policy_note.caveat: Methodology, dataset composition, and scoring rubrics are not publicly disclosed, making external reproduction or cross-lab comparison impossible. Scores are expressed only as relative deltas against specific Gemini baselines, so the same model evaluated against different baselines yields incomparable numbers. The 'text-to-text' qualifier implies a separate multimodal safety track exists, but label boundaries between the two are not formally specified in public documentation.
policy_note.measures: An internal Google/DeepMind safety evaluation measuring a model's propensity to produce harmful or policy-violating outputs given text-only inputs. Results are reported as relative comparisons against a named Gemini baseline (e.g., Gemini 1.5 Pro 002 or Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash) rather than as absolute scores; dataset size and task format are not publicly documented.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher (more positive delta) is better, indicating lower rates of unsafe outputs relative to the named baseline. Because scores are relative, a result of '+X% vs Gemini 2.5 Flash' cannot be directly compared to '+X% vs Gemini 1.5 Pro 002' without knowing the absolute safety level of each baseline.
policy_note.intended_for: Primarily intended for readers of Gemini-family model cards who want to compare safety regressions or improvements between successive Gemini releases; not designed for external benchmarking.

policy_note.measures: ThinkFollow evaluates whether language models follow user instructions faithfully during extended chain-of-thought or 'thinking' traces, probing whether reasoning steps respect stated constraints rather than ignoring them mid-thought. It targets the gap between a model appearing to comply in its final answer while violating instructions in its internal reasoning.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better instruction adherence during reasoning; specific scale and frontier ranges are not well-documented in public sources.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and evaluators assessing instruction-following reliability in reasoning or 'thinking' models, particularly those with visible scratchpad outputs.

policy_note.caveat: The label 'hard variant' is not standardized across the literature; different papers use it to mean longer horizons, noisier series, or out-of-distribution splits, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. Without a canonical dataset card it is unclear whether the hard split is held fixed or constructed dynamically, which affects reproducibility. Scores are sensitive to the specific error metric used (MAE, MSE, CRPS, MASE), so comparisons across reported results require confirming metric alignment.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to predict future values in multivariate or univariate time series under conditions explicitly selected for difficulty — typically longer forecast horizons, higher noise, irregular seasonality, or distributional shift. The 'hard' variant filters or reweights examples where standard models historically underperform.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower error (MAE/MSE/MAPE) or higher probabilistic accuracy (CRPS) is better depending on the reported metric. Hard-variant scores are expected to be notably worse than standard-variant baselines; a model that closes this gap substantially is considered strong.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating foundation or fine-tuned models on challenging real-world forecasting scenarios beyond standard benchmark splits.

policy_note.caveat: Performance is sensitive to the choice of demonstration example under the 1-shot evaluation variant, making cross-system comparisons unreliable unless the same shot is held constant. Reddit-sourced summaries vary widely in quality and reflect informal writing conventions, and ROUGE-based scoring may reward n-gram overlap over factual accuracy or coherence. Frontier models saturate automatic metrics on short-form summarization tasks.
policy_note.measures: TLDR9+ measures abstractive summarization quality on Reddit posts, where models must generate concise TL;DR summaries of longer user-written text. It probes whether models can condense informal, real-world prose into accurate and fluent short summaries, typically evaluated with ROUGE metrics.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; typically reported as ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, or ROUGE-L F1 scores on a 0–100 scale. Frontier models tend to cluster near the top of automatic metrics, so fine-grained differentiation between strong models is limited.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers benchmarking language model summarization capabilities, particularly in few-shot settings.

policy_note.caveat: Scores are inherently baseline-dependent and non-portable: a result labeled 'vs Gemini 2.5 Pro' is incomparable to one labeled 'relative to Gemini 1.5 Pro 002' without knowing the absolute quality of the anchoring model. The evaluation methodology, annotator guidelines, and dataset are not publicly documented, making independent replication impossible. Label conflation is common—different model cards may use different rater pools, prompt distributions, or aggregation methods under the same 'Tone' heading.
policy_note.measures: Tone measures human-preference ratings for the appropriateness, style, and affective quality of model-generated text responses. Scores are reported as relative win-rates or preference deltas against a named Gemini baseline model rather than on an absolute scale.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher (more positive) relative scores are better, indicating the evaluated model is preferred over the named baseline on tone. A score near zero means rough parity with the baseline; negative values indicate the baseline is preferred. Interpret only within the specific baseline stated—cross-baseline comparisons are not valid without normalization.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners comparing conversational or instruction-following models on stylistic and affective response quality, primarily within Google's internal evaluation suite context.

policy_note.caveat: The generic slug 'tooluse' appears across model cards without a shared canonical dataset, making cross-model comparisons unreliable. Scores can reflect different evaluation harnesses, tool inventories, or agentic scaffolds, so a score labeled 'Tool Use' from one lab may not be commensurable with the same label from another.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to correctly select and invoke tools (function calls) given a natural-language user request, covering tool selection accuracy, argument formatting, and in some variants multi-step tool chaining. Dataset size and task distribution vary by implementation — no single canonical benchmark owns this slug.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are typically reported as accuracy percentages (0–100%). Frontier models generally range from roughly 70–95% depending on task complexity, number of available tools, and whether parallel or nested calls are required.
policy_note.intended_for: ML practitioners evaluating models for agentic, function-calling, or API-integration deployments.

policy_note.caveat: This does not correspond to a widely recognized public benchmark; it appears to be an internal or proprietary evaluation. Without a public spec, results are not reproducible or comparable across organizations, and the label taxonomy, dataset size, and scoring methodology are unknown.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates a model's ability to assign text passages to predefined topical categories, probing whether the model can correctly identify the subject domain or theme of a given input. Dataset size and exact taxonomy are not publicly documented for this benchmark.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate better topical classification accuracy. Without a public leaderboard or known frontier range, scores from different organizations cannot be meaningfully compared.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers or product teams assessing a model's general-purpose text categorization capability, typically as a proxy for instruction-following and domain-awareness in classification tasks.

policy_note.caveat: Human annotation agreement on the original dataset was low, leading to a revised human-annotated subset; results on the full set vs. the cleaner subset are not directly comparable. The benchmark targets English only and covers a fixed set of 13 demographic groups, leaving other axes of harm unmeasured. Frontier models have approached saturation on the cleaner subset.
policy_note.measures: ToxiGen tests a model's ability to detect implicit and adversarial toxicity across ~274,000 machine-generated statements targeting 13 minority groups. The task is binary classification: toxic vs. non-toxic, with an emphasis on subtle, not overtly hateful language.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher accuracy is better. Frontier models typically score in the high-80s to low-90s (%) on the human-annotated subset; scores near or above 90% signal strong implicit toxicity detection. Random baseline is ~50%.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model card authors evaluating a model's tendency to generate or fail to detect implicit hate speech and adversarial toxicity.

policy_note.caveat: High contamination risk: questions are drawn from publicly available trivia websites that predate most LLM training cutoffs, likely inflating scores for models trained on large web crawls. Saturation is a concern at the frontier — top models score in the 85–92% range, compressing the signal between strong models. Note also that the standard closed-book LLM evaluation differs meaningfully from the original reading-comprehension formulation (which supplied Wikipedia or web evidence passages), so scores are not directly comparable across the two settings.
policy_note.measures: TriviaQA tests closed-book factoid question answering using ~95K questions sourced from trivia enthusiasts and quiz leagues. In the standard 5-shot LLM evaluation (as used in lm-evaluation-harness), models answer questions from memory without retrieved passages, probing breadth of factual world knowledge.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scored by token-level exact match (EM) after light answer normalization. In the 5-shot closed-book setting, frontier models typically fall in the 82–92% range; scores below ~70% indicate materially weaker factual recall.
policy_note.intended_for: ML researchers comparing language model factual recall and world-knowledge breadth; commonly used as a standard slot in LLM leaderboard suites.

policy_note.measures: TroubleshootingBench evaluates a model's ability to diagnose and resolve technical problems, typically presented as multi-step scenarios requiring root-cause identification and corrective action. It probes practical reasoning under realistic fault conditions rather than abstract problem-solving.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Specific frontier ranges are not well-documented in public literature; compare scores only within the same evaluation setup, as task framing and available tools can shift results substantially.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners assessing AI systems for applied technical support, IT operations, or agentic troubleshooting workflows.

policy_note.caveat: The expert threshold is anchored to a specific expert cohort; different sampling of human raters could shift the 80th-percentile bar, making cross-report comparisons sensitive to whose expert pool was used. The variant label '80th percentile' may be applied inconsistently across model cards — some may report raw score, others whether the model clears the threshold.
policy_note.measures: TroubleshootingBench evaluates models on multi-step technical diagnosis and problem-resolution tasks, requiring models to identify root causes and propose fixes. The Expert Threshold variant marks the 80th-percentile score achieved by human domain experts, used as a reference bar for assessing expert-level performance.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The primary reference point is the expert threshold (80th-percentile human expert score); a model clearing that threshold is considered expert-level. Scores are typically reported as a percentage or pass/fail relative to the threshold.
policy_note.intended_for: AI researchers and product teams evaluating whether models reach professional-grade diagnostic reasoning; useful for deployment decisions in technical support or engineering assistant contexts.

policy_note.caveat: The '80th percentile' label is a specific human-calibration variant, not the full benchmark ceiling; scores above it do not imply superhuman troubleshooting across all domains. Expert pool composition and domain coverage can materially shift the baseline, so cross-paper comparisons should verify that the same baseline definition was used.
policy_note.measures: TroubleshootingBench evaluates a model's ability to diagnose and resolve technical problems, with the human expert baseline anchored at the 80th-percentile score of domain experts on the same tasks. Performance is expressed relative to that human reference point.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better. The human expert 80th-percentile score serves as a calibration anchor; a model at or above that score is performing at or above the level of a strong human expert on this benchmark's tasks.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating AI systems on practical diagnostic and problem-solving reasoning, particularly for comparison against skilled human performance.

policy_note.caveat: Saturation is a concern: frontier models now routinely score above 85–90% on mc1, leaving little headroom to differentiate top systems. The mc1 and mc2 variants measure subtly different things (single correct answer vs. probability mass on all true answers) and should not be compared across cards that mix them. Questions were written in 2021 and some factual answers may have since changed, creating silent label rot.
policy_note.measures: TruthfulQA tests whether a model gives truthful answers to 817 questions spanning 38 categories (health, law, finance, conspiracy, etc.) that are deliberately crafted to elicit common human misconceptions. The mc1 variant scores single-best-answer multiple-choice accuracy: the model must select the one correct answer from a set of plausible-sounding options.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; mc1 is a 0–100% accuracy score. Weak models (circa 2021 GPT-3) scored near 20–30%; strong frontier models now cluster around 85–95%, so differences below ~5 points at the top are rarely meaningful.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and practitioners evaluating model honesty and resistance to imitating popular falsehoods; safety-focused model evaluation.

policy_note.caveat: TTFT is highly sensitive to infrastructure choices (hardware, batching strategy, network proximity, quantization) rather than model architecture alone, making cross-provider comparisons unreliable. Values reported on model cards likely reflect a specific serving setup at a point in time and can shift substantially with load or provider optimizations. It is not a capability benchmark.
policy_note.measures: TTFT (Time To First Token) measures the latency from when a complete prompt is submitted to when the model produces its first output token, typically in milliseconds. It captures perceived responsiveness in streaming deployments rather than any cognitive capability of the model.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better. Typical frontier-model TTFT ranges from ~200 ms to several seconds depending on prompt length, hardware, and provider; values below 500 ms are generally considered responsive for interactive use.
policy_note.intended_for: Engineers and product teams evaluating inference latency and user-perceived responsiveness for streaming LLM deployments.

policy_note.caveat: Possible training-data contamination given public availability since 2020. The GoldP task is one of three TyDi QA subtasks — results are not interchangeable with the Minimum Answer Span or Passage Selection tasks. Performance varies widely by language; aggregate scores can mask near-random performance on low-resource languages like Swahili or Telugu. Frontier models may show saturation on high-resource subsets.
policy_note.measures: TyDi QA Gold Passage (GoldP) measures extractive reading comprehension across 11 typologically diverse languages (Arabic, Bengali, Finnish, Indonesian, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Swahili, Telugu, Thai, English). Given a gold passage and a question, models must identify a short answer span or signal no answer; evaluated with F1 over token overlap.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher is better; scores are F1 (0–100). Frontier models typically report overall averages in the high 60s to low 80s under 1-shot prompting, with substantial per-language variance; lower-resource languages routinely drag aggregate scores 10–20 points below high-resource ones.
policy_note.intended_for: NLP researchers and model evaluators assessing multilingual extractive QA capability, especially across morphologically complex and typologically non-English languages.

policy_note.caveat: Performance is highly sensitive to whether and how much Hausa text appeared in a model's pretraining corpus, making cross-model comparisons conflate language coverage decisions with model capability. Most frontier models are trained predominantly on English and European languages, so scores here reflect both general reasoning ability and Hausa-specific training data — these factors are difficult to disentangle.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates large language model performance on Hausa-language NLP tasks, probing capabilities such as reading comprehension, natural language inference, or general language understanding in Hausa, a major West African language spoken by roughly 70–100 million people. The benchmark is part of the broader Uhura-Eval suite targeting African languages underrepresented in standard evaluation sets.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores are better. Expect frontier model scores to be substantially lower than on English counterparts of similar tasks; a score competitive with human baselines would be notable. The benchmark provides meaningful differentiation in a range where English-centric benchmarks show saturation.
policy_note.intended_for: Researchers and developers assessing multilingual LLM capabilities on African and low-resource languages; useful for teams building or selecting models for Hausa-speaking users.

name: UK AISI Expert Narrow Cyber Tasks

policy_note.caveat: Task counts in published UK AISI evaluation rounds have been small (typically tens of tasks), making scores sensitive to individual item variance. Scaffold and prompting strategy can meaningfully shift pass rates; results are not directly comparable across labs' self-reported evaluations using different harnesses. The 'narrow' framing means scores may understate or overstate general cyber uplift risk depending on which sub-skills are sampled.
policy_note.measures: Measures the ability of AI models to complete expert-designed, narrowly-scoped cybersecurity subtasks — such as CTF-style challenges, vulnerability analysis, and specific technical operations — that require specialist domain knowledge. Tasks are curated by cyber experts and intended to probe targeted, operationally-relevant skills rather than broad security awareness.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores (percent of tasks completed) indicate greater cyber task capability. Frontier models in early published rounds completed roughly 20–70% of tasks depending on difficulty tier; scores are best interpreted relative to a human expert baseline reported alongside them rather than as absolute percentages.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policymakers, and pre-deployment evaluators assessing whether frontier models could provide meaningful uplift to cyber threat actors; primarily used in UK AISI / DSIT pre-deployment safety evaluations.

policy_note.caveat: Frontier models are likely to saturate the lower-difficulty tier, limiting differentiation between leading systems. Scores are scaffold-dependent: agentic framework choice (tool availability, retry logic, shell access) can substantially shift pass rates. The benchmark is not publicly released in full, so independent contamination audits are not possible. Results reported in model cards may reflect different scaffolding configurations than AISI's internal runs, making cross-card comparisons unreliable.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates AI models on a curated set of entry-to-intermediate cybersecurity tasks developed by the UK AI Safety Institute, covering skills such as basic vulnerability identification, simple exploitation, and CTF-style challenges. Tasks are calibrated to be tractable for capable non-expert humans, probing whether models can provide meaningful uplift on lower-end offensive cyber operations.
policy_note.how_to_read: Higher scores indicate greater autonomous cyber capability — from a safety standpoint, lower is preferable. Frontier models as of 2024–2025 tend to score in the 50–80% range on lower-difficulty tiers; a score near ceiling warrants escalation to higher-difficulty variants. Absolute pass rates matter more than ranking here, since the policy question is whether a threshold is crossed, not which model ranks first.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers, policymakers, and frontier-lab evaluators assessing dangerous-capability thresholds for pre-deployment or post-deployment risk assessment.

name: Ungrounded Inference and Sensitive Trait Attribution

policy_note.caveat: The adversarial and non-adversarial variants are not directly comparable: the adversarial split uses prompts specifically engineered to elicit sensitive-trait attribution, while the non-adversarial split uses naturalistic phrasings; reporting a single aggregate number without specifying the variant conflates meaningfully different difficulty levels. Scores are also sensitive to system-prompt framing and refusal tuning, so results reflect policy and instruction-following behavior as much as underlying model tendency.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model makes ungrounded inferences about sensitive personal attributes—such as race, gender, religion, sexual orientation, or political affiliation—from context that does not explicitly state those traits. Tasks present scenarios or personas and probe whether the model attributes sensitive characteristics without textual grounding.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower rates of ungrounded attribution are better. Adversarial-variant scores are typically higher (worse) than non-adversarial; always confirm which variant is being cited before comparing across models or reports.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing fairness, stereotyping risk, and discriminatory-inference behavior in language models.

policy_note.caveat: No canonical public paper or standardized dataset is widely associated with this exact benchmark name; it may be an internal or proprietary evaluation, or a sub-task within a broader safety suite. Scoring methodology and dataset composition vary significantly across implementations, making cross-lab comparisons unreliable. The line between a reasonable contextual inference and an ungrounded attribution can be ambiguous, leading to labeler disagreement.
policy_note.measures: Evaluates whether a model makes unjustified inferences about individuals' sensitive personal characteristics—such as race, religion, political affiliation, health status, or sexual orientation—from context that does not support such conclusions. Tasks typically present a scenario or passage and assess whether the model attributes protected or sensitive traits without grounding evidence in the provided text.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower rates of ungrounded sensitive trait attribution are better. Scores typically represent the fraction of prompts on which the model avoids making the unjustified inference; a score of 1.0 (or 100%) means the model never made an ungrounded attribution. Frontier model ranges are not well-publicized for this benchmark.
policy_note.intended_for: AI safety researchers and model developers assessing whether models exhibit presumptuous or biased behavior when reasoning about people's personal characteristics.

policy_note.caveat: Results are not comparable across variants: 'non-egregious', 'System Jailbreak', and 'User Jailbreak' probe qualitatively different conditions (benign baseline requests vs. adversarial framing designed to induce over-caution) and should be read separately. The evaluation appears to be Anthropic-internal; the prompt set and labeling criteria are not publicly audited, making third-party replication difficult. Comparative figures (e.g. 'vs Gemini 2.5 Flash') reflect a single provider's test harness and may not generalize.
policy_note.measures: Measures the rate at which a model incorrectly refuses legitimate, non-harmful requests — the over-refusal failure mode. Prompts span everyday tasks and edge-case phrasings; a lower refusal rate on these items indicates better calibration between helpfulness and safety.
policy_note.how_to_read: Lower is better — a lower score means fewer unjustified refusals. Scores are typically expressed as a percentage of prompts incorrectly refused. Frontier models vary meaningfully in this range; differences of a few percentage points between variants or models are considered significant given the policy implications.
